Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 28, verses 1–3:

Meccan, [except from verse 52 to verse 55, which are Medinan, and verse 85, which was revealed at al-Juhfa during the Hijra]; its verses are 88. [It was revealed after Surat al-Naml.] In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

﴿Of the news of Musa and Fir'awn﴾: an object of "natlu" (We recite), meaning: We recite to you some of the account of the two of them, ﴿with truth﴾: in a truthful manner, like His saying ﴿tanbutu bil-duhn﴾ (it grows with oil). ﴿For a people who believe﴾: for those whom We know in advance will believe, because the recitation benefits only these and not others.

**Al-Zamakhshari, *al-Kashshaf*, on Surah 28, verse 4:**

﴿Indeed, Pharaoh⦈ is a resumptive clause (*jumla mustaʾnafa*, a new sentence that begins a fresh statement), serving as an explanation of what was stated in summary, as if someone had asked: "And how was their story?" So He said:

﴿Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the earth﴾, meaning the land of his kingdom, ﴿and he made its people into factions (*shiyaʿan*), groups, who follow him in what he wills and obey him, none of them able to turn his neck away.﴾ al-Aʿsha said:

*"And a land that the guide (al-jawwab) fears, its night-journeys,*
*until you see him in it seeking the mirage (al-shiyaʿ),*
*I bore its unknown, and my resolve aided me,*
*my aspiration upon it when its mirages shone,*
*with a vigorous, thick-necked she-camel, if she stumbles,*
*then "ruin" is more fitting for her than to be said "ah, may you rise" to her."*

Meaning: "And many a desert wasteland, which the guide fears, its traverser (*jabbat*, from *jabta al-arḍ*, "he crossed the land by travel") is one who journeys much. The night-journey (*dalja*) comes from *dalaja* and *adlaja* (form *iftaʿala*) and *adlaja* (form *akrama*): it means to travel by night, and *dalja* is an hour of the night. That is: the one accustomed to travel fears its journey by night, until he seeks companions to help him on it. I burdened myself with traversing its unknown part, and my resolve helped me to cross it at the time its mirages (*ālih*, the *sarab*, which appears in intense heat as if it were water) shone, although the midday journey is harder than the night journey." Then he said: "with a she-camel possessing strength." *Lauth* is also used for weakness, so it is one of the words with opposite meanings (*al-aḍdād*). *ʿAfranā* means thick. For one who stumbles (*al-ʿāʾir*) they say *laʿan lak*, a prayer for him to rise up. *Taʿsan lahu* is a prayer against him, for him to fall. He means that she does not stumble, and if she did stumble, then a prayer against her is more fitting for her than a prayer for her.

Or: ﴿some of them make others follow them in obedience to him.﴾ Or: ﴿categories (*aṣnāf*) in his service: he subjugates one category to building, another to tilling, another to digging, and whoever does not serve him, the poll-tax (*jizya*) is imposed upon him.﴾ Or: ﴿distinct groups among whom he had incited enmity, and they were the Children of Israel and the Copts.﴾

﴿A group among them he deemed weak﴾: they were the Children of Israel. The reason for slaughtering the sons was that a soothsayer (*kāhin*) told him: "A boy will be born among the Children of Israel, and your kingdom will be lost at his hands." In this is clear evidence of the depth of Pharaoh's foolishness, for if the soothsayer was truthful, killing would not prevent what was destined to happen, and if he was lying, what is the justification for killing?

﴿He deemed weak﴾ (*yastaḍʿifu*) is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the pronoun in *wa-jaʿala*, or it is a qualifier of *shiyaʿan*, or it is a new independent sentence. ﴿Slaughtering﴾ (*yudhabbiḥu*) is a substitute (*badal*) for *yastaḍʿifu*.

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, he was among the corrupters﴾ is an explanation that the killing was nothing but the act of corrupters alone, because it is an act with no benefit in it, whether the soothsayer was truthful or lying.

If you ask: to what is the clause ﴿and We wish to bestow﴾ (*wa-nuridu an namunna*) conjoined, and is its conjunction to ﴿We recite﴾ (*natlū*) and ﴿He oppresses﴾ (*yastadʿifu*) not sound? I answer: it is a clause conjoined to His saying ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land﴾, because it is parallel to ﴿Those﴾ (*tilka*) in its being an explanation of the account of Moses and Pharaoh and a narration of it. ﴿And We wish﴾ is a narration of a past situation (*ḥikāyat ḥāl*, the grammatical device of recounting a past state as if it were present). It is also permissible that it be a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from ﴿He oppresses﴾, meaning: Pharaoh oppresses them, while We wish to bestow favour upon them. If you ask: how can their oppression be combined with God's wish to bestow favour upon them? And when God wills something, it comes to be and is not delayed until another time? I answer: since God's favour of delivering them from Pharaoh was near in occurrence, its willed occurrence was treated as if it were concurrent with their oppression. ﴿Leaders﴾ (*a'immah*), advanced in religion and worldly affairs, whom people will follow in their footsteps. From Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both: leaders who are followed in good. From Mujahid, may God be pleased with him: callers to good. From Qatadah, may God be pleased with him: rulers, like His saying ﴿and made you kings﴾. ﴿The inheritors﴾: they inherit Pharaoh and his people's dominion and all that was theirs. *Makkana lahu* means: when one makes a place for him to sit or lie down, and he treads on it and prepares it; its parallel is *arrada lahu*. The meaning of ﴿establishing them﴾ (*tamkīn*, granting firm establishment) in the land, which is the land of Egypt and Syria, is that He makes it such that it does not repel them nor become hostile (*lā tughuth*) to them, as it was in the days of the tyrants, and that their command is executed, and that He releases their hands and empowers them. [[Your saying "and does not become hostile to them", i.e., does not corrupt and become foul. Related from al-Sihah (ʿ)]]

It is also read: ﴿and Pharaoh and Haman and their hosts see﴾, meaning: they see from them what they feared, namely the loss of their dominion and their destruction at the hand of a boy from among them.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 28, verse 7:

Al-yamm (al-yamm): the sea. It is said: it is the Nile of Egypt. If you ask: what is meant by the two fears, such that he made one of them obligatory and forbade the other? I answer: as for the first, it is fear for him of being killed, because if he cried out, they feared the neighbours would hear his voice and inform on him. As for the second, it is fear for him of drowning, of getting lost, of falling into the hand of some of the spies dispatched by Pharaoh in search of the infant boys, and other such fears. If you ask:

What is the difference between khawf (fear) and huzn (grief)? I answer: khawf is distress that befalls a person over something anticipated; huzn is distress that befalls him over something that has occurred, namely his separation from the child and the news of it. So you were forbidden from both of them. You were assured through the revelation to her, and promised what would console her, calm her heart, and fill her with joy and delight: that he would be returned to her and made one of the messengers.

It is narrated that ninety thousand infant boys were slaughtered in the search for Musa (peace be upon him). It is also narrated that when she drew near to delivery and the pains of labour seized her, one of the midwives assigned to the pregnant women of the Children of Israel, who was friendly with her, said to her: "Let your love for me benefit me today." So she attended to her. When he fell to the ground, a light between his eyes overwhelmed her, every joint of her body trembled, and his love entered her heart. Then she said: "I have only come to deliver your child and to inform Pharaoh, but I have found for your son a love the like of which I have never found, so keep him safe." When she went out, Pharaoh's spies came, so she wrapped him in a cloth and placed him in a heated oven (tannur masjur) [[The commentator's gloss on "placed him in a heated oven": in al-Sihah, "al-tannur" is that in which bread is baked. Also in it: "sajjartu al-tannur sajran" means I heated it. (Gloss)]], not knowing what she was doing, for her reason had been bewildered. They searched and found nothing, so they left, while she did not know where he was. Then she heard his crying from the oven, went to him, and God had made the fire cool and safe for him. When Pharaoh pressed the search for the infant boys, God revealed to her, and she cast him into the yamm. It is also related that she nursed him for three months in a chest of papyrus (bardi) [[The commentator's gloss on "a chest of papyrus smeared with bitumen": in al-Sihah, "al-bardi" with a fatha is a well-known plant; let it be examined. (Gloss)]] smeared with pitch on its inside.

The lam in liyakūna ("so that it might become") is the lam of kay (lam al-ta'lil), meaning causation, as in your saying: "I came to you so that you would honour me" (ji'tuka li-tukrimanī). However, the sense of causation in it comes by way of metaphor (majāz) and not literally (ḥaqīqa), because what motivated them to pick him up was not that he should become for them an enemy and a source of grief, but rather love and adoption. Yet since that was the result (natīja) and fruit (thamara) of their picking him up, it was likened to the motive for which an agent performs an act, just as the honour that is the result of coming, and the discipline that is the fruit of striking, in your saying: "I struck him so that he would learn discipline" (ḍarabtuhu li-yata'addaba). Its clarification: the ruling of this lam is the ruling of the lion (al-asad), in that it is borrowed for what resembles causation, just as the word "lion" is borrowed for one who resembles a lion.

It is recited as wa-ḥazanan, and both are two dialects (lughatān), like al-'adam and al-'adam (ʿadam/ʿudm, "lack"). They were sinners (kānū khāṭi'īna) in everything, so their error in raising their enemy was nothing novel from them. Or they were guilty and criminal, so God punished them by having their enemy, who was the cause of their destruction, raised by their own hands. It is also recited as khāṭīn, a lightened form of khāṭi'īn, or khāṭīn meaning those who turn the right into the wrong.

It is related that when they picked up the chest, they tried to open it but could not. They tried to break it, but failed. Then Asiya drew near and saw a light inside the chest. She worked on it and opened it, and there was a boy whose light shone between his eyes, sucking his thumb for milk. They loved him. Pharaoh had a daughter who had leprosy (*barṣā'*), and the physicians told him: "She will not be cured except by [something] from, before the sea, [a creature] resembling a human, whose saliva is her remedy." So the leprous woman smeared her leprosy with his saliva, and she was cured [[The phrase "fa-bara'at" (so she was cured). In *al-Sihah* (the lexicon of al-Jawhari): "bari'tu min al-marad bar'an" with a damma. The people of the Hijaz say "bara'tu min al-marad bar'an" with a fatha. "Asbaha fulan bari'an min maradih" (so-and-so became one who has recovered from his illness) (ʿ)]]. It is also said that when she looked at his face, she was cured, and she said: "Indeed, this is a blessed soul." This was one of the things that inclined them toward him. But the deviants among his people said: "This is the boy we were warned about. Permit us to kill him." Pharaoh was about to do so, but Asiya said: ﴿A delight of the eye for me and for you﴾. Pharaoh said: "For you, not for me."

It is related in a hadith: "If he had said, 'He is a delight of the eye for me as he is for you,' Allah would have guided him as He guided her." This is a portion of the lengthy narration of the trials (*ḥadīth al-futūn*). We have mentioned in [the commentary on] Ṭā Hā that al-Nasa'i transmitted it from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas, in which: she came to Pharaoh and said, "A delight of the eye for me and for you." Pharaoh said, "Let it be for you; as for me, I have no need of him." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By the One by whom I swear, if Pharaoh had acknowledged that he could be a delight of the eye for him as his wife acknowledged, Allah would have guided him as He guided her, but Allah denied him that."

This is by way of supposition and estimation, meaning: if he had not been sealed upon his heart, like Asiya, he would have said the same as she said, and would have embraced Islam as she did. This is its interpretation, if the hadith is authentic, and Allah knows best its authenticity.

It is related that she said to him: "Perhaps he is from another people, not from the Children of Israel." "A delight of the eye" is the predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject (*mubtada'*). It is not strong to make it the subject with "do not kill him" as the predicate; had it been put in the accusative, it would have been stronger. The reading of Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) is evidence that it is a predicate: he recited "Do not kill him, a delight of the eye for me and for you," placing "lā taqtulūhu" [i.e., do not kill him] after it.

﴿Perhaps he will benefit us﴾: indeed, in him are signs of good fortune and indications of benefit to his people, because of what she witnessed of the light, the sucking of the thumb, and the healing of the leprous woman. Perhaps she discerned in his features the nobility that announced he would be a beneficent one.

﴿Or we may adopt him﴾: for he is fit to be adopted, and to be the son of one of the kings. If you say: "﴿while they do not perceive﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*); what is its governing element (*dhū ḥāl*)?" I say: its governing element is the family of Pharaoh. The sense of the sentence is: the family of Pharaoh picked him up so that he might become an enemy and a source of grief for them, and the wife of Pharaoh said what she said, while they did not perceive that they were in a great error in picking him up, in hoping for benefit from him, and in adopting him. As for His saying, ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh...﴾ (the verse), it is a parenthetical clause (*jumla i'tirāḍiyya*) placed between the conjoined element and that to which it is conjoined, confirming the meaning of their error. How excellent is the composition of this speech to one who is versed in the science of the beauties of composition.

Empty, void of reason. The meaning is: when she heard that he had fallen into the hand of Pharaoh, her reason flew away because of the overwhelming anguish and bewilderment that came upon her. Similar to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and their hearts were air﴾ [Qur'an 14:43], meaning hollow, with no minds in them. And from this is the verse of Hassan:

"Surely convey to Abu Sufyan from me... for you are hollow, empty, air."
[[The explanation of this witness was mentioned earlier among the verses in the second part, page 563, so refer to it if you wish. Its corrector.]]

This is because hearts are the seats of reason. Do you not see His saying: ﴿so that they would have hearts with which they understand﴾ [Qur'an 22:46]? It is supported by the reading of the one who read: "fargha" (فرغا). And it was read "qarʿan" (قرعا), meaning empty, from their saying: "We seek refuge in Allah from the emptiness of the vessel (صفر الإناء) and the bareness of the courtyard (قرع الفناء)."
[[His saying "from the emptiness of the vessel and the bareness of the courtyard": "ṣafar al-iná'" is its being empty; it is the verbal noun of ṣafira al-shay' (with kasra), meaning it became empty.

"Qara' al-fanā'" is its being free of what covers it; it is the verbal noun of qari'a (with kasra), meaning it became empty. (ʿ)]].
And "farighan" comes from their saying: "Their blood is fargh among them," meaning wasted, i.e., her heart was nullified and gone, and it remained with no heart at all because of the severity of what befell her. ﴿to disclose it﴾, i.e., to reveal it, [[His saying "to reveal it": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, "aṣḥara al-rajul" means he went out into the open desert; here it means to proclaim it openly and not conceal his affair (ʿ)]] by it. The pronoun refers to Moses, and what is meant is his affair and his story, and that he was her son. ﴿Had We not bound fast upon her heart﴾, by inspiring patience, as one ties up a thing that has slipped away so that it settles and is calmed, ﴿that she might be among the believers﴾, among those who affirm the promise of Allah, which is His saying: ﴿Surely We shall return him to you﴾ [Qur'an 28:7].

It is also permissible to say: "And her heart became empty of worry when she heard that Pharaoh had shown kindness to him and adopted him," ﴿if she was almost about to disclose that he was her son﴾, because she could not control herself out of joy and gladness at what she heard, ﴿had We not calmed her heart and quieted her restlessness that arose from the severity of joy and exultation, that she might be among the believers, the ones who trust in the promise of Allah, not in Pharaoh's adoption and kindness.

It was read "mu’sā" (مؤسى) with a hamza: the damma on the letter after the waw, which is the mīm, was placed as if it were in it, so the waw was made into a hamza as the waw in "wujūh" is made into a hamza. ﴿Follow his trail﴾, i.e., follow his track and seek out his news.

It was read "fabasurat" (فبصرت) with a kasra, as in "baṣurtu bihi ʿan janbin" and "ʿan janābatin," meaning from a distance. It was read "ʿan jānib" and "ʿan janb." Al-janb means the side. It is said: "He sat at his side and at his flank," meaning: she looked at him sidelong, furtively, deceptively. [[His saying "furtively, deceptively": mutajānifa means inclining aside; mukhātila means deceiving. Stated in al-Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿ)]] And they did not perceive that she was his sister, and her name was Maryam.

(ʿ)]] And they did not perceive that she was his sister, and her name was Maryam.

Tahrim (prohibition) is a metaphor (*isti'arah*) for prevention, because whoever is forbidden something has been prevented from it. Do you not see their saying: *mahzur* (forbidden)?

And *hajr* (prohibition). This is because God prevented him from suckling any breast, so he would never accept the breast of any wet-nurse at all, until this worried them.

*Al-maraḍi'* (wet-nurses): the plural of *murḍi'*, the woman who suckles. Or it is the plural of *mirḍa'*, which is the place of suckling, meaning the breast, or the suckling. *Min qablu* (﴿from before﴾): from before her narration of his story, its trace.

It is reported that when she said ﴿and they are sincere to him﴾, Haman said: "She surely knows him and knows his family." So she said: "I only meant: ﴿and they are sincere to the king﴾." [[Mahmud said: "They accused her when she said ﴿and they are sincere to him﴾ of knowing Moses, peace be upon him. So she said: 'I only meant: ﴿and they are sincere to the king, Pharaoh﴾, and so she was cleared of the accusation." Ahmad said: "I cited this *tawriyah* (double meaning, a deliberate ambiguity) out of admiration for her cleverness, and because she was of the household of prophethood and the sister of a prophet, so it is fitting for her."]]

*Al-nusḥ* (sincerity) is the purification of the act from any admixture of corruption.

So she went to her mother with their command, and she came with her, while the boy was in Pharaoh's hand, who was coaxing him out of compassion for him, and he was crying, seeking suckling. When he smelled her scent, he was comforted and took hold of her breast. Then Pharaoh said to her: "Who are you to him? Every breast has been refused by him except yours?" She said: "I am a woman of good scent and good milk. No child is brought to me except that he suckles from me." So he gave him to her and paid her a wage, and she went with him to her house. God fulfilled His promise of the return, so it was established and settled in her knowledge that he would be a prophet. This is His saying ﴿and that she might know that the promise of God is true﴾, meaning: so that her knowledge would be confirmed and firmly rooted.

His saying ﴿but most of them do not know﴾ falls under her knowledge. The meaning: ﴿that she might know that the promise of God is true, but most people do not know that it is true, so they doubt.﴾

It resembles an allusion to what had occurred from her when she heard the news of Moses, and became distressed, and ﴿her heart became empty﴾. It is reported that when she cast him into the river, Satan came to her and said: "O mother of Moses, you disliked that Pharaoh should kill Moses, so you will be rewarded, then you went and yourself took charge of his killing." Then when the news reached her that Pharaoh had seized him, she said: "He has fallen into the hand of the enemy," and she forgot the promise of God.

It is also permissible that ﴿but﴾ be connected to His saying ﴿that she might know﴾, and its meaning is: the return was only for this religious purpose, which is her knowledge of the truth of God's promise. But most do not know that this is the original purpose, to which everything else is subordinate, namely:

﴿the delight of the eye and the removal of grief﴾.

Tahrim (prohibition) is a metaphor (*isti'arah*) for prevention, because whoever is forbidden something has been prevented from it. Do you not see their saying: *mahzur* (forbidden)?

And *hajr* (prohibition). This is because God prevented him from suckling any breast, so he would never accept the breast of any wet-nurse at all, until this worried them.

*Al-maraḍi'* (wet-nurses): the plural of *murḍi'*, the woman who suckles. Or it is the plural of *mirḍa'*, which is the place of suckling, meaning the breast, or the suckling. *Min qablu* (﴿from before﴾): from before her narration of his story, its trace.

It is reported that when she said ﴿and they are sincere to him﴾, Haman said: "She surely knows him and knows his family." So she said: "I only meant: ﴿and they are sincere to the king﴾." [[Mahmud said: "They accused her when she said ﴿and they are sincere to him﴾ of knowing Moses, peace be upon him. So she said: 'I only meant: ﴿and they are sincere to the king, Pharaoh﴾, and so she was cleared of the accusation." Ahmad said: "I cited this *tawriyah* (double meaning, a deliberate ambiguity) out of admiration for her cleverness, and because she was of the household of prophethood and the sister of a prophet, so it is fitting for her."]]

*Al-nusḥ* (sincerity) is the purification of the act from any admixture of corruption.

So she went to her mother with their command, and she came with her, while the boy was in Pharaoh's hand, who was coaxing him out of compassion for him, and he was crying, seeking suckling. When he smelled her scent, he was comforted and took hold of her breast. Then Pharaoh said to her: "Who are you to him? Every breast has been refused by him except yours?" She said: "I am a woman of good scent and good milk. No child is brought to me except that he suckles from me." So he gave him to her and paid her a wage, and she went with him to her house. ﴿وَاسْتَوى﴾ means he reached maturity, became balanced, and his strength was fully established, arriving at the point beyond which nothing more is added, as Luqayt said:

*So bear your affair, by your God, O you of excellence,*
*the sharp (shizr) of the bitter one (al-marira), neither senile nor feeble.*

[[For Luqayt. It is narrated as: "wa-stahkamū" (and they made it firm). Al-shizr: severe killing, or a severe thing; it is a verbal noun or an adjective. Al-marīra derives from al-marra, which means strength. Al-marīr: a rope tightly twisted. Al-qaḥm: an old man of advanced age who suffers from senility and dementia. Al-ḍaraʿ: soft and humiliated, from al-ḍarāʿa, which means humility and submission. He says: entrust the affair of your caliphate to a man of firm resolve and strong determination, not a decrepit man of disordered judgment, nor a weak one. Wa-llāhi darruKum: a parenthetical clause (jumla iʿtirāḍiyya), meaning: by God, your best and your righteous deeds.]]

It is said that this verse is a patchwork compiled from what Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Mubarrad narrated in his *al-Kāmil*, and from it:

*So entrust your affair, by your God, to one of wide stride, bold in the affair of war, rising to it,*
*who kept milking this age of its portions, sometimes following and sometimes followed,*
*until he became established on the sharp of its bitterness, firm in judgment, neither senile nor feeble.*

[[Raḥb al-dhirāʿ: one of long reach and broad breast, meaning brave and generous. Iḍṭalaʿa bi-kadhā: he was strong enough for it and firmly able to bear it, from al-ḍalāʿa, which means strength and the ability to bear heavy burdens. Shaṭṭarat al-nāqa shaṭran: he milked half of her milk and left the other half, meaning half. What is here is borrowed from that: he tested the age and its varied conditions of good and evil passed over him, so he acquired from it what made his opinion sound. Al-ashṭar: the plural of shaṭr, a substitute (badal) for al-dahr. It is permissible that ḥalaba transitively takes two objects, even by implication (tadmīn). Mutbaʿ, the first, is a passive participle, and the second is an active participle, meaning: at times a follower and at times a leader. Ustumirrat marīratuhu: his resolve strengthened and his affair became firm upon the sharp, meaning strength and sincerity of purpose.]]

And that is forty years. It is reported that no prophet was sent except at the age of forty. [[I have not found it.]]

Al-ʿilm: knowledge. Al-Tawrāt: the Torah.

Al-ḥukm: the Sunnah. The wisdom (ḥikmat) of the prophets is their Sunnah. God the Exalted said: ﴿And remember what is recited in your houses of the signs of God and the wisdom﴾ (33:34). It is also said: its meaning is that We gave him the conduct and disposition of wise scholars before his commission, so he would not do any act for which he could be considered ignorant.

The city: Egypt. It was also said: the city of Memphis in the land of Egypt. "At a time of their heedlessness": between the two evening prayers (maghrib and 'isha').

It was said: at the time of the midday rest. It was said: a festival day for them, when they were occupied with their amusements. It was said: when he grew up and came to reason, he began to speak the truth and denounce them, so they feared him, and therefore he would not enter a town except when they were heedless.

Sibawayh read فاستعانه (so he sought his help) مِنْ شِيعَتِهِ, meaning: from among his faction, those who followed him in his religion, from the Children of Israel. It was said: he was the Samiri. ﴿عَلَى الَّذِي مِنْ عَدُوِّهِ﴾ (against the one from his enemy): from his opponents among the Copts. He was Fatun, and he used to conscript the Israelite to carry firewood to Pharaoh's kitchen.

Al-wakz (a shove or punch) is pushing with the tips of the fingers. It was said: with the palm gathered together. Ibn Mas'ud read فلكزه, with a lam. ﴿فَقَضَى عَلَيْهِ﴾ (So he dealt a decisive blow to him), ﴿فَقَتَلَهُ﴾ (and killed him).

If you ask: why did he make the killing of the disbeliever ﴿مِنْ عَمَلِ الشَّيْطَانِ﴾ (the work of Satan), call it wronging himself ﴿رَبِّ إِنِّي ظَلَمْتُ نَفْسِي﴾ (My Lord, I have wronged myself), and seek forgiveness for it? I say: because he killed him before he had been permitted to kill, so it was a sin for which he sought forgiveness.

On the authority of Ibn Jurayj: a prophet is not to kill what he has not been commanded to kill. ﴿قَالَ رَبِّ بِمَا أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيَّ فَلَنْ أَكُونَ ظَهِيراً لِلْمُجْرِمِينَ﴾ (He said: My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me, I will never be a supporter of the criminals). [[It is said in the verse: "He said: My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me, I will never be a supporter of the criminals." Ahmad said: he has disassociated himself from a great thing, for the supporter of criminals is their partner in what they are engaged in. It is narrated that on the Day of Resurrection it will be said: Where are the oppressors and the helpers of the oppressors? They will be brought, even those who tied an ink-knot for them or sharpened a pen for them, and they will be placed in an iron chest and thrown into the Fire.]] It may also be an oath whose answer is omitted, its sense being: I swear by Your bounty upon me of forgiveness that I will surely repent, so I will never be a supporter of the criminals. It may also be an appeal: "Lord, preserve me by the right of what You have bestowed upon me of forgiveness, so that I will never be (if You preserve me) a supporter of the criminals."

By supporting the criminals he meant either accompanying Pharaoh, being incorporated into his company and increasing his numbers, since he would ride with his mount like a child with a father, and he was called Pharaoh's son; or supporting those whose support leads to sin and wrongdoing, like the Israelite's support that led to a killing which was not lawful for him.

From Ibn 'Abbas: he did not make an exception (by saying "if God wills"), so he was tested with it again, meaning he did not say: "I will never (do so), if God wills." This is like His saying ﴿وَلَا تَرْكَنُوا إِلَى الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا﴾ (And do not incline toward those who did wrong).

From 'Ata': a man said to him: my brother strikes with his pen and does not exceed his provision. He said: then from the head, meaning, who writes for him? He said: Khalid ibn 'Abdullah al-Qasri said: Then where is the statement of Moses? And he recited this verse.

It is recorded in a hadith: "A caller will call out on the Day of Resurrection: Where are the wrongdoers, and those like the wrongdoers, and the helpers of the wrongdoers, even those who held an inkwell for them or mended a pen for them? They will be gathered in an iron chest, and it will be thrown into Hell." [[Mentioned by the author of al-Firdaws from a hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]

It was also said that its meaning is: "By what You have bestowed upon me of strength, I will not use it except in supporting Your friends, the people of Your obedience, and those who believe in You."

He was watchful, fearing (the consequences of) the matter, expecting retaliation from it, or (fearing) the report and what would be said about it. The Israelite is described as "the one seeking help" (al-ghawi) because he was the cause of a man's death while he was fighting another. It is also read as yabtish (with a dammah on the ya'), meaning "to strike". "The one who is an enemy to both of them" is the Copt, because he was not upon their religion, and because the Copts were enemies of the Children of Israel. "Al-Jabbar" (the tyrant) is one who does whatever he wishes of striking and killing by way of injustice, who does not consider the consequences and does not repel (evil) with what is better. It was also said: he is the one who magnifies himself and does not humble himself before the command of God. When he said this, he disclosed (the matter) about Musa, and the story spread in the city and reached Pharaoh, and they resolved to kill him.

When he said this, he disclosed (the matter) about Musa, and the story spread in the city and reached Pharaoh, and they resolved to kill him.

Some say: "the man" was the believer from Pharaoh's family, who was a cousin of Pharaoh. "Yas'a" (running) may be parsed as either a description (sifah) of "rajul" (man) or as a circumstantial accusative (hal) relating to him. Since he has been specified by the description given in His words ﴿from the farthest part of the city﴾, and if the phrase is taken as a relative clause (silah) of "jā'a" (came), then with "yas'a" only the reading as a description is permissible. Al-i'timar means consultation (al-tashawur). It is said: "The two men are consulting one another (yata'marani) and taking counsel (ya'tamirani)," because each of them commands the other to do something or advises him on a matter. The meaning is: they are consulting about you. ﴿Laka﴾ ("for you") is an explanatory complement (bayan), and it is not a silah (relative clause) of ﴿al-nasihin﴾ ("the advisers").
He was watching out for an encounter with him on the road, or for him to catch up.

Toward Madyan (tilqa'a Madyan): he intended it and headed in its direction. Madyan was the town of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him. It was named after Madyan ibn Ibrahim. It was not under the authority of Pharaoh, and the distance between it and Egypt was eight days' journey. Musa did not know the road to it. Ibn 'Abbas said: he set out without any knowledge of the way, relying only on his good opinion of his Lord. "The right way" (sawa' al-sabil): its middle and the main part of its path.

It has also been said: he set out barefoot, living on nothing but tree leaves, and he did not arrive until the sole of his foot had worn away.

It has also been said: a angel came to him on a horse, holding a staff ('anza), and set off with him toward Madyan.

﴿...﴾ the water of Madyan, the water from which they drew. It was a well, according to what is narrated. Wurud (arriving) means coming to it and reaching it. ﴿He found upon it a community (ummah) of people﴾, a dense, large group of people of various kinds, ﴿and beside them he found two women driving back﴾, in a place lower than theirs. Al-dhawd means driving away and pushing back. The two women were driving back (their flock) because there were stronger people at the water who would prevent them from watering. It is also said that they disliked crowding at the water. It is also said that they did this so that their sheep would not mix with the sheep of the others. It is also said that they were driving back (the sheep) and screening their faces from a viewer's gaze. ﴿What is your matter (khatbukuma)?﴾ meaning, what is your affair? Its literal sense is "what is your maktub (the thing sought)," i.e., your objective, from al-dhawd. So the sought thing is called khatb, just as the affair (sha'n) is called sha'n in your saying "ma sha'nuka?" It is said: sha'nat sha'nahu, meaning, I aimed at his aim. It has been read as ﴿lā nasqī﴾ (we do not water) and ﴿yuṣdira﴾ (until the shepherds send back). And al-ri'a', with a damma on the nun, the ya' and the ra': al-ri'a' is a collective noun like al-rikhal and al-tha'a'.[[His statement "lā nasqī, yuṣdira, al-ri'ā' with a damma on the nūn, the yā' and the rā'" indicates that the well-known reading is with a fatḥa on the nūn and the yā' and a kasra on the rā'. Al-rikhāl: its singular is rakhl, which is the female of young sheep. Al-tha'ā': the tether of a camel or the like, from a twisted rope, as stated in al-Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿ)]]

As for al-ri'ā' with a kasra, it is analogical, like ṣiyām and qiyām. ﴿An old man﴾, meaning, an elderly man of great age. ﴿So he watered for them﴾, meaning he watered their flock on their behalf. It is narrated that the shepherds used to place upon the mouth of the well a stone which only seven men could lift. It is said: ten. It is said: forty. It is said: a hundred. Yet he lifted it alone. It is narrated that he asked them for a bucket of water, and they gave him their bucket and said: "Draw water with it." It was a bucket that only forty men could draw up. He drew water with it, poured it into the trough, and prayed for blessing, and he gave their flock drink and sent them back. It is narrated that he pushed them away from the water until he had watered for the two women. It is also said there was another well, over which was a stone. He did this out of eagerness for doing good and relieving the distressed. The meaning is: he reached that water when a community of people of differing, dense numbers had crowded around it, and he saw the two weak women behind them with their small flock, waiting for them to finish. His resolve did not fail to seize that opportunity in the religion of God, despite the fatigue he had, the tearing of the sole of his foot, and his hunger. Rather, he showed them mercy and relieved them, and he took care of the watering for them in such a crowd by the strength of his heart and the strength of his arm, and by the excellence God had given him in firmness of nature and solidity of constitution. And in this, together with the intent to relate his story and the strength and power he had been given, and what he did not neglect despite his exhaustion, there is an encouragement to goodness, a seizing of its opportunities, and an impulse to follow the righteous in that and to take up their conduct and ways.

If you ask: why was the object omitted in ﴿yasquna﴾ and ﴿tadhūdāni﴾ and ﴿lā nasqī﴾? I answer: because the purpose is the act, not the object of it. Do you not see that he showed mercy to them only because they were driving back while the others were watering, and he did not show mercy because their flock was of sheep and the others' was of camels, for example? Likewise their saying ﴿lā nasqī ḥattā yuṣdira al-ri'āʾ﴾, where what is intended is the watering, not the watered thing.

If you ask: how did their answer correspond to his question? I answer: he asked them about the reason for their driving back, and they said: the reason for that is that we are two weak women, veiled, unable to compete (musājala) with men or crowd with them, so we must delay watering until they finish. We have no man to do that, and our father is an old man whom age has weakened, so he is not fit to do it. So they presented their excuse for taking on the watering themselves.[[His statement "abalatā ilayhi ʿudhrahumā" is probably a distortion; its original is abdatā, as in the wording of al-Nasafī. (ʿ)]]

If you ask: how was it permissible for the prophet of God, who is Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, to be content for his two daughters to water the livestock? I answer: the matter in itself is not forbidden, and religion does not reject it. As for manliness (murū'ah), people differ in that, and customs vary regarding it. The condition of the Arabs in this differs from that of non-Arabs, and the custom of the people of the desert differs from that of the people of the settled towns, especially when the situation is one of necessity.

﴿Indeed, I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need﴾, whether little or much, lean or fat. Faqīr is followed by lām because it implies the meaning of "one who asks" and "one who seeks." It is said: he mentioned that, though the greenness of the herb showed through his belly from emaciation, he asked God only for a single meal. It may also mean: "I am poor in worldly things, on account of what You have sent down to me of the good of religion, which is salvation from the wrongdoers," because he had been in wealth and prosperity at Pharaoh's court. He said that out of contentment with the noble exchange, joy in it, and gratitude for it.

﴿And the shade was the shade of a sumur tree﴾ and ﴿she came walking to him with modesty﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: modestly, shyly, veiled. It is said: she had drawn her garment about her.

It is narrated that when the two of them returned to their father earlier than the people, their flock came back with full udders. He said to them: "What has hastened you?" They said: "We found a righteous man who had pity on us and watered for us." So he said to one of them: "Go and call him for me." Then Musa followed her, but the wind pressed her garment against her body, and she described him. So he said to her: "Walk behind me and direct me to the way." When he related his story to him, he said: "Do not fear; there is no authority of Pharaoh in our land."

If you ask: how was it permissible for Musa to act on the word of a woman, and to walk with her though she was a stranger? I answer: as for acting on the word of a woman, it is like acting on the word of one (single reporter) in reports, whether free or slave, male or female. She was only reporting about her father that he was calling him to reward him. As for walking with a foreign woman, there is no harm in it in similar circumstances, together with caution and abstinence.

If you ask: how was it valid for him to take a wage for righteousness and kindness? I answer: it is possible that he did that for the sake of God and as a form of righteousness and kindness. It is also said that Shu'ayb's feeding him and his beneficence was not in the manner of taking a wage, but as an accepting of a kindness begun by him. How (could it be otherwise), since he had related his story to him and he had made him know that he was of the house of prophethood, from the descendants of Ya'qub? Such a man deserves to be hosted and honored, especially in the house of a prophet of God's prophets. And it is not objectionable that he should do so out of the necessity of poverty and need, seeking reward.

And there is narrated something that supports both views: it is reported that when she said "that he may reward you," he disliked that. And when the food was set before him, he refused and said: "We are a household that does not sell its religion for the filling of the earth with gold, nor do we take a price for kindness." Until Shu'ayb said: "This is our custom with everyone who comes down upon us."

It is related from ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib: he raised his voice in supplication so that they would hear him. That is why it was said to him: ﴿that he may reward you for what you watered﴾, i.e., the recompense for your watering.

Al-qaṣaṣ (the story) is a verbal noun like al-ʿilal, and the narrated account is named after it.

The elder of the two was called Ṣafrāʾ, and the younger Ṣufayrāʾ. Ṣafrāʾ is the one who went with him and asked her father to hire him, and she is the one he married.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās that Shu'ayb was seized by jealousy and said: "And what do you know of his strength and trustworthiness?" So she mentioned the lifting of the stone and the drawing of the bucket, and that he lowered his head when his message reached him and when her father commanded her to walk behind him.

Her saying ﴿Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong, the trustworthy﴾ is a wise, comprehensive statement to which nothing can be added, because when these two qualities are combined, I mean sufficiency and trustworthiness in the one who manages your affair, your mind is at ease and your goal is achieved. She has been content with sending this saying, whose context is that of a proverb, and the wisdom is that you say: hire him for his strength and his trustworthiness.[[Mahmud said: "This is a wise and comprehensive statement to which nothing can be added, because if strength and trustworthiness are combined in the one who manages your affair, your mind is at rest, and she has been content with sending this saying, whose context is that of a proverb and maxim, rather than saying: 'He is strong and trustworthy.'" Aḥmad said: This is also more beautiful as praise by women of men than specific praise, and more preserving of modesty, especially if she understood that her father's aim, peace be upon him, was to marry her to him. How well the Fārūq (ʿUmar), may God be pleased with him, took this meaning when he said: "I complain to God of the weakness of the trustworthy and the treachery of the strong." In the content of this complaint is a request to God that He grant him one who combines the two qualities, strong and trustworthy, whom he could rely upon in what he was undertaking, may God be pleased with him. And this ambiguity, from the daughter of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, was also taken by Zulaykha with Yusuf, peace be upon him. But how different is natural modesty from acquired modesty: kohl in the eyes is not like the kohl. When she said to her master: ﴿What is the recompense of one who intended evil to your wife, except that he be imprisoned or a painful punishment?﴾, she meant: what is the recompense of Yusuf for having intended evil toward me, except that you imprison him or punish him with a painful punishment? But shame and modesty prevented her husband's mind from her speaking the word of chastity while attributing the indecency to herself, indicating that this modesty in her, which prevented her from speaking this matter, prevented her from soliciting Yusuf by a more fitting and better means. And God knows best.]]

If you ask: how did he make ﴿the best you hire﴾ the subject of ﴿inna﴾ and ﴿the strong, the trustworthy﴾ the predicate? I answer: it is like his saying:

"Surely the best of people, alive and dead, is the captive of Thaqīf among them in chains."[[Surely the best of people, living and dead, is the captive of Thaqīf among them in chains. By my life, if you have made the prison abode of Khalid and made him tread it with the tread of one burdened. He was one who rose up to every calamity, and gave generous gifts, great in bounty, abundant in extra gifts. This is by Abu al-Shaghb al-ʿAbsī, lamenting over Khalid ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī when Yusuf ibn ʿUmar captured him. "The best of people" is an elative in the form of a comparative, annexed to a definite with al, and it is the subject of inna. "Living and dead" (ḥayyan wa-mayyitan), and in one narration "perishing" (hālikan), are two circumstantial clauses from it. "Captive" (asīr) is the predicate of inna, annexed to Thaqīf, the name of the tribe. A proper name is more definite than what is definite by al, so the predicate annexed to the proper noun is more definite than its subject which is annexed to the definite by al, and there is no obstacle to this when both refer to the same thing intended by the speaker. "Among them in chains" is a circumstantial clause or a predicate after a predicate. "By my life" is an oath. "If you have made...": that is, you put Khalid into prison and settled him there. "And made him tread it": that is, you made him tread the ground with his foot like the tread of one burdened with something heavy, meaning you put the shackles on his feet, so this is a metaphor for that. "He was one who rose up..." is the answer to the oath. The answer to the condition is omitted, meaning he was quick to rise to every heavy calamity. "Giver of al-lahā" with a fatḥa is the plural of lahāh, like ḥaṣā and ḥaṣāh, meaning the piece of flesh at the farthest part of the mouth, but here it means the mouth itself. The more likely is that with a ḍamma it is the plural of luhwah, like ghuraf, plural of ghurfah, meaning gift of any kind. "Ghamran" means abundant overflowing gift, and he was one with many additions in giving. He treated "muʿṭī" in the manner of a nominative for the sake of the meter.]] in that care is the cause of the fronting, and she has spoken truly, so that what is more worthy of being the predicate was made a noun. And the verb's coming in the past tense indicates that it is a matter that has been tested and known. From this is their saying: "The least of what you have worked with is the tongue of one who disowns."[[His statement "the least of what you have worked with is the tongue of one who disowns (mamkh)" in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: tamakhkhaytu min al-shayʾ and amkhaytu minhu: when one disowns something. So perhaps mamkh is an active participle from amkhaytu. (ʿ)]]

It is narrated from Ibn Masʿūd, may God be pleased with him: "The shrewdest of people are three: the daughter of Shu'ayb; the companion of Yusuf in his saying ﴿perhaps he will benefit us﴾; and Abu Bakr concerning ʿUmar."

It is narrated that he married him to Ṣafrāʾ.

His saying ﴿these two﴾ (hātayn) is evidence that he had other daughters besides them. ﴿That you hire me﴾ (ta'jurunī) is from ajara, meaning to hire someone out, if you were his hired man, like your saying abawtuhu if you were his father. ﴿Eight years﴾ (thamāniya ḥijaj) is its adverbial object. Or it is from ajartuhu kadhā, when I gave it to him as a wage. From this is the condolence of the Messenger of God, ﷺ: "May God reward you (ajarakum) and have mercy on you."[[It was recorded by Abu Nuʿaym in Taʾrīkh Aṣbahān from the route of Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn Ibrāhīm ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Ibrāhīm ibn al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, from his fathers, Ibrāhīm ibn al-Ḥasan, from Fāṭimah bint al-Ḥusayn, from her father, who said: "When the Messenger of God ﷺ offered condolence he would say: 'Ajarakum Allāh wa-raḥimakum,' and when he congratulated he would say: 'Bārak Allāh lakum wa-bārak ʿalaykum.'" It has a supporting mursal report recorded by Ibn Abī Shaybah from the narration of Ibn Khālid al-Wālibī: that the Prophet ﷺ offered condolence to a man and said to him: "May God have mercy on him and reward you." In al-Ḍuʿafāʾ by Ibn Ḥibbān from Ibn ʿUmar: that the Prophet ﷺ offered condolence to a Muslim for a dhimmi who had died to him, and said: "May God reward you and increase your reward." Its chain includes Ismāʿīl ibn Yaḥyā al-Taymī, who is discarded (sāqiṭ). (ʿ)]] "Eight years" is the object, and its meaning is: the pasturing of eight years.

If you ask: how is it valid that he marries him one of his two daughters without specifying? I answer: that was not a contract of marriage, but a promise and a description of a matter he had resolved upon.[[His statement "but a promise and a description (muwāṣafah) of a matter he had resolved upon" is probably muwāḍaʿah (agreement). (ʿ)]] If it had been a contract, he would have said: "I have married you," and he did not say: "I intend to marry you."

If you ask: how is it valid that he gives as her dowry the hire of his own labor in pasturing sheep, when the delivery of what is property is necessary? Do you not see how Abu Ḥanīfah prohibited a man marrying a woman on condition that he serve her for a year?[[Mahmud said: "It is quoted from Abu Ḥanīfah's school that marriage is forbidden upon his personal service, but permitted upon the service of his slave for a year, and he made a distinction: in the first case he has given himself, which is not property, while in the second he has given his slave, which is property. It is quoted from al-Shāfiʿī that marriage upon known benefits is permitted absolutely." Aḥmad said: The school of Mālik has three positions: prohibition, disapproval, and permissibility. The marvel is Abu Ḥanīfah's permission of marriage upon the benefits of a slave, but not upon the benefits of the husband, while the verse permitted marriage upon the benefits of the husband and did not touch on anything else. This is only to favor the meaning that al-Zamakhsharī pointed to, or on the basis that there is no evidence in the law of those before us, or for other reasons. And God knows best.]] He permitted that he marry her by serving her, his slave, for a year, or by housing her in his house for a year, because in the first case...

Hired himself out, not for property. In the second case, he is hired for property, which is a slave or a house. I say: the matter stands on Abu Hanifa's school as you have mentioned. As for al-Shafi'i, he permitted marriage in exchange for a hire (ijara) for certain works and services, provided that the thing the employer hires or the service rendered is a known matter. Perhaps that was permitted in that earlier law (shari'a).

The dower may be something else. He wanted him to tend his sheep for this period, and he wanted to marry him his daughter. So he mentioned the two desired things and tied the marriage to the tending, meaning: "I will do this if you do that," as a mutual pledge (mu'ahada) and not as a binding contract (mu'aqada). It is also possible that he hired him to tend for eight years at a known sum, paid it to him, and then married his daughter to him for that. His words ﴿on condition that you hire yourself to me for eight years﴾ are an expression of what passed between them. ﴿And if you complete ten years, it is from you﴾: so its completion is from you. Its meaning is: it is from you, not from me. That is, I do not obligate you to it or impose it upon you, but if you do it, it is a favour and a voluntary gift from you; and if not, there is no blame on you. ﴿And I do not want to burden you﴾ by obligating you to complete the longer of the two terms and making it binding.

If you ask: what is the reality of their saying "I burdened him" (shaqqa 'alayhi) and "the matter burdened him" (shadda 'alayhi)? I say: its reality is that when a matter becomes great for you, it is as if it has burdened you, since you are in doubt; you say at one time, "I can bear it," and at another, "I cannot bear it." Or his promise of leniency and easygoing dealing from himself, meaning that he would not burden him in what he hired him for, in tending his sheep, and would not do what the difficult employers do with those they hire, such as quibbling over observing times, strictness in demanding the completion of tasks, and assigning the shepherds labours beyond the limit of the condition. Thus the prophets, peace be upon them, always adopted the most lenient course in their dealings with people. From this is the hadith: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was my partner, and he was the best of partners; he was not stubborn, did not dispute, and did not quarrel." [[Narrated by Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah from the hadith of al-Sa'ib, that he said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "You were my partner, and you were the best partner; you were not stubborn and did not dispute."]] His words ﴿you will find me, if Allah wills, among the righteous﴾ indicate this. By righteousness he means good dealing, gentleness of manner and softness of disposition. [[His words "gentleness of manner and softness of disposition": in al-Sihah (the lexicon of al-Jawhari), "wati'a" (softness) means "gentle, easy." (Ibn Hajar? no; the marginal note reads: (ʿ).)]] It is also possible that he means righteousness in general, which includes good dealing. The purpose of conditioning the will of Allah on the righteousness he promised is reliance on Allah's granting him success in it and His help, not that he would perform righteousness "if Allah wills," and if He wills, He would make him do the opposite.

﴿That﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿between me and you﴾ is its predicate, and it refers to what Shu'ayb covenanted with him. He means: what you said and covenanted with me and stipulated upon me remains established between us both, and neither of us departs from it, neither I from what you stipulated upon me, nor you from what you stipulated upon yourself.

Then he said: ﴿whichever of the two terms I fulfil﴾, that is, the longer of them, which is the ten years, or the shorter, which is the eight years, ﴿there shall be no injustice against me﴾, that is, no one shall transgress against me by seeking more than it. If you ask: the imagining of injustice applies only to one of the two terms, the shorter one, which is the demand for completing the ten years, so what is the meaning of attaching injustice to both of them together? I say: its meaning is that just as, if I were required to add to the ten years, that would certainly be an injustice, so likewise if I were required to add to the eight years. He intended by this to establish the matter of choice (khiyar), that it is firm and fixed, and that the two terms are equal: either this or that, with no difference between them in fulfilment. As for the completion, it is left to my judgement: if I wish, I will do it, and if not, I will not be compelled to it. It was also said: the meaning is "then I am not a transgressor," and this is in negating transgression from himself, like your saying, "there is no sin upon me, and no consequence upon me."

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "whichever of the two terms I have fulfilled." It was also read as "ayyama" with a sukun on the ya', as in the verse:

*I waited for Nasr and the two Simaks, whichever of them*
*its heavy rains pour upon me.* [[By al-Farazdaq. Nasr is the son of Sayyar, king of the two Iraqs. The two Simaks are two stars: al-Simak al-A'zal, which has no star in front of it, and al-Simak al-Ramih, which has stars in front of it. The word "ayyuhuma" originally had a doubled letter, which was made quiescent out of necessity. Then it may be that it is in the accusative as a substitute for what precedes it, and that it governs a deleted element, meaning: "I do not know which of them," and it is a relative pronoun. It is also possible that it is an interrogative, and in that case it is in the nominative as the subject, and the pronoun in it refers to Nasr and the two Simaks, meaning: "I awaited Nasr and the two Simaks, whichever of them its rains pour down upon me from the cloud." "Istahalla" means its pouring became intense. "Mawatir" are clouds, and "ghayth" is rain. In linking Nasr with the two Simaks there is an indication of comparing him to them in goodness, and of the interrogative sense, so it is of the type of "feigning ignorance of one who knows" (tajahul al-arif); and likewise it denies knowledge.]]

It is also reported from Ibn Qutayb: "'udwan" with a kasra. If you ask: what is the difference between the two positions of the extra "ma" in the two readings? I say: in the widely transmitted reading it occurs as an emphasis on the indefiniteness, meaning that "ayyu" is made more general by it; and in the irregular reading it is an emphasis on the decree, as if he said: "whichever of the two terms I have resolved upon fulfilling, and I have set my firm resolve upon it."

"Al-wakil" is the one to whom the matter has been entrusted. When it is used in the place of "witness," "guardian" (muhaymin) and "sustainer" (muqit), it takes "'ala" by virtue of that. [[His words "muhaymin and muqit": that is, the powerful one (al-muqtadir), or the guardian (al-hafiz). (ʿ)]]

It is reported that Shu'ayb had the staff of the prophets with him, and he said to Musa at night: "Enter that room and take a staff from those staffs." So he took a staff that Adam had descended with from Paradise, and the prophets had continued to inherit it until it came into the possession of Shu'ayb. He touched it, and he was blind, and he was reluctant to give it up, saying: "Take another." But nothing came into his hand except it, seven times, so he knew that it had a significance.

It was also said: Gabriel took it after the death of Adam, and it remained with him until he brought it to Musa at night. And it was also said: an angel in the form of a man entrusted it to Shu'ayb, and he commanded his daughter to bring him a staff, and she brought it to him, and he threw it back seven times, and nothing came into her hand except it, so he gave it to him. Then he regretted it, because it was a deposit (wadi'a), and he followed him, and they disputed over it. They agreed that whoever arrived first should judge between them, and the angel came to them and said: "Cast it down; whoever lifts it, it is his." The old man struggled with it and could not manage it, and Musa lifted it.

From al-Hasan: it was nothing but a staff of wood that came in his way by chance. From al-Kalbi: the tree from which he was called was a thorn-bush (shajarat al-'awsaj), and from it was his staff.

When morning came, Shu'ayb said to him: "When you reach the fork in the road, do not take on your right, for although there is more pasture there, in it is a serpent (tinnin) [[His words "a serpent": that is, a large snake (tha'ban). (ʿ)]] I fear for you and for the sheep." So the sheep took the right, and he could not restrain them, so he walked in their tracks, and there was pasture and lush greenery the like of which he had never seen. He slept, and suddenly the serpent came, and the staff fought it until it killed it, and returned to Musa's side, bloodied. When he saw it bloodied and the serpent dead, he was pleased with that. When he returned to Shu'ayb, he touched the sheep and found them full-bellied and abundant in milk, and Musa informed him, and he rejoiced and knew that Musa and the staff had a significance. He said to him: "I have given you of the young of my flock this year every spotted and speckled one."

Then in a dream it was revealed to him: "Strike your staff against the watering-place of the sheep." He did so, and then he watered them, and not one of them missed without bearing spotted and speckled young, and so he fulfilled his condition to him.

﴿...﴾ the water of Madyan, the water from which they drew. It was a well, according to what is narrated. Wurud (arriving) means coming to it and reaching it. ﴿He found upon it a community (ummah) of people﴾, a dense, large group of people of various kinds, ﴿and beside them he found two women driving back﴾, in a place lower than theirs. Al-dhawd means driving away and pushing back. The two women were driving back (their flock) because there were stronger people at the water who would prevent them from watering. It is also said that they disliked crowding at the water. It is also said that they did this so that their sheep would not mix with the sheep of the others. It is also said that they were driving back (the sheep) and screening their faces from a viewer's gaze. ﴿What is your matter (khatbukuma)?﴾ meaning, what is your affair? Its literal sense is "what is your maktub (the thing sought)," i.e., your objective, from al-dhawd. So the sought thing is called khatb, just as the affair (sha'n) is called sha'n in your saying "ma sha'nuka?" It is said: sha'nat sha'nahu, meaning, I aimed at his aim. It has been read as ﴿lā nasqī﴾ (we do not water) and ﴿yuṣdira﴾ (until the shepherds send back). And al-ri'a', with a damma on the nun, the ya' and the ra': al-ri'a' is a collective noun like al-rikhal and al-tha'a'.[[His statement "lā nasqī, yuṣdira, al-ri'ā' with a damma on the nūn, the yā' and the rā'" indicates that the well-known reading is with a fatḥa on the nūn and the yā' and a kasra on the rā'. Al-rikhāl: its singular is rakhl, which is the female of young sheep. Al-tha'ā': the tether of a camel or the like, from a twisted rope, as stated in al-Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿ)]]

As for al-ri'ā' with a kasra, it is analogical, like ṣiyām and qiyām. ﴿An old man﴾, meaning, an elderly man of great age. ﴿So he watered for them﴾, meaning he watered their flock on their behalf. It is narrated that the shepherds used to place upon the mouth of the well a stone which only seven men could lift. It is said: ten. It is said: forty. It is said: a hundred. Yet he lifted it alone. It is narrated that he asked them for a bucket of water, and they gave him their bucket and said: "Draw water with it." It was a bucket that only forty men could draw up. He drew water with it, poured it into the trough, and prayed for blessing, and he gave their flock drink and sent them back. It is narrated that he pushed them away from the water until he had watered for the two women. It is also said there was another well, over which was a stone. He did this out of eagerness for doing good and relieving the distressed. The meaning is: he reached that water when a community of people of differing, dense numbers had crowded around it, and he saw the two weak women behind them with their small flock, waiting for them to finish. His resolve did not fail to seize that opportunity in the religion of God, despite the fatigue he had, the tearing of the sole of his foot, and his hunger. Rather, he showed them mercy and relieved them, and he took care of the watering for them in such a crowd by the strength of his heart and the strength of his arm, and by the excellence God had given him in firmness of nature and solidity of constitution. And in this, together with the intent to relate his story and the strength and power he had been given, and what he did not neglect despite his exhaustion, there is an encouragement to goodness, a seizing of its opportunities, and an impulse to follow the righteous in that and to take up their conduct and ways.

If you ask: why was the object omitted in ﴿yasquna﴾ and ﴿tadhūdāni﴾ and ﴿lā nasqī﴾? I answer: because the purpose is the act, not the object of it. Do you not see that he showed mercy to them only because they were driving back while the others were watering, and he did not show mercy because their flock was of sheep and the others' was of camels, for example? Likewise their saying ﴿lā nasqī ḥattā yuṣdira al-ri'āʾ﴾, where what is intended is the watering, not the watered thing.

If you ask: how did their answer correspond to his question? I answer: he asked them about the reason for their driving back, and they said: the reason for that is that we are two weak women, veiled, unable to compete (musājala) with men or crowd with them, so we must delay watering until they finish. We have no man to do that, and our father is an old man whom age has weakened, so he is not fit to do it. So they presented their excuse for taking on the watering themselves.[[His statement "abalatā ilayhi ʿudhrahumā" is probably a distortion; its original is abdatā, as in the wording of al-Nasafī. (ʿ)]]

If you ask: how was it permissible for the prophet of God, who is Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, to be content for his two daughters to water the livestock? I answer: the matter in itself is not forbidden, and religion does not reject it. As for manliness (murū'ah), people differ in that, and customs vary regarding it. The condition of the Arabs in this differs from that of non-Arabs, and the custom of the people of the desert differs from that of the people of the settled towns, especially when the situation is one of necessity.

﴿Indeed, I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need﴾, whether little or much, lean or fat. Faqīr is followed by lām because it implies the meaning of "one who asks" and "one who seeks." It is said: he mentioned that, though the greenness of the herb showed through his belly from emaciation, he asked God only for a single meal. It may also mean: "I am poor in worldly things, on account of what You have sent down to me of the good of religion, which is salvation from the wrongdoers," because he had been in wealth and prosperity at Pharaoh's court. He said that out of contentment with the noble exchange, joy in it, and gratitude for it.

﴿And the shade was the shade of a sumur tree﴾ and ﴿she came walking to him with modesty﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: modestly, shyly, veiled. It is said: she had drawn her garment about her.

It is narrated that when the two of them returned to their father earlier than the people, their flock came back with full udders. He said to them: "What has hastened you?" They said: "We found a righteous man who had pity on us and watered for us." So he said to one of them: "Go and call him for me." Then Musa followed her, but the wind pressed her garment against her body, and she described him. So he said to her: "Walk behind me and direct me to the way." When he related his story to him, he said: "Do not fear; there is no authority of Pharaoh in our land."

If you ask: how was it permissible for Musa to act on the word of a woman, and to walk with her though she was a stranger? I answer: as for acting on the word of a woman, it is like acting on the word of one (single reporter) in reports, whether free or slave, male or female. She was only reporting about her father that he was calling him to reward him. As for walking with a foreign woman, there is no harm in it in similar circumstances, together with caution and abstinence.

If you ask: how was it valid for him to take a wage for righteousness and kindness? I answer: it is possible that he did that for the sake of God and as a form of righteousness and kindness. It is also said that Shu'ayb's feeding him and his beneficence was not in the manner of taking a wage, but as an accepting of a kindness begun by him. How (could it be otherwise), since he had related his story to him and he had made him know that he was of the house of prophethood, from the descendants of Ya'qub? Such a man deserves to be hosted and honored, especially in the house of a prophet of God's prophets. And it is not objectionable that he should do so out of the necessity of poverty and need, seeking reward.

And there is narrated something that supports both views: it is reported that when she said "that he may reward you," he disliked that. And when the food was set before him, he refused and said: "We are a household that does not sell its religion for the filling of the earth with gold, nor do we take a price for kindness." Until Shu'ayb said: "This is our custom with everyone who comes down upon us."

It is related from ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib: he raised his voice in supplication so that they would hear him. That is why it was said to him: ﴿that he may reward you for what you watered﴾, i.e., the recompense for your watering.

Al-qaṣaṣ (the story) is a verbal noun like al-ʿilal, and the narrated account is named after it.

The elder of the two was called Ṣafrāʾ, and the younger Ṣufayrāʾ. Ṣafrāʾ is the one who went with him and asked her father to hire him, and she is the one he married.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās that Shu'ayb was seized by jealousy and said: "And what do you know of his strength and trustworthiness?" So she mentioned the lifting of the stone and the drawing of the bucket, and that he lowered his head when his message reached him and when her father commanded her to walk behind him.

Her saying ﴿Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong, the trustworthy﴾ is a wise, comprehensive statement to which nothing can be added, because when these two qualities are combined, I mean sufficiency and trustworthiness in the one who manages your affair, your mind is at ease and your goal is achieved. She has been content with sending this saying, whose context is that of a proverb, and the wisdom is that you say: hire him for his strength and his trustworthiness.[[Mahmud said: "This is a wise and comprehensive statement to which nothing can be added, because if strength and trustworthiness are combined in the one who manages your affair, your mind is at rest, and she has been content with sending this saying, whose context is that of a proverb and maxim, rather than saying: 'He is strong and trustworthy.'" Aḥmad said: This is also more beautiful as praise by women of men than specific praise, and more preserving of modesty, especially if she understood that her father's aim, peace be upon him, was to marry her to him. How well the Fārūq (ʿUmar), may God be pleased with him, took this meaning when he said: "I complain to God of the weakness of the trustworthy and the treachery of the strong." In the content of this complaint is a request to God that He grant him one who combines the two qualities, strong and trustworthy, whom he could rely upon in what he was undertaking, may God be pleased with him. And this ambiguity, from the daughter of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, was also taken by Zulaykha with Yusuf, peace be upon him. But how different is natural modesty from acquired modesty: kohl in the eyes is not like the kohl. When she said to her master: ﴿What is the recompense of one who intended evil to your wife, except that he be imprisoned or a painful punishment?﴾, she meant: what is the recompense of Yusuf for having intended evil toward me, except that you imprison him or punish him with a painful punishment? But shame and modesty prevented her husband's mind from her speaking the word of chastity while attributing the indecency to herself, indicating that this modesty in her, which prevented her from speaking this matter, prevented her from soliciting Yusuf by a more fitting and better means. And God knows best.]]

If you ask: how did he make ﴿the best you hire﴾ the subject of ﴿inna﴾ and ﴿the strong, the trustworthy﴾ the predicate? I answer: it is like his saying:

"Surely the best of people, alive and dead, is the captive of Thaqīf among them in chains."[[Surely the best of people, living and dead, is the captive of Thaqīf among them in chains. By my life, if you have made the prison abode of Khalid and made him tread it with the tread of one burdened. He was one who rose up to every calamity, and gave generous gifts, great in bounty, abundant in extra gifts. This is by Abu al-Shaghb al-ʿAbsī, lamenting over Khalid ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī when Yusuf ibn ʿUmar captured him. "The best of people" is an elative in the form of a comparative, annexed to a definite with al, and it is the subject of inna. "Living and dead" (ḥayyan wa-mayyitan), and in one narration "perishing" (hālikan), are two circumstantial clauses from it. "Captive" (asīr) is the predicate of inna, annexed to Thaqīf, the name of the tribe. A proper name is more definite than what is definite by al, so the predicate annexed to the proper noun is more definite than its subject which is annexed to the definite by al, and there is no obstacle to this when both refer to the same thing intended by the speaker. "Among them in chains" is a circumstantial clause or a predicate after a predicate. "By my life" is an oath. "If you have made...": that is, you put Khalid into prison and settled him there. "And made him tread it": that is, you made him tread the ground with his foot like the tread of one burdened with something heavy, meaning you put the shackles on his feet, so this is a metaphor for that. "He was one who rose up..." is the answer to the oath. The answer to the condition is omitted, meaning he was quick to rise to every heavy calamity. "Giver of al-lahā" with a fatḥa is the plural of lahāh, like ḥaṣā and ḥaṣāh, meaning the piece of flesh at the farthest part of the mouth, but here it means the mouth itself. The more likely is that with a ḍamma it is the plural of luhwah, like ghuraf, plural of ghurfah, meaning gift of any kind. "Ghamran" means abundant overflowing gift, and he was one with many additions in giving. He treated "muʿṭī" in the manner of a nominative for the sake of the meter.]] in that care is the cause of the fronting, and she has spoken truly, so that what is more worthy of being the predicate was made a noun. And the verb's coming in the past tense indicates that it is a matter that has been tested and known. From this is their saying: "The least of what you have worked with is the tongue of one who disowns."[[His statement "the least of what you have worked with is the tongue of one who disowns (mamkh)" in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: tamakhkhaytu min al-shayʾ and amkhaytu minhu: when one disowns something. So perhaps mamkh is an active participle from amkhaytu. (ʿ)]]

It is narrated from Ibn Masʿūd, may God be pleased with him: "The shrewdest of people are three: the daughter of Shu'ayb; the companion of Yusuf in his saying ﴿perhaps he will benefit us﴾; and Abu Bakr concerning ʿUmar."

It is narrated that he married him to Ṣafrāʾ.

His saying ﴿these two﴾ (hātayn) is evidence that he had other daughters besides them. ﴿That you hire me﴾ (ta'jurunī) is from ajara, meaning to hire someone out, if you were his hired man, like your saying abawtuhu if you were his father. ﴿Eight years﴾ (thamāniya ḥijaj) is its adverbial object. Or it is from ajartuhu kadhā, when I gave it to him as a wage. From this is the condolence of the Messenger of God, ﷺ: "May God reward you (ajarakum) and have mercy on you."[[It was recorded by Abu Nuʿaym in Taʾrīkh Aṣbahān from the route of Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn Ibrāhīm ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Ibrāhīm ibn al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, from his fathers, Ibrāhīm ibn al-Ḥasan, from Fāṭimah bint al-Ḥusayn, from her father, who said: "When the Messenger of God ﷺ offered condolence he would say: 'Ajarakum Allāh wa-raḥimakum,' and when he congratulated he would say: 'Bārak Allāh lakum wa-bārak ʿalaykum.'" It has a supporting mursal report recorded by Ibn Abī Shaybah from the narration of Ibn Khālid al-Wālibī: that the Prophet ﷺ offered condolence to a man and said to him: "May God have mercy on him and reward you." In al-Ḍuʿafāʾ by Ibn Ḥibbān from Ibn ʿUmar: that the Prophet ﷺ offered condolence to a Muslim for a dhimmi who had died to him, and said: "May God reward you and increase your reward." Its chain includes Ismāʿīl ibn Yaḥyā al-Taymī, who is discarded (sāqiṭ). (ʿ)]] "Eight years" is the object, and its meaning is: the pasturing of eight years.

If you ask: how is it valid that he marries him one of his two daughters without specifying? I answer: that was not a contract of marriage, but a promise and a description of a matter he had resolved upon.[[His statement "but a promise and a description (muwāṣafah) of a matter he had resolved upon" is probably muwāḍaʿah (agreement). (ʿ)]] If it had been a contract, he would have said: "I have married you," and he did not say: "I intend to marry you."

If you ask: how is it valid that he gives as her dowry the hire of his own labor in pasturing sheep, when the delivery of what is property is necessary? Do you not see how Abu Ḥanīfah prohibited a man marrying a woman on condition that he serve her for a year?[[Mahmud said: "It is quoted from Abu Ḥanīfah's school that marriage is forbidden upon his personal service, but permitted upon the service of his slave for a year, and he made a distinction: in the first case he has given himself, which is not property, while in the second he has given his slave, which is property. It is quoted from al-Shāfiʿī that marriage upon known benefits is permitted absolutely." Aḥmad said: The school of Mālik has three positions: prohibition, disapproval, and permissibility. The marvel is Abu Ḥanīfah's permission of marriage upon the benefits of a slave, but not upon the benefits of the husband, while the verse permitted marriage upon the benefits of the husband and did not touch on anything else. This is only to favor the meaning that al-Zamakhsharī pointed to, or on the basis that there is no evidence in the law of those before us, or for other reasons. And God knows best.]] He permitted that he marry her by serving her, his slave, for a year, or by housing her in his house for a year, because in the first case...

Hired himself out, not for property. In the second case, he is hired for property, which is a slave or a house. I say: the matter stands on Abu Hanifa's school as you have mentioned. As for al-Shafi'i, he permitted marriage in exchange for a hire (ijara) for certain works and services, provided that the thing the employer hires or the service rendered is a known matter. Perhaps that was permitted in that earlier law (shari'a).

The dower may be something else. He wanted him to tend his sheep for this period, and he wanted to marry him his daughter. So he mentioned the two desired things and tied the marriage to the tending, meaning: "I will do this if you do that," as a mutual pledge (mu'ahada) and not as a binding contract (mu'aqada). It is also possible that he hired him to tend for eight years at a known sum, paid it to him, and then married his daughter to him for that. His words ﴿on condition that you hire yourself to me for eight years﴾ are an expression of what passed between them. ﴿And if you complete ten years, it is from you﴾: so its completion is from you. Its meaning is: it is from you, not from me. That is, I do not obligate you to it or impose it upon you, but if you do it, it is a favour and a voluntary gift from you; and if not, there is no blame on you. ﴿And I do not want to burden you﴾ by obligating you to complete the longer of the two terms and making it binding.

If you ask: what is the reality of their saying "I burdened him" (shaqqa 'alayhi) and "the matter burdened him" (shadda 'alayhi)? I say: its reality is that when a matter becomes great for you, it is as if it has burdened you, since you are in doubt; you say at one time, "I can bear it," and at another, "I cannot bear it."
