Or his promise of leniency and easygoing dealing from himself, meaning that he would not burden him in what he hired him for, in tending his sheep, and would not do what the difficult employers do with those they hire, such as quibbling over observing times, strictness in demanding the completion of tasks, and assigning the shepherds labours beyond the limit of the condition. Thus the prophets, peace be upon them, always adopted the most lenient course in their dealings with people. From this is the hadith: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was my partner, and he was the best of partners; he was not stubborn, did not dispute, and did not quarrel." [[Narrated by Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah from the hadith of al-Sa'ib, that he said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "You were my partner, and you were the best partner; you were not stubborn and did not dispute."]] His words ﴿you will find me, if Allah wills, among the righteous﴾ indicate this. By righteousness he means good dealing, gentleness of manner and softness of disposition. [[His words "gentleness of manner and softness of disposition": in al-Sihah (the lexicon of al-Jawhari), "wati'a" (softness) means "gentle, easy." (Ibn Hajar? no; the marginal note reads: (ʿ).)]] It is also possible that he means righteousness in general, which includes good dealing. The purpose of conditioning the will of Allah on the righteousness he promised is reliance on Allah's granting him success in it and His help, not that he would perform righteousness "if Allah wills," and if He wills, He would make him do the opposite.

﴿That﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿between me and you﴾ is its predicate, and it refers to what Shu'ayb covenanted with him. He means: what you said and covenanted with me and stipulated upon me remains established between us both, and neither of us departs from it, neither I from what you stipulated upon me, nor you from what you stipulated upon yourself.

Then he said: ﴿whichever of the two terms I fulfil﴾, that is, the longer of them, which is the ten years, or the shorter, which is the eight years, ﴿there shall be no injustice against me﴾, that is, no one shall transgress against me by seeking more than it. If you ask: the imagining of injustice applies only to one of the two terms, the shorter one, which is the demand for completing the ten years, so what is the meaning of attaching injustice to both of them together? I say: its meaning is that just as, if I were required to add to the ten years, that would certainly be an injustice, so likewise if I were required to add to the eight years. He intended by this to establish the matter of choice (khiyar), that it is firm and fixed, and that the two terms are equal: either this or that, with no difference between them in fulfilment. As for the completion, it is left to my judgement: if I wish, I will do it, and if not, I will not be compelled to it. It was also said: the meaning is "then I am not a transgressor," and this is in negating transgression from himself, like your saying, "there is no sin upon me, and no consequence upon me."

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "whichever of the two terms I have fulfilled." It was also read as "ayyama" with a sukun on the ya', as in the verse:

*I waited for Nasr and the two Simaks, whichever of them*
*its heavy rains pour upon me.* [[By al-Farazdaq. Nasr is the son of Sayyar, king of the two Iraqs. The two Simaks are two stars: al-Simak al-A'zal, which has no star in front of it, and al-Simak al-Ramih, which has stars in front of it. The word "ayyuhuma" originally had a doubled letter, which was made quiescent out of necessity. Then it may be that it is in the accusative as a substitute for what precedes it, and that it governs a deleted element, meaning: "I do not know which of them," and it is a relative pronoun. It is also possible that it is an interrogative, and in that case it is in the nominative as the subject, and the pronoun in it refers to Nasr and the two Simaks, meaning: "I awaited Nasr and the two Simaks, whichever of them its rains pour down upon me from the cloud." "Istahalla" means its pouring became intense. "Mawatir" are clouds, and "ghayth" is rain. In linking Nasr with the two Simaks there is an indication of comparing him to them in goodness, and of the interrogative sense, so it is of the type of "feigning ignorance of one who knows" (tajahul al-arif); and likewise it denies knowledge.]]

It is also reported from Ibn Qutayb: "'udwan" with a kasra. If you ask: what is the difference between the two positions of the extra "ma" in the two readings? I say: in the widely transmitted reading it occurs as an emphasis on the indefiniteness, meaning that "ayyu" is made more general by it; and in the irregular reading it is an emphasis on the decree, as if he said: "whichever of the two terms I have resolved upon fulfilling, and I have set my firm resolve upon it."

"Al-wakil" is the one to whom the matter has been entrusted. When it is used in the place of "witness," "guardian" (muhaymin) and "sustainer" (muqit), it takes "'ala" by virtue of that. [[His words "muhaymin and muqit": that is, the powerful one (al-muqtadir), or the guardian (al-hafiz). (ʿ)]]

It is reported that Shu'ayb had the staff of the prophets with him, and he said to Musa at night: "Enter that room and take a staff from those staffs." So he took a staff that Adam had descended with from Paradise, and the prophets had continued to inherit it until it came into the possession of Shu'ayb. He touched it, and he was blind, and he was reluctant to give it up, saying: "Take another." But nothing came into his hand except it, seven times, so he knew that it had a significance.

It was also said: Gabriel took it after the death of Adam, and it remained with him until he brought it to Musa at night. And it was also said: an angel in the form of a man entrusted it to Shu'ayb, and he commanded his daughter to bring him a staff, and she brought it to him, and he threw it back seven times, and nothing came into her hand except it, so he gave it to him. Then he regretted it, because it was a deposit (wadi'a), and he followed him, and they disputed over it. They agreed that whoever arrived first should judge between them, and the angel came to them and said: "Cast it down; whoever lifts it, it is his." The old man struggled with it and could not manage it, and Musa lifted it.

From al-Hasan: it was nothing but a staff of wood that came in his way by chance. From al-Kalbi: the tree from which he was called was a thorn-bush (shajarat al-'awsaj), and from it was his staff.

When morning came, Shu'ayb said to him: "When you reach the fork in the road, do not take on your right, for although there is more pasture there, in it is a serpent (tinnin) [[His words "a serpent": that is, a large snake (tha'ban). (ʿ)]] I fear for you and for the sheep." So the sheep took the right, and he could not restrain them, so he walked in their tracks, and there was pasture and lush greenery the like of which he had never seen. He slept, and suddenly the serpent came, and the staff fought it until it killed it, and returned to Musa's side, bloodied. When he saw it bloodied and the serpent dead, he was pleased with that. When he returned to Shu'ayb, he touched the sheep and found them full-bellied and abundant in milk, and Musa informed him, and he rejoiced and knew that Musa and the staff had a significance. He said to him: "I have given you of the young of my flock this year every spotted and speckled one."

Then in a dream it was revealed to him: "Strike your staff against the watering-place of the sheep." He did so, and then he watered them, and not one of them missed without bearing spotted and speckled young, and so he fulfilled his condition to him.

﴿...﴾ the water of Madyan, the water from which they drew. It was a well, according to what is narrated. Wurud (arriving) means coming to it and reaching it. ﴿He found upon it a community (ummah) of people﴾, a dense, large group of people of various kinds, ﴿and beside them he found two women driving back﴾, in a place lower than theirs. Al-dhawd means driving away and pushing back. The two women were driving back (their flock) because there were stronger people at the water who would prevent them from watering. It is also said that they disliked crowding at the water. It is also said that they did this so that their sheep would not mix with the sheep of the others. It is also said that they were driving back (the sheep) and screening their faces from a viewer's gaze. ﴿What is your matter (khatbukuma)?﴾ meaning, what is your affair? Its literal sense is "what is your maktub (the thing sought)," i.e., your objective, from al-dhawd. So the sought thing is called khatb, just as the affair (sha'n) is called sha'n in your saying "ma sha'nuka?" It is said: sha'nat sha'nahu, meaning, I aimed at his aim. It has been read as ﴿lā nasqī﴾ (we do not water) and ﴿yuṣdira﴾ (until the shepherds send back). And al-ri'a', with a damma on the nun, the ya' and the ra': al-ri'a' is a collective noun like al-rikhal and al-tha'a'.[[His statement "lā nasqī, yuṣdira, al-ri'ā' with a damma on the nūn, the yā' and the rā'" indicates that the well-known reading is with a fatḥa on the nūn and the yā' and a kasra on the rā'. Al-rikhāl: its singular is rakhl, which is the female of young sheep. Al-tha'ā': the tether of a camel or the like, from a twisted rope, as stated in al-Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿ)]]

As for al-ri'ā' with a kasra, it is analogical, like ṣiyām and qiyām. ﴿An old man﴾, meaning, an elderly man of great age. ﴿So he watered for them﴾, meaning he watered their flock on their behalf. It is narrated that the shepherds used to place upon the mouth of the well a stone which only seven men could lift. It is said: ten. It is said: forty. It is said: a hundred. Yet he lifted it alone. It is narrated that he asked them for a bucket of water, and they gave him their bucket and said: "Draw water with it." It was a bucket that only forty men could draw up. He drew water with it, poured it into the trough, and prayed for blessing, and he gave their flock drink and sent them back. It is narrated that he pushed them away from the water until he had watered for the two women. It is also said there was another well, over which was a stone. He did this out of eagerness for doing good and relieving the distressed. The meaning is: he reached that water when a community of people of differing, dense numbers had crowded around it, and he saw the two weak women behind them with their small flock, waiting for them to finish. His resolve did not fail to seize that opportunity in the religion of God, despite the fatigue he had, the tearing of the sole of his foot, and his hunger. Rather, he showed them mercy and relieved them, and he took care of the watering for them in such a crowd by the strength of his heart and the strength of his arm, and by the excellence God had given him in firmness of nature and solidity of constitution. And in this, together with the intent to relate his story and the strength and power he had been given, and what he did not neglect despite his exhaustion, there is an encouragement to goodness, a seizing of its opportunities, and an impulse to follow the righteous in that and to take up their conduct and ways.

If you ask: why was the object omitted in ﴿yasquna﴾ and ﴿tadhūdāni﴾ and ﴿lā nasqī﴾? I answer: because the purpose is the act, not the object of it. Do you not see that he showed mercy to them only because they were driving back while the others were watering, and he did not show mercy because their flock was of sheep and the others' was of camels, for example? Likewise their saying ﴿lā nasqī ḥattā yuṣdira al-ri'āʾ﴾, where what is intended is the watering, not the watered thing.

If you ask: how did their answer correspond to his question? I answer: he asked them about the reason for their driving back, and they said: the reason for that is that we are two weak women, veiled, unable to compete (musājala) with men or crowd with them, so we must delay watering until they finish. We have no man to do that, and our father is an old man whom age has weakened, so he is not fit to do it. So they presented their excuse for taking on the watering themselves.[[His statement "abalatā ilayhi ʿudhrahumā" is probably a distortion; its original is abdatā, as in the wording of al-Nasafī. (ʿ)]]

If you ask: how was it permissible for the prophet of God, who is Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, to be content for his two daughters to water the livestock? I answer: the matter in itself is not forbidden, and religion does not reject it. As for manliness (murū'ah), people differ in that, and customs vary regarding it. The condition of the Arabs in this differs from that of non-Arabs, and the custom of the people of the desert differs from that of the people of the settled towns, especially when the situation is one of necessity.

﴿Indeed, I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need﴾, whether little or much, lean or fat. Faqīr is followed by lām because it implies the meaning of "one who asks" and "one who seeks." It is said: he mentioned that, though the greenness of the herb showed through his belly from emaciation, he asked God only for a single meal. It may also mean: "I am poor in worldly things, on account of what You have sent down to me of the good of religion, which is salvation from the wrongdoers," because he had been in wealth and prosperity at Pharaoh's court. He said that out of contentment with the noble exchange, joy in it, and gratitude for it.

﴿And the shade was the shade of a sumur tree﴾ and ﴿she came walking to him with modesty﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: modestly, shyly, veiled. It is said: she had drawn her garment about her.

It is narrated that when the two of them returned to their father earlier than the people, their flock came back with full udders. He said to them: "What has hastened you?" They said: "We found a righteous man who had pity on us and watered for us." So he said to one of them: "Go and call him for me." Then Musa followed her, but the wind pressed her garment against her body, and she described him. So he said to her: "Walk behind me and direct me to the way." When he related his story to him, he said: "Do not fear; there is no authority of Pharaoh in our land."

If you ask: how was it permissible for Musa to act on the word of a woman, and to walk with her though she was a stranger? I answer: as for acting on the word of a woman, it is like acting on the word of one (single reporter) in reports, whether free or slave, male or female. She was only reporting about her father that he was calling him to reward him. As for walking with a foreign woman, there is no harm in it in similar circumstances, together with caution and abstinence.

If you ask: how was it valid for him to take a wage for righteousness and kindness? I answer: it is possible that he did that for the sake of God and as a form of righteousness and kindness. It is also said that Shu'ayb's feeding him and his beneficence was not in the manner of taking a wage, but as an accepting of a kindness begun by him. How (could it be otherwise), since he had related his story to him and he had made him know that he was of the house of prophethood, from the descendants of Ya'qub? Such a man deserves to be hosted and honored, especially in the house of a prophet of God's prophets. And it is not objectionable that he should do so out of the necessity of poverty and need, seeking reward.

And there is narrated something that supports both views: it is reported that when she said "that he may reward you," he disliked that. And when the food was set before him, he refused and said: "We are a household that does not sell its religion for the filling of the earth with gold, nor do we take a price for kindness." Until Shu'ayb said: "This is our custom with everyone who comes down upon us."

It is related from ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib: he raised his voice in supplication so that they would hear him. That is why it was said to him: ﴿that he may reward you for what you watered﴾, i.e., the recompense for your watering.

Al-qaṣaṣ (the story) is a verbal noun like al-ʿilal, and the narrated account is named after it.

The elder of the two was called Ṣafrāʾ, and the younger Ṣufayrāʾ. Ṣafrāʾ is the one who went with him and asked her father to hire him, and she is the one he married.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās that Shu'ayb was seized by jealousy and said: "And what do you know of his strength and trustworthiness?" So she mentioned the lifting of the stone and the drawing of the bucket, and that he lowered his head when his message reached him and when her father commanded her to walk behind him.

Her saying ﴿Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong, the trustworthy﴾ is a wise, comprehensive statement to which nothing can be added, because when these two qualities are combined, I mean sufficiency and trustworthiness in the one who manages your affair, your mind is at ease and your goal is achieved. She has been content with sending this saying, whose context is that of a proverb, and the wisdom is that you say: hire him for his strength and his trustworthiness.[[Mahmud said: "This is a wise and comprehensive statement to which nothing can be added, because if strength and trustworthiness are combined in the one who manages your affair, your mind is at rest, and she has been content with sending this saying, whose context is that of a proverb and maxim, rather than saying: 'He is strong and trustworthy.'" Aḥmad said: This is also more beautiful as praise by women of men than specific praise, and more preserving of modesty, especially if she understood that her father's aim, peace be upon him, was to marry her to him. How well the Fārūq (ʿUmar), may God be pleased with him, took this meaning when he said: "I complain to God of the weakness of the trustworthy and the treachery of the strong." In the content of this complaint is a request to God that He grant him one who combines the two qualities, strong and trustworthy, whom he could rely upon in what he was undertaking, may God be pleased with him. And this ambiguity, from the daughter of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, was also taken by Zulaykha with Yusuf, peace be upon him. But how different is natural modesty from acquired modesty: kohl in the eyes is not like the kohl. When she said to her master: ﴿What is the recompense of one who intended evil to your wife, except that he be imprisoned or a painful punishment?﴾, she meant: what is the recompense of Yusuf for having intended evil toward me, except that you imprison him or punish him with a painful punishment? But shame and modesty prevented her husband's mind from her speaking the word of chastity while attributing the indecency to herself, indicating that this modesty in her, which prevented her from speaking this matter, prevented her from soliciting Yusuf by a more fitting and better means. And God knows best.]]

If you ask: how did he make ﴿the best you hire﴾ the subject of ﴿inna﴾ and ﴿the strong, the trustworthy﴾ the predicate? I answer: it is like his saying:

"Surely the best of people, alive and dead, is the captive of Thaqīf among them in chains."[[Surely the best of people, living and dead, is the captive of Thaqīf among them in chains. By my life, if you have made the prison abode of Khalid and made him tread it with the tread of one burdened. He was one who rose up to every calamity, and gave generous gifts, great in bounty, abundant in extra gifts. This is by Abu al-Shaghb al-ʿAbsī, lamenting over Khalid ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī when Yusuf ibn ʿUmar captured him. "The best of people" is an elative in the form of a comparative, annexed to a definite with al, and it is the subject of inna. "Living and dead" (ḥayyan wa-mayyitan), and in one narration "perishing" (hālikan), are two circumstantial clauses from it. "Captive" (asīr) is the predicate of inna, annexed to Thaqīf, the name of the tribe. A proper name is more definite than what is definite by al, so the predicate annexed to the proper noun is more definite than its subject which is annexed to the definite by al, and there is no obstacle to this when both refer to the same thing intended by the speaker. "Among them in chains" is a circumstantial clause or a predicate after a predicate. "By my life" is an oath. "If you have made...": that is, you put Khalid into prison and settled him there. "And made him tread it": that is, you made him tread the ground with his foot like the tread of one burdened with something heavy, meaning you put the shackles on his feet, so this is a metaphor for that. "He was one who rose up..." is the answer to the oath. The answer to the condition is omitted, meaning he was quick to rise to every heavy calamity. "Giver of al-lahā" with a fatḥa is the plural of lahāh, like ḥaṣā and ḥaṣāh, meaning the piece of flesh at the farthest part of the mouth, but here it means the mouth itself. The more likely is that with a ḍamma it is the plural of luhwah, like ghuraf, plural of ghurfah, meaning gift of any kind. "Ghamran" means abundant overflowing gift, and he was one with many additions in giving. He treated "muʿṭī" in the manner of a nominative for the sake of the meter.]] in that care is the cause of the fronting, and she has spoken truly, so that what is more worthy of being the predicate was made a noun. And the verb's coming in the past tense indicates that it is a matter that has been tested and known. From this is their saying: "The least of what you have worked with is the tongue of one who disowns."[[His statement "the least of what you have worked with is the tongue of one who disowns (mamkh)" in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: tamakhkhaytu min al-shayʾ and amkhaytu minhu: when one disowns something. So perhaps mamkh is an active participle from amkhaytu. (ʿ)]]

It is narrated from Ibn Masʿūd, may God be pleased with him: "The shrewdest of people are three: the daughter of Shu'ayb; the companion of Yusuf in his saying ﴿perhaps he will benefit us﴾; and Abu Bakr concerning ʿUmar."

It is narrated that he married him to Ṣafrāʾ.

His saying ﴿these two﴾ (hātayn) is evidence that he had other daughters besides them. ﴿That you hire me﴾ (ta'jurunī) is from ajara, meaning to hire someone out, if you were his hired man, like your saying abawtuhu if you were his father. ﴿Eight years﴾ (thamāniya ḥijaj) is its adverbial object. Or it is from ajartuhu kadhā, when I gave it to him as a wage. From this is the condolence of the Messenger of God, ﷺ: "May God reward you (ajarakum) and have mercy on you."[[It was recorded by Abu Nuʿaym in Taʾrīkh Aṣbahān from the route of Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn Ibrāhīm ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Ibrāhīm ibn al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, from his fathers, Ibrāhīm ibn al-Ḥasan, from Fāṭimah bint al-Ḥusayn, from her father, who said: "When the Messenger of God ﷺ offered condolence he would say: 'Ajarakum Allāh wa-raḥimakum,' and when he congratulated he would say: 'Bārak Allāh lakum wa-bārak ʿalaykum.'" It has a supporting mursal report recorded by Ibn Abī Shaybah from the narration of Ibn Khālid al-Wālibī: that the Prophet ﷺ offered condolence to a man and said to him: "May God have mercy on him and reward you." In al-Ḍuʿafāʾ by Ibn Ḥibbān from Ibn ʿUmar: that the Prophet ﷺ offered condolence to a Muslim for a dhimmi who had died to him, and said: "May God reward you and increase your reward." Its chain includes Ismāʿīl ibn Yaḥyā al-Taymī, who is discarded (sāqiṭ). (ʿ)]] "Eight years" is the object, and its meaning is: the pasturing of eight years.

If you ask: how is it valid that he marries him one of his two daughters without specifying? I answer: that was not a contract of marriage, but a promise and a description of a matter he had resolved upon.[[His statement "but a promise and a description (muwāṣafah) of a matter he had resolved upon" is probably muwāḍaʿah (agreement). (ʿ)]] If it had been a contract, he would have said: "I have married you," and he did not say: "I intend to marry you."

If you ask: how is it valid that he gives as her dowry the hire of his own labor in pasturing sheep, when the delivery of what is property is necessary? Do you not see how Abu Ḥanīfah prohibited a man marrying a woman on condition that he serve her for a year?[[Mahmud said: "It is quoted from Abu Ḥanīfah's school that marriage is forbidden upon his personal service, but permitted upon the service of his slave for a year, and he made a distinction: in the first case he has given himself, which is not property, while in the second he has given his slave, which is property. It is quoted from al-Shāfiʿī that marriage upon known benefits is permitted absolutely." Aḥmad said: The school of Mālik has three positions: prohibition, disapproval, and permissibility. The marvel is Abu Ḥanīfah's permission of marriage upon the benefits of a slave, but not upon the benefits of the husband, while the verse permitted marriage upon the benefits of the husband and did not touch on anything else. This is only to favor the meaning that al-Zamakhsharī pointed to, or on the basis that there is no evidence in the law of those before us, or for other reasons. And God knows best.]] He permitted that he marry her by serving her, his slave, for a year, or by housing her in his house for a year, because in the first case...

Hired himself out, not for property. In the second case, he is hired for property, which is a slave or a house. I say: the matter stands on Abu Hanifa's school as you have mentioned. As for al-Shafi'i, he permitted marriage in exchange for a hire (ijara) for certain works and services, provided that the thing the employer hires or the service rendered is a known matter. Perhaps that was permitted in that earlier law (shari'a).

The dower may be something else. He wanted him to tend his sheep for this period, and he wanted to marry him his daughter. So he mentioned the two desired things and tied the marriage to the tending, meaning: "I will do this if you do that," as a mutual pledge (mu'ahada) and not as a binding contract (mu'aqada). It is also possible that he hired him to tend for eight years at a known sum, paid it to him, and then married his daughter to him for that. His words ﴿on condition that you hire yourself to me for eight years﴾ are an expression of what passed between them. ﴿And if you complete ten years, it is from you﴾: so its completion is from you. Its meaning is: it is from you, not from me. That is, I do not obligate you to it or impose it upon you, but if you do it, it is a favour and a voluntary gift from you; and if not, there is no blame on you. ﴿And I do not want to burden you﴾ by obligating you to complete the longer of the two terms and making it binding.

If you ask: what is the reality of their saying "I burdened him" (shaqqa 'alayhi) and "the matter burdened him" (shadda 'alayhi)? I say: its reality is that when a matter becomes great for you, it is as if it has burdened you, since you are in doubt; you say at one time, "I can bear it," and at another, "I cannot bear it." Or his promise of leniency and easygoing dealing from himself, meaning that he would not burden him in what he hired him for, in tending his sheep, and would not do what the difficult employers do with those they hire, such as quibbling over observing times, strictness in demanding the completion of tasks, and assigning the shepherds labours beyond the limit of the condition. Thus the prophets, peace be upon them, always adopted the most lenient course in their dealings with people. From this is the hadith: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was my partner, and he was the best of partners; he was not stubborn, did not dispute, and did not quarrel." [[Narrated by Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah from the hadith of al-Sa'ib, that he said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "You were my partner, and you were the best partner; you were not stubborn and did not dispute."]] His words ﴿you will find me, if Allah wills, among the righteous﴾ indicate this. By righteousness he means good dealing, gentleness of manner and softness of disposition. [[His words "gentleness of manner and softness of disposition": in al-Sihah (the lexicon of al-Jawhari), "wati'a" (softness) means "gentle, easy." (Ibn Hajar? no; the marginal note reads: (ʿ).)]] It is also possible that he means righteousness in general, which includes good dealing. The purpose of conditioning the will of Allah on the righteousness he promised is reliance on Allah's granting him success in it and His help, not that he would perform righteousness "if Allah wills," and if He wills, He would make him do the opposite.

﴿That﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿between me and you﴾ is its predicate, and it refers to what Shu'ayb covenanted with him. He means: what you said and covenanted with me and stipulated upon me remains established between us both, and neither of us departs from it, neither I from what you stipulated upon me, nor you from what you stipulated upon yourself.

Then he said: ﴿whichever of the two terms I fulfil﴾, that is, the longer of them, which is the ten years, or the shorter, which is the eight years, ﴿there shall be no injustice against me﴾, that is, no one shall transgress against me by seeking more than it. If you ask: the imagining of injustice applies only to one of the two terms, the shorter one, which is the demand for completing the ten years, so what is the meaning of attaching injustice to both of them together? I say: its meaning is that just as, if I were required to add to the ten years, that would certainly be an injustice, so likewise if I were required to add to the eight years. He intended by this to establish the matter of choice (khiyar), that it is firm and fixed, and that the two terms are equal: either this or that, with no difference between them in fulfilment. As for the completion, it is left to my judgement: if I wish, I will do it, and if not, I will not be compelled to it. It was also said: the meaning is "then I am not a transgressor," and this is in negating transgression from himself, like your saying, "there is no sin upon me, and no consequence upon me."

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "whichever of the two terms I have fulfilled." It was also read as "ayyama" with a sukun on the ya', as in the verse:

*I waited for Nasr and the two Simaks, whichever of them*
*its heavy rains pour upon me.* [[By al-Farazdaq. Nasr is the son of Sayyar, king of the two Iraqs. The two Simaks are two stars: al-Simak al-A'zal, which has no star in front of it, and al-Simak al-Ramih, which has stars in front of it. The word "ayyuhuma" originally had a doubled letter, which was made quiescent out of necessity. Then it may be that it is in the accusative as a substitute for what precedes it, and that it governs a deleted element, meaning: "I do not know which of them," and it is a relative pronoun. It is also possible that it is an interrogative, and in that case it is in the nominative as the subject, and the pronoun in it refers to Nasr and the two Simaks, meaning: "I awaited Nasr and the two Simaks, whichever of them its rains pour down upon me from the cloud." "Istahalla" means its pouring became intense. "Mawatir" are clouds, and "ghayth" is rain. In linking Nasr with the two Simaks there is an indication of comparing him to them in goodness, and of the interrogative sense, so it is of the type of "feigning ignorance of one who knows" (tajahul al-arif); and likewise it denies knowledge.]]

It is also reported from Ibn Qutayb: "'udwan" with a kasra. If you ask: what is the difference between the two positions of the extra "ma" in the two readings? I say: in the widely transmitted reading it occurs as an emphasis on the indefiniteness, meaning that "ayyu" is made more general by it; and in the irregular reading it is an emphasis on the decree, as if he said: "whichever of the two terms I have resolved upon fulfilling, and I have set my firm resolve upon it."

"Al-wakil" is the one to whom the matter has been entrusted. When it is used in the place of "witness," "guardian" (muhaymin) and "sustainer" (muqit), it takes "'ala" by virtue of that. [[His words "muhaymin and muqit": that is, the powerful one (al-muqtadir), or the guardian (al-hafiz). (ʿ)]]

It is reported that Shu'ayb had the staff of the prophets with him, and he said to Musa at night: "Enter that room and take a staff from those staffs." So he took a staff that Adam had descended with from Paradise, and the prophets had continued to inherit it until it came into the possession of Shu'ayb. He touched it, and he was blind, and he was reluctant to give it up, saying: "Take another." But nothing came into his hand except it, seven times, so he knew that it had a significance.

It was also said: Gabriel took it after the death of Adam, and it remained with him until he brought it to Musa at night. And it was also said: an angel in the form of a man entrusted it to Shu'ayb, and he commanded his daughter to bring him a staff, and she brought it to him, and he threw it back seven times, and nothing came into her hand except it, so he gave it to him. Then he regretted it, because it was a deposit (wadi'a), and he followed him, and they disputed over it. They agreed that whoever arrived first should judge between them, and the angel came to them and said: "Cast it down; whoever lifts it, it is his." The old man struggled with it and could not manage it, and Musa lifted it.

From al-Hasan: it was nothing but a staff of wood that came in his way by chance. From al-Kalbi: the tree from which he was called was a thorn-bush (shajarat al-'awsaj), and from it was his staff.

When morning came, Shu'ayb said to him: "When you reach the fork in the road, do not take on your right, for although there is more pasture there, in it is a serpent (tinnin) [[His words "a serpent": that is, a large snake (tha'ban). (ʿ)]] I fear for you and for the sheep." So the sheep took the right, and he could not restrain them, so he walked in their tracks, and there was pasture and lush greenery the like of which he had never seen. He slept, and suddenly the serpent came, and the staff fought it until it killed it, and returned to Musa's side, bloodied. When he saw it bloodied and the serpent dead, he was pleased with that. When he returned to Shu'ayb, he touched the sheep and found them full-bellied and abundant in milk, and Musa informed him, and he rejoiced and knew that Musa and the staff had a significance. He said to him: "I have given you of the young of my flock this year every spotted and speckled one."

Then in a dream it was revealed to him: "Strike your staff against the watering-place of the sheep." He did so, and then he watered them, and not one of them missed without bearing spotted and speckled young, and so he fulfilled his condition to him.

﴿...﴾ the water of Madyan, the water from which they drew. It was a well, according to what is narrated. Wurud (arriving) means coming to it and reaching it. ﴿He found upon it a community (ummah) of people﴾, a dense, large group of people of various kinds, ﴿and beside them he found two women driving back﴾, in a place lower than theirs. Al-dhawd means driving away and pushing back. The two women were driving back (their flock) because there were stronger people at the water who would prevent them from watering. It is also said that they disliked crowding at the water. It is also said that they did this so that their sheep would not mix with the sheep of the others. It is also said that they were driving back (the sheep) and screening their faces from a viewer's gaze. ﴿What is your matter (khatbukuma)?﴾ meaning, what is your affair? Its literal sense is "what is your maktub (the thing sought)," i.e., your objective, from al-dhawd. So the sought thing is called khatb, just as the affair (sha'n) is called sha'n in your saying "ma sha'nuka?" It is said: sha'nat sha'nahu, meaning, I aimed at his aim. It has been read as ﴿lā nasqī﴾ (we do not water) and ﴿yuṣdira﴾ (until the shepherds send back). And al-ri'a', with a damma on the nun, the ya' and the ra': al-ri'a' is a collective noun like al-rikhal and al-tha'a'.[[His statement "lā nasqī, yuṣdira, al-ri'ā' with a damma on the nūn, the yā' and the rā'" indicates that the well-known reading is with a fatḥa on the nūn and the yā' and a kasra on the rā'. Al-rikhāl: its singular is rakhl, which is the female of young sheep. Al-tha'ā': the tether of a camel or the like, from a twisted rope, as stated in al-Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿ)]]

As for al-ri'ā' with a kasra, it is analogical, like ṣiyām and qiyām. ﴿An old man﴾, meaning, an elderly man of great age. ﴿So he watered for them﴾, meaning he watered their flock on their behalf. It is narrated that the shepherds used to place upon the mouth of the well a stone which only seven men could lift. It is said: ten. It is said: forty. It is said: a hundred. Yet he lifted it alone. It is narrated that he asked them for a bucket of water, and they gave him their bucket and said: "Draw water with it." It was a bucket that only forty men could draw up. He drew water with it, poured it into the trough, and prayed for blessing, and he gave their flock drink and sent them back. It is narrated that he pushed them away from the water until he had watered for the two women. It is also said there was another well, over which was a stone. He did this out of eagerness for doing good and relieving the distressed. The meaning is: he reached that water when a community of people of differing, dense numbers had crowded around it, and he saw the two weak women behind them with their small flock, waiting for them to finish. His resolve did not fail to seize that opportunity in the religion of God, despite the fatigue he had, the tearing of the sole of his foot, and his hunger. Rather, he showed them mercy and relieved them, and he took care of the watering for them in such a crowd by the strength of his heart and the strength of his arm, and by the excellence God had given him in firmness of nature and solidity of constitution. And in this, together with the intent to relate his story and the strength and power he had been given, and what he did not neglect despite his exhaustion, there is an encouragement to goodness, a seizing of its opportunities, and an impulse to follow the righteous in that and to take up their conduct and ways.

If you ask: why was the object omitted in ﴿yasquna﴾ and ﴿tadhūdāni﴾ and ﴿lā nasqī﴾? I answer: because the purpose is the act, not the object of it. Do you not see that he showed mercy to them only because they were driving back while the others were watering, and he did not show mercy because their flock was of sheep and the others' was of camels, for example? Likewise their saying ﴿lā nasqī ḥattā yuṣdira al-ri'āʾ﴾, where what is intended is the watering, not the watered thing.

If you ask: how did their answer correspond to his question? I answer: he asked them about the reason for their driving back, and they said: the reason for that is that we are two weak women, veiled, unable to compete (musājala) with men or crowd with them, so we must delay watering until they finish. We have no man to do that, and our father is an old man whom age has weakened, so he is not fit to do it. So they presented their excuse for taking on the watering themselves.[[His statement "abalatā ilayhi ʿudhrahumā" is probably a distortion; its original is abdatā, as in the wording of al-Nasafī. (ʿ)]]

If you ask: how was it permissible for the prophet of God, who is Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, to be content for his two daughters to water the livestock? I answer: the matter in itself is not forbidden, and religion does not reject it. As for manliness (murū'ah), people differ in that, and customs vary regarding it. The condition of the Arabs in this differs from that of non-Arabs, and the custom of the people of the desert differs from that of the people of the settled towns, especially when the situation is one of necessity.

﴿Indeed, I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need﴾, whether little or much, lean or fat. Faqīr is followed by lām because it implies the meaning of "one who asks" and "one who seeks." It is said: he mentioned that, though the greenness of the herb showed through his belly from emaciation, he asked God only for a single meal. It may also mean: "I am poor in worldly things, on account of what You have sent down to me of the good of religion, which is salvation from the wrongdoers," because he had been in wealth and prosperity at Pharaoh's court. He said that out of contentment with the noble exchange, joy in it, and gratitude for it.

﴿And the shade was the shade of a sumur tree﴾ and ﴿she came walking to him with modesty﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: modestly, shyly, veiled. It is said: she had drawn her garment about her.

It is narrated that when the two of them returned to their father earlier than the people, their flock came back with full udders. He said to them: "What has hastened you?" They said: "We found a righteous man who had pity on us and watered for us." So he said to one of them: "Go and call him for me." Then Musa followed her, but the wind pressed her garment against her body, and she described him. So he said to her: "Walk behind me and direct me to the way." When he related his story to him, he said: "Do not fear; there is no authority of Pharaoh in our land."

If you ask: how was it permissible for Musa to act on the word of a woman, and to walk with her though she was a stranger? I answer: as for acting on the word of a woman, it is like acting on the word of one (single reporter) in reports, whether free or slave, male or female. She was only reporting about her father that he was calling him to reward him. As for walking with a foreign woman, there is no harm in it in similar circumstances, together with caution and abstinence.

If you ask: how was it valid for him to take a wage for righteousness and kindness? I answer: it is possible that he did that for the sake of God and as a form of righteousness and kindness. It is also said that Shu'ayb's feeding him and his beneficence was not in the manner of taking a wage, but as an accepting of a kindness begun by him. How (could it be otherwise), since he had related his story to him and he had made him know that he was of the house of prophethood, from the descendants of Ya'qub? Such a man deserves to be hosted and honored, especially in the house of a prophet of God's prophets. And it is not objectionable that he should do so out of the necessity of poverty and need, seeking reward.

And there is narrated something that supports both views: it is reported that when she said "that he may reward you," he disliked that. And when the food was set before him, he refused and said: "We are a household that does not sell its religion for the filling of the earth with gold, nor do we take a price for kindness." Until Shu'ayb said: "This is our custom with everyone who comes down upon us."

It is related from ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib: he raised his voice in supplication so that they would hear him. That is why it was said to him: ﴿that he may reward you for what you watered﴾, i.e., the recompense for your watering.

Al-qaṣaṣ (the story) is a verbal noun like al-ʿilal, and the narrated account is named after it.

The elder of the two was called Ṣafrāʾ, and the younger Ṣufayrāʾ. Ṣafrāʾ is the one who went with him and asked her father to hire him, and she is the one he married.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās that Shu'ayb was seized by jealousy and said: "And what do you know of his strength and trustworthiness?" So she mentioned the lifting of the stone and the drawing of the bucket, and that he lowered his head when his message reached him and when her father commanded her to walk behind him.

Her saying ﴿Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong, the trustworthy﴾ is a wise, comprehensive statement to which nothing can be added, because when these two qualities are combined, I mean sufficiency and trustworthiness in the one who manages your affair, your mind is at ease and your goal is achieved. She has been content with sending this saying, whose context is that of a proverb, and the wisdom is that you say: hire him for his strength and his trustworthiness.[[Mahmud said: "This is a wise and comprehensive statement to which nothing can be added, because if strength and trustworthiness are combined in the one who manages your affair, your mind is at rest, and she has been content with sending this saying, whose context is that of a proverb and maxim, rather than saying: 'He is strong and trustworthy.'" Aḥmad said: This is also more beautiful as praise by women of men than specific praise, and more preserving of modesty, especially if she understood that her father's aim, peace be upon him, was to marry her to him. How well the Fārūq (ʿUmar), may God be pleased with him, took this meaning when he said: "I complain to God of the weakness of the trustworthy and the treachery of the strong." In the content of this complaint is a request to God that He grant him one who combines the two qualities, strong and trustworthy, whom he could rely upon in what he was undertaking, may God be pleased with him. And this ambiguity, from the daughter of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, was also taken by Zulaykha with Yusuf, peace be upon him. But how different is natural modesty from acquired modesty: kohl in the eyes is not like the kohl. When she said to her master: ﴿What is the recompense of one who intended evil to your wife, except that he be imprisoned or a painful punishment?﴾, she meant: what is the recompense of Yusuf for having intended evil toward me, except that you imprison him or punish him with a painful punishment? But shame and modesty prevented her husband's mind from her speaking the word of chastity while attributing the indecency to herself, indicating that this modesty in her, which prevented her from speaking this matter, prevented her from soliciting Yusuf by a more fitting and better means. And God knows best.]]

If you ask: how did he make ﴿the best you hire﴾ the subject of ﴿inna﴾ and ﴿the strong, the trustworthy﴾ the predicate? I answer: it is like his saying:

"Surely the best of people, alive and dead, is the captive of Thaqīf among them in chains."[[Surely the best of people, living and dead, is the captive of Thaqīf among them in chains. By my life, if you have made the prison abode of Khalid and made him tread it with the tread of one burdened. He was one who rose up to every calamity, and gave generous gifts, great in bounty, abundant in extra gifts. This is by Abu al-Shaghb al-ʿAbsī, lamenting over Khalid ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī when Yusuf ibn ʿUmar captured him. "The best of people" is an elative in the form of a comparative, annexed to a definite with al, and it is the subject of inna. "Living and dead" (ḥayyan wa-mayyitan), and in one narration "perishing" (hālikan), are two circumstantial clauses from it. "Captive" (asīr) is the predicate of inna, annexed to Thaqīf, the name of the tribe. A proper name is more definite than what is definite by al, so the predicate annexed to the proper noun is more definite than its subject which is annexed to the definite by al, and there is no obstacle to this when both refer to the same thing intended by the speaker. "Among them in chains" is a circumstantial clause or a predicate after a predicate. "By my life" is an oath. "If you have made...": that is, you put Khalid into prison and settled him there. "And made him tread it": that is, you made him tread the ground with his foot like the tread of one burdened with something heavy, meaning you put the shackles on his feet, so this is a metaphor for that. "He was one who rose up..." is the answer to the oath. The answer to the condition is omitted, meaning he was quick to rise to every heavy calamity. "Giver of al-lahā" with a fatḥa is the plural of lahāh, like ḥaṣā and ḥaṣāh, meaning the piece of flesh at the farthest part of the mouth, but here it means the mouth itself. The more likely is that with a ḍamma it is the plural of luhwah, like ghuraf, plural of ghurfah, meaning gift of any kind. "Ghamran" means abundant overflowing gift, and he was one with many additions in giving. He treated "muʿṭī" in the manner of a nominative for the sake of the meter.]] in that care is the cause of the fronting, and she has spoken truly, so that what is more worthy of being the predicate was made a noun. And the verb's coming in the past tense indicates that it is a matter that has been tested and known. From this is their saying: "The least of what you have worked with is the tongue of one who disowns."[[His statement "the least of what you have worked with is the tongue of one who disowns (mamkh)" in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: tamakhkhaytu min al-shayʾ and amkhaytu minhu: when one disowns something. So perhaps mamkh is an active participle from amkhaytu. (ʿ)]]

It is narrated from Ibn Masʿūd, may God be pleased with him: "The shrewdest of people are three: the daughter of Shu'ayb; the companion of Yusuf in his saying ﴿perhaps he will benefit us﴾; and Abu Bakr concerning ʿUmar."

It is narrated that he married him to Ṣafrāʾ.

His saying ﴿these two﴾ (hātayn) is evidence that he had other daughters besides them. ﴿That you hire me﴾ (ta'jurunī) is from ajara, meaning to hire someone out, if you were his hired man, like your saying abawtuhu if you were his father. ﴿Eight years﴾ (thamāniya ḥijaj) is its adverbial object. Or it is from ajartuhu kadhā, when I gave it to him as a wage. From this is the condolence of the Messenger of God, ﷺ: "May God reward you (ajarakum) and have mercy on you."[[It was recorded by Abu Nuʿaym in Taʾrīkh Aṣbahān from the route of Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn Ibrāhīm ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Ibrāhīm ibn al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, from his fathers, Ibrāhīm ibn al-Ḥasan, from Fāṭimah bint al-Ḥusayn, from her father, who said: "When the Messenger of God ﷺ offered condolence he would say: 'Ajarakum Allāh wa-raḥimakum,' and when he congratulated he would say: 'Bārak Allāh lakum wa-bārak ʿalaykum.'" It has a supporting mursal report recorded by Ibn Abī Shaybah from the narration of Ibn Khālid al-Wālibī: that the Prophet ﷺ offered condolence to a man and said to him: "May God have mercy on him and reward you." In al-Ḍuʿafāʾ by Ibn Ḥibbān from Ibn ʿUmar: that the Prophet ﷺ offered condolence to a Muslim for a dhimmi who had died to him, and said: "May God reward you and increase your reward." Its chain includes Ismāʿīl ibn Yaḥyā al-Taymī, who is discarded (sāqiṭ). (ʿ)]] "Eight years" is the object, and its meaning is: the pasturing of eight years.

If you ask: how is it valid that he marries him one of his two daughters without specifying? I answer: that was not a contract of marriage, but a promise and a description of a matter he had resolved upon.[[His statement "but a promise and a description (muwāṣafah) of a matter he had resolved upon" is probably muwāḍaʿah (agreement). (ʿ)]] If it had been a contract, he would have said: "I have married you," and he did not say: "I intend to marry you."

If you ask: how is it valid that he gives as her dowry the hire of his own labor in pasturing sheep, when the delivery of what is property is necessary? Do you not see how Abu Ḥanīfah prohibited a man marrying a woman on condition that he serve her for a year?[[Mahmud said: "It is quoted from Abu Ḥanīfah's school that marriage is forbidden upon his personal service, but permitted upon the service of his slave for a year, and he made a distinction: in the first case he has given himself, which is not property, while in the second he has given his slave, which is property. It is quoted from al-Shāfiʿī that marriage upon known benefits is permitted absolutely." Aḥmad said: The school of Mālik has three positions: prohibition, disapproval, and permissibility. The marvel is Abu Ḥanīfah's permission of marriage upon the benefits of a slave, but not upon the benefits of the husband, while the verse permitted marriage upon the benefits of the husband and did not touch on anything else. This is only to favor the meaning that al-Zamakhsharī pointed to, or on the basis that there is no evidence in the law of those before us, or for other reasons. And God knows best.]] He permitted that he marry her by serving her, his slave, for a year, or by housing her in his house for a year, because in the first case...

Hired himself out, not for property. In the second case, he is hired for property, which is a slave or a house. I say: the matter stands on Abu Hanifa's school as you have mentioned. As for al-Shafi'i, he permitted marriage in exchange for a hire (ijara) for certain works and services, provided that the thing the employer hires or the service rendered is a known matter. Perhaps that was permitted in that earlier law (shari'a).

The dower may be something else. He wanted him to tend his sheep for this period, and he wanted to marry him his daughter. So he mentioned the two desired things and tied the marriage to the tending, meaning: "I will do this if you do that," as a mutual pledge (mu'ahada) and not as a binding contract (mu'aqada). It is also possible that he hired him to tend for eight years at a known sum, paid it to him, and then married his daughter to him for that. His words ﴿on condition that you hire yourself to me for eight years﴾ are an expression of what passed between them. ﴿And if you complete ten years, it is from you﴾: so its completion is from you. Its meaning is: it is from you, not from me. That is, I do not obligate you to it or impose it upon you, but if you do it, it is a favour and a voluntary gift from you; and if not, there is no blame on you. ﴿And I do not want to burden you﴾ by obligating you to complete the longer of the two terms and making it binding.

If you ask: what is the reality of their saying "I burdened him" (shaqqa 'alayhi) and "the matter burdened him" (shadda 'alayhi)? I say: its reality is that when a matter becomes great for you, it is as if it has burdened you, since you are in doubt; you say at one time, "I can bear it," and at another, "I cannot bear it." Or his promise of leniency and easygoing dealing from himself, meaning that he would not burden him in what he hired him for, in tending his sheep, and would not do what the difficult employers do with those they hire, such as quibbling over observing times, strictness in demanding the completion of tasks, and assigning the shepherds labours beyond the limit of the condition. Thus the prophets, peace be upon them, always adopted the most lenient course in their dealings with people. From this is the hadith: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was my partner, and he was the best of partners; he was not stubborn, did not dispute, and did not quarrel." [[Narrated by Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah from the hadith of al-Sa'ib, that he said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "You were my partner, and you were the best partner; you were not stubborn and did not dispute."]] His words ﴿you will find me, if Allah wills, among the righteous﴾ indicate this. By righteousness he means good dealing, gentleness of manner and softness of disposition. [[His words "gentleness of manner and softness of disposition": in al-Sihah (the lexicon of al-Jawhari), "wati'a" (softness) means "gentle, easy." (Ibn Hajar? no; the marginal note reads: (ʿ).)]] It is also possible that he means righteousness in general, which includes good dealing. The purpose of conditioning the will of Allah on the righteousness he promised is reliance on Allah's granting him success in it and His help, not that he would perform righteousness "if Allah wills," and if He wills, He would make him do the opposite.

﴿That﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿between me and you﴾ is its predicate, and it refers to what Shu'ayb covenanted with him. He means: what you said and covenanted with me and stipulated upon me remains established between us both, and neither of us departs from it, neither I from what you stipulated upon me, nor you from what you stipulated upon yourself.

Then he said: ﴿whichever of the two terms I fulfil﴾, that is, the longer of them, which is the ten years, or the shorter, which is the eight years, ﴿there shall be no injustice against me﴾, that is, no one shall transgress against me by seeking more than it. If you ask: the imagining of injustice applies only to one of the two terms, the shorter one, which is the demand for completing the ten years, so what is the meaning of attaching injustice to both of them together? I say: its meaning is that just as, if I were required to add to the ten years, that would certainly be an injustice, so likewise if I were required to add to the eight years. He intended by this to establish the matter of choice (khiyar), that it is firm and fixed, and that the two terms are equal: either this or that, with no difference between them in fulfilment. As for the completion, it is left to my judgement: if I wish, I will do it, and if not, I will not be compelled to it. It was also said: the meaning is "then I am not a transgressor," and this is in negating transgression from himself, like your saying, "there is no sin upon me, and no consequence upon me."

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "whichever of the two terms I have fulfilled." It was also read as "ayyama" with a sukun on the ya', as in the verse:

*I waited for Nasr and the two Simaks, whichever of them*
*its heavy rains pour upon me.* [[By al-Farazdaq. Nasr is the son of Sayyar, king of the two Iraqs. The two Simaks are two stars: al-Simak al-A'zal, which has no star in front of it, and al-Simak al-Ramih, which has stars in front of it. The word "ayyuhuma" originally had a doubled letter, which was made quiescent out of necessity. Then it may be that it is in the accusative as a substitute for what precedes it, and that it governs a deleted element, meaning: "I do not know which of them," and it is a relative pronoun. It is also possible that it is an interrogative, and in that case it is in the nominative as the subject, and the pronoun in it refers to Nasr and the two Simaks, meaning: "I awaited Nasr and the two Simaks, whichever of them its rains pour down upon me from the cloud." "Istahalla" means its pouring became intense. "Mawatir" are clouds, and "ghayth" is rain. In linking Nasr with the two Simaks there is an indication of comparing him to them in goodness, and of the interrogative sense, so it is of the type of "feigning ignorance of one who knows" (tajahul al-arif); and likewise it denies knowledge.]]

It is also reported from Ibn Qutayb: "'udwan" with a kasra. If you ask: what is the difference between the two positions of the extra "ma" in the two readings? I say: in the widely transmitted reading it occurs as an emphasis on the indefiniteness, meaning that "ayyu" is made more general by it; and in the irregular reading it is an emphasis on the decree, as if he said: "whichever of the two terms I have resolved upon fulfilling, and I have set my firm resolve upon it."

"Al-wakil" is the one to whom the matter has been entrusted. When it is used in the place of "witness," "guardian" (muhaymin) and "sustainer" (muqit), it takes "'ala" by virtue of that. [[His words "muhaymin and muqit": that is, the powerful one (al-muqtadir), or the guardian (al-hafiz). (ʿ)]]

It is reported that Shu'ayb had the staff of the prophets with him, and he said to Musa at night: "Enter that room and take a staff from those staffs." So he took a staff that Adam had descended with from Paradise, and the prophets had continued to inherit it until it came into the possession of Shu'ayb. He touched it, and he was blind, and he was reluctant to give it up, saying: "Take another." But nothing came into his hand except it, seven times, so he knew that it had a significance.

It was also said: Gabriel took it after the death of Adam, and it remained with him until he brought it to Musa at night. And it was also said: an angel in the form of a man entrusted it to Shu'ayb, and he commanded his daughter to bring him a staff, and she brought it to him, and he threw it back seven times, and nothing came into her hand except it, so he gave it to him. Then he regretted it, because it was a deposit (wadi'a), and he followed him, and they disputed over it. They agreed that whoever arrived first should judge between them, and the angel came to them and said: "Cast it down; whoever lifts it, it is his." The old man struggled with it and could not manage it, and Musa lifted it.

From al-Hasan: it was nothing but a staff of wood that came in his way by chance. From al-Kalbi: the tree from which he was called was a thorn-bush (shajarat al-'awsaj), and from it was his staff.

When morning came, Shu'ayb said to him: "When you reach the fork in the road, do not take on your right, for although there is more pasture there, in it is a serpent (tinnin) [[His words "a serpent": that is, a large snake (tha'ban). (ʿ)]] I fear for you and for the sheep." So the sheep took the right, and he could not restrain them, so he walked in their tracks, and there was pasture and lush greenery the like of which he had never seen. He slept, and suddenly the serpent came, and the staff fought it until it killed it, and returned to Musa's side, bloodied. When he saw it bloodied and the serpent dead, he was pleased with that. When he returned to Shu'ayb, he touched the sheep and found them full-bellied and abundant in milk, and Musa informed him, and he rejoiced and knew that Musa and the staff had a significance. He said to him: "I have given you of the young of my flock this year every spotted and speckled one."

Then in a dream it was revealed to him: "Strike your staff against the watering-place of the sheep." He did so, and then he watered them, and not one of them missed without bearing spotted and speckled young, and so he fulfilled his condition to him.

﴿...﴾ the water of Madyan, the water from which they drew. It was a well, according to what is narrated. Wurud (arriving) means coming to it and reaching it. ﴿He found upon it a community (ummah) of people﴾, a dense, large group of people of various kinds, ﴿and beside them he found two women driving back﴾, in a place lower than theirs. Al-dhawd means driving away and pushing back. The two women were driving back (their flock) because there were stronger people at the water who would prevent them from watering. It is also said that they disliked crowding at the water. It is also said that they did this so that their sheep would not mix with the sheep of the others. It is also said that they were driving back (the sheep) and screening their faces from a viewer's gaze. ﴿What is your matter (khatbukuma)?﴾ meaning, what is your affair? Its literal sense is "what is your maktub (the thing sought)," i.e., your objective, from al-dhawd. So the sought thing is called khatb, just as the affair (sha'n) is called sha'n in your saying "ma sha'nuka?" It is said: sha'nat sha'nahu, meaning, I aimed at his aim. It has been read as ﴿lā nasqī﴾ (we do not water) and ﴿yuṣdira﴾ (until the shepherds send back). And al-ri'a', with a damma on the nun, the ya' and the ra': al-ri'a' is a collective noun like al-rikhal and al-tha'a'.[[His statement "lā nasqī, yuṣdira, al-ri'ā' with a damma on the nūn, the yā' and the rā'" indicates that the well-known reading is with a fatḥa on the nūn and the yā' and a kasra on the rā'. Al-rikhāl: its singular is rakhl, which is the female of young sheep. Al-tha'ā': the tether of a camel or the like, from a twisted rope, as stated in al-Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿ)]]

As for al-ri'ā' with a kasra, it is analogical, like ṣiyām and qiyām. ﴿An old man﴾, meaning, an elderly man of great age. ﴿So he watered for them﴾, meaning he watered their flock on their behalf. It is narrated that the shepherds used to place upon the mouth of the well a stone which only seven men could lift. It is said: ten. It is said: forty. It is said: a hundred. Yet he lifted it alone. It is narrated that he asked them for a bucket of water, and they gave him their bucket and said: "Draw water with it." It was a bucket that only forty men could draw up. He drew water with it, poured it into the trough, and prayed for blessing, and he gave their flock drink and sent them back. It is narrated that he pushed them away from the water until he had watered for the two women. It is also said there was another well, over which was a stone. He did this out of eagerness for doing good and relieving the distressed. The meaning is: he reached that water when a community of people of differing, dense numbers had crowded around it, and he saw the two weak women behind them with their small flock, waiting for them to finish. His resolve did not fail to seize that opportunity in the religion of God, despite the fatigue he had, the tearing of the sole of his foot, and his hunger. Rather, he showed them mercy and relieved them, and he took care of the watering for them in such a crowd by the strength of his heart and the strength of his arm, and by the excellence God had given him in firmness of nature and solidity of constitution. And in this, together with the intent to relate his story and the strength and power he had been given, and what he did not neglect despite his exhaustion, there is an encouragement to goodness, a seizing of its opportunities, and an impulse to follow the righteous in that and to take up their conduct and ways.

If you ask: why was the object omitted in ﴿yasquna﴾ and ﴿tadhūdāni﴾ and ﴿lā nasqī﴾? I answer: because the purpose is the act, not the object of it. Do you not see that he showed mercy to them only because they were driving back while the others were watering, and he did not show mercy because their flock was of sheep and the others' was of camels, for example? Likewise their saying ﴿lā nasqī ḥattā yuṣdira al-ri'āʾ﴾, where what is intended is the watering, not the watered thing.

If you ask: how did their answer correspond to his question? I answer: he asked them about the reason for their driving back, and they said: the reason for that is that we are two weak women, veiled, unable to compete (musājala) with men or crowd with them, so we must delay watering until they finish. We have no man to do that, and our father is an old man whom age has weakened, so he is not fit to do it. So they presented their excuse for taking on the watering themselves.[[His statement "abalatā ilayhi ʿudhrahumā" is probably a distortion; its original is abdatā, as in the wording of al-Nasafī. (ʿ)]]

If you ask: how was it permissible for the prophet of God, who is Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, to be content for his two daughters to water the livestock? I answer: the matter in itself is not forbidden, and religion does not reject it. As for manliness (murū'ah), people differ in that, and customs vary regarding it. The condition of the Arabs in this differs from that of non-Arabs, and the custom of the people of the desert differs from that of the people of the settled towns, especially when the situation is one of necessity.

﴿Indeed, I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need﴾, whether little or much, lean or fat. Faqīr is followed by lām because it implies the meaning of "one who asks" and "one who seeks." It is said: he mentioned that, though the greenness of the herb showed through his belly from emaciation, he asked God only for a single meal. It may also mean: "I am poor in worldly things, on account of what You have sent down to me of the good of religion, which is salvation from the wrongdoers," because he had been in wealth and prosperity at Pharaoh's court. He said that out of contentment with the noble exchange, joy in it, and gratitude for it.

﴿And the shade was the shade of a sumur tree﴾ and ﴿she came walking to him with modesty﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: modestly, shyly, veiled. It is said: she had drawn her garment about her.

It is narrated that when the two of them returned to their father earlier than the people, their flock came back with full udders. He said to them: "What has hastened you?" They said: "We found a righteous man who had pity on us and watered for us." So he said to one of them: "Go and call him for me." Then Musa followed her, but the wind pressed her garment against her body, and she described him. So he said to her: "Walk behind me and direct me to the way." When he related his story to him, he said: "Do not fear; there is no authority of Pharaoh in our land."

If you ask: how was it permissible for Musa to act on the word of a woman, and to walk with her though she was a stranger? I answer: as for acting on the word of a woman, it is like acting on the word of one (single reporter) in reports, whether free or slave, male or female. She was only reporting about her father that he was calling him to reward him. As for walking with a foreign woman, there is no harm in it in similar circumstances, together with caution and abstinence.

If you ask: how was it valid for him to take a wage for righteousness and kindness? I answer: it is possible that he did that for the sake of God and as a form of righteousness and kindness. It is also said that Shu'ayb's feeding him and his beneficence was not in the manner of taking a wage, but as an accepting of a kindness begun by him. How (could it be otherwise), since he had related his story to him and he had made him know that he was of the house of prophethood, from the descendants of Ya'qub? Such a man deserves to be hosted and honored, especially in the house of a prophet of God's prophets. And it is not objectionable that he should do so out of the necessity of poverty and need, seeking reward.

And there is narrated something that supports both views: it is reported that when she said "that he may reward you," he disliked that. And when the food was set before him, he refused and said: "We are a household that does not sell its religion for the filling of the earth with gold, nor do we take a price for kindness." Until Shu'ayb said: "This is our custom with everyone who comes down upon us."

It is related from ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib: he raised his voice in supplication so that they would hear him. That is why it was said to him: ﴿that he may reward you for what you watered﴾, i.e., the recompense for your watering.

Al-qaṣaṣ (the story) is a verbal noun like al-ʿilal, and the narrated account is named after it.

The elder of the two was called Ṣafrāʾ, and the younger Ṣufayrāʾ. Ṣafrāʾ is the one who went with him and asked her father to hire him, and she is the one he married.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās that Shu'ayb was seized by jealousy and said: "And what do you know of his strength and trustworthiness?" So she mentioned the lifting of the stone and the drawing of the bucket, and that he lowered his head when his message reached him and when her father commanded her to walk behind him.

Her saying ﴿Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong, the trustworthy﴾ is a wise, comprehensive statement to which nothing can be added, because when these two qualities are combined, I mean sufficiency and trustworthiness in the one who manages your affair, your mind is at ease and your goal is achieved. She has been content with sending this saying, whose context is that of a proverb, and the wisdom is that you say: hire him for his strength and his trustworthiness.[[Mahmud said: "This is a wise and comprehensive statement to which nothing can be added, because if strength and trustworthiness are combined in the one who manages your affair, your mind is at rest, and she has been content with sending this saying, whose context is that of a proverb and maxim, rather than saying: 'He is strong and trustworthy.'" Aḥmad said: This is also more beautiful as praise by women of men than specific praise, and more preserving of modesty, especially if she understood that her father's aim, peace be upon him, was to marry her to him. How well the Fārūq (ʿUmar), may God be pleased with him, took this meaning when he said: "I complain to God of the weakness of the trustworthy and the treachery of the strong." In the content of this complaint is a request to God that He grant him one who combines the two qualities, strong and trustworthy, whom he could rely upon in what he was undertaking, may God be pleased with him. And this ambiguity, from the daughter of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, was also taken by Zulaykha with Yusuf, peace be upon him. But how different is natural modesty from acquired modesty: kohl in the eyes is not like the kohl. When she said to her master: ﴿What is the recompense of one who intended evil to your wife, except that he be imprisoned or a painful punishment?﴾, she meant: what is the recompense of Yusuf for having intended evil toward me, except that you imprison him or punish him with a painful punishment? But shame and modesty prevented her husband's mind from her speaking the word of chastity while attributing the indecency to herself, indicating that this modesty in her, which prevented her from speaking this matter, prevented her from soliciting Yusuf by a more fitting and better means. And God knows best.]]

If you ask: how did he make ﴿the best you hire﴾ the subject of ﴿inna﴾ and ﴿the strong, the trustworthy﴾ the predicate? I answer: it is like his saying:

"Surely the best of people, alive and dead, is the captive of Thaqīf among them in chains."[[Surely the best of people, living and dead, is the captive of Thaqīf among them in chains. By my life, if you have made the prison abode of Khalid and made him tread it with the tread of one burdened. He was one who rose up to every calamity, and gave generous gifts, great in bounty, abundant in extra gifts. This is by Abu al-Shaghb al-ʿAbsī, lamenting over Khalid ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī when Yusuf ibn ʿUmar captured him. "The best of people" is an elative in the form of a comparative, annexed to a definite with al, and it is the subject of inna. "Living and dead" (ḥayyan wa-mayyitan), and in one narration "perishing" (hālikan), are two circumstantial clauses from it. "Captive" (asīr) is the predicate of inna, annexed to Thaqīf, the name of the tribe. A proper name is more definite than what is definite by al, so the predicate annexed to the proper noun is more definite than its subject which is annexed to the definite by al, and there is no obstacle to this when both refer to the same thing intended by the speaker. "Among them in chains" is a circumstantial clause or a predicate after a predicate. "By my life" is an oath. "If you have made...": that is, you put Khalid into prison and settled him there. "And made him tread it": that is, you made him tread the ground with his foot like the tread of one burdened with something heavy, meaning you put the shackles on his feet, so this is a metaphor for that. "He was one who rose up..." is the answer to the oath. The answer to the condition is omitted, meaning he was quick to rise to every heavy calamity. "Giver of al-lahā" with a fatḥa is the plural of lahāh, like ḥaṣā and ḥaṣāh, meaning the piece of flesh at the farthest part of the mouth, but here it means the mouth itself. The more likely is that with a ḍamma it is the plural of luhwah, like ghuraf, plural of ghurfah, meaning gift of any kind. "Ghamran" means abundant overflowing gift, and he was one with many additions in giving. He treated "muʿṭī" in the manner of a nominative for the sake of the meter.]] in that care is the cause of the fronting, and she has spoken truly, so that what is more worthy of being the predicate was made a noun. And the verb's coming in the past tense indicates that it is a matter that has been tested and known. From this is their saying: "The least of what you have worked with is the tongue of one who disowns."[[His statement "the least of what you have worked with is the tongue of one who disowns (mamkh)" in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: tamakhkhaytu min al-shayʾ and amkhaytu minhu: when one disowns something. So perhaps mamkh is an active participle from amkhaytu. (ʿ)]]

It is narrated from Ibn Masʿūd, may God be pleased with him: "The shrewdest of people are three: the daughter of Shu'ayb; the companion of Yusuf in his saying ﴿perhaps he will benefit us﴾; and Abu Bakr concerning ʿUmar."

It is narrated that he married him to Ṣafrāʾ.

His saying ﴿these two﴾ (hātayn) is evidence that he had other daughters besides them. ﴿That you hire me﴾ (ta'jurunī) is from ajara, meaning to hire someone out, if you were his hired man, like your saying abawtuhu if you were his father. ﴿Eight years﴾ (thamāniya ḥijaj) is its adverbial object. Or it is from ajartuhu kadhā, when I gave it to him as a wage. From this is the condolence of the Messenger of God, ﷺ: "May God reward you (ajarakum) and have mercy on you."[[It was recorded by Abu Nuʿaym in Taʾrīkh Aṣbahān from the route of Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn Ibrāhīm ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Ibrāhīm ibn al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, from his fathers, Ibrāhīm ibn al-Ḥasan, from Fāṭimah bint al-Ḥusayn, from her father, who said: "When the Messenger of God ﷺ offered condolence he would say: 'Ajarakum Allāh wa-raḥimakum,' and when he congratulated he would say: 'Bārak Allāh lakum wa-bārak ʿalaykum.'" It has a supporting mursal report recorded by Ibn Abī Shaybah from the narration of Ibn Khālid al-Wālibī: that the Prophet ﷺ offered condolence to a man and said to him: "May God have mercy on him and reward you." In al-Ḍuʿafāʾ by Ibn Ḥibbān from Ibn ʿUmar: that the Prophet ﷺ offered condolence to a Muslim for a dhimmi who had died to him, and said: "May God reward you and increase your reward." Its chain includes Ismāʿīl ibn Yaḥyā al-Taymī, who is discarded (sāqiṭ). (ʿ)]] "Eight years" is the object, and its meaning is: the pasturing of eight years.

If you ask: how is it valid that he marries him one of his two daughters without specifying? I answer: that was not a contract of marriage, but a promise and a description of a matter he had resolved upon.[[His statement "but a promise and a description (muwāṣafah) of a matter he had resolved upon" is probably muwāḍaʿah (agreement). (ʿ)]] If it had been a contract, he would have said: "I have married you," and he did not say: "I intend to marry you."

If you ask: how is it valid that he gives as her dowry the hire of his own labor in pasturing sheep, when the delivery of what is property is necessary? Do you not see how Abu Ḥanīfah prohibited a man marrying a woman on condition that he serve her for a year?[[Mahmud said: "It is quoted from Abu Ḥanīfah's school that marriage is forbidden upon his personal service, but permitted upon the service of his slave for a year, and he made a distinction: in the first case he has given himself, which is not property, while in the second he has given his slave, which is property. It is quoted from al-Shāfiʿī that marriage upon known benefits is permitted absolutely." Aḥmad said: The school of Mālik has three positions: prohibition, disapproval, and permissibility. The marvel is Abu Ḥanīfah's permission of marriage upon the benefits of a slave, but not upon the benefits of the husband, while the verse permitted marriage upon the benefits of the husband and did not touch on anything else. This is only to favor the meaning that al-Zamakhsharī pointed to, or on the basis that there is no evidence in the law of those before us, or for other reasons. And God knows best.]] He permitted that he marry her by serving her, his slave, for a year, or by housing her in his house for a year, because in the first case...
