Hired himself out, not for property. In the second case, he is hired for property, which is a slave or a house. I say: the matter stands on Abu Hanifa's school as you have mentioned. As for al-Shafi'i, he permitted marriage in exchange for a hire (ijara) for certain works and services, provided that the thing the employer hires or the service rendered is a known matter. Perhaps that was permitted in that earlier law (shari'a).

The dower may be something else. He wanted him to tend his sheep for this period, and he wanted to marry him his daughter. So he mentioned the two desired things and tied the marriage to the tending, meaning: "I will do this if you do that," as a mutual pledge (mu'ahada) and not as a binding contract (mu'aqada). It is also possible that he hired him to tend for eight years at a known sum, paid it to him, and then married his daughter to him for that. His words ﴿on condition that you hire yourself to me for eight years﴾ are an expression of what passed between them. ﴿And if you complete ten years, it is from you﴾: so its completion is from you. Its meaning is: it is from you, not from me. That is, I do not obligate you to it or impose it upon you, but if you do it, it is a favour and a voluntary gift from you; and if not, there is no blame on you. ﴿And I do not want to burden you﴾ by obligating you to complete the longer of the two terms and making it binding.

If you ask: what is the reality of their saying "I burdened him" (shaqqa 'alayhi) and "the matter burdened him" (shadda 'alayhi)? I say: its reality is that when a matter becomes great for you, it is as if it has burdened you, since you are in doubt; you say at one time, "I can bear it," and at another, "I cannot bear it." Or his promise of leniency and easygoing dealing from himself, meaning that he would not burden him in what he hired him for, in tending his sheep, and would not do what the difficult employers do with those they hire, such as quibbling over observing times, strictness in demanding the completion of tasks, and assigning the shepherds labours beyond the limit of the condition. Thus the prophets, peace be upon them, always adopted the most lenient course in their dealings with people. From this is the hadith: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was my partner, and he was the best of partners; he was not stubborn, did not dispute, and did not quarrel." [[Narrated by Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah from the hadith of al-Sa'ib, that he said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "You were my partner, and you were the best partner; you were not stubborn and did not dispute."]] His words ﴿you will find me, if Allah wills, among the righteous﴾ indicate this. By righteousness he means good dealing, gentleness of manner and softness of disposition. [[His words "gentleness of manner and softness of disposition": in al-Sihah (the lexicon of al-Jawhari), "wati'a" (softness) means "gentle, easy." (Ibn Hajar? no; the marginal note reads: (ʿ).)]] It is also possible that he means righteousness in general, which includes good dealing. The purpose of conditioning the will of Allah on the righteousness he promised is reliance on Allah's granting him success in it and His help, not that he would perform righteousness "if Allah wills," and if He wills, He would make him do the opposite.

﴿That﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿between me and you﴾ is its predicate, and it refers to what Shu'ayb covenanted with him. He means: what you said and covenanted with me and stipulated upon me remains established between us both, and neither of us departs from it, neither I from what you stipulated upon me, nor you from what you stipulated upon yourself.

Then he said: ﴿whichever of the two terms I fulfil﴾, that is, the longer of them, which is the ten years, or the shorter, which is the eight years, ﴿there shall be no injustice against me﴾, that is, no one shall transgress against me by seeking more than it. If you ask: the imagining of injustice applies only to one of the two terms, the shorter one, which is the demand for completing the ten years, so what is the meaning of attaching injustice to both of them together? I say: its meaning is that just as, if I were required to add to the ten years, that would certainly be an injustice, so likewise if I were required to add to the eight years. He intended by this to establish the matter of choice (khiyar), that it is firm and fixed, and that the two terms are equal: either this or that, with no difference between them in fulfilment. As for the completion, it is left to my judgement: if I wish, I will do it, and if not, I will not be compelled to it. It was also said: the meaning is "then I am not a transgressor," and this is in negating transgression from himself, like your saying, "there is no sin upon me, and no consequence upon me."

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "whichever of the two terms I have fulfilled." It was also read as "ayyama" with a sukun on the ya', as in the verse:

*I waited for Nasr and the two Simaks, whichever of them*
*its heavy rains pour upon me.* [[By al-Farazdaq. Nasr is the son of Sayyar, king of the two Iraqs. The two Simaks are two stars: al-Simak al-A'zal, which has no star in front of it, and al-Simak al-Ramih, which has stars in front of it. The word "ayyuhuma" originally had a doubled letter, which was made quiescent out of necessity. Then it may be that it is in the accusative as a substitute for what precedes it, and that it governs a deleted element, meaning: "I do not know which of them," and it is a relative pronoun. It is also possible that it is an interrogative, and in that case it is in the nominative as the subject, and the pronoun in it refers to Nasr and the two Simaks, meaning: "I awaited Nasr and the two Simaks, whichever of them its rains pour down upon me from the cloud." "Istahalla" means its pouring became intense. "Mawatir" are clouds, and "ghayth" is rain. In linking Nasr with the two Simaks there is an indication of comparing him to them in goodness, and of the interrogative sense, so it is of the type of "feigning ignorance of one who knows" (tajahul al-arif); and likewise it denies knowledge.]]

It is also reported from Ibn Qutayb: "'udwan" with a kasra. If you ask: what is the difference between the two positions of the extra "ma" in the two readings? I say: in the widely transmitted reading it occurs as an emphasis on the indefiniteness, meaning that "ayyu" is made more general by it; and in the irregular reading it is an emphasis on the decree, as if he said: "whichever of the two terms I have resolved upon fulfilling, and I have set my firm resolve upon it."

"Al-wakil" is the one to whom the matter has been entrusted. When it is used in the place of "witness," "guardian" (muhaymin) and "sustainer" (muqit), it takes "'ala" by virtue of that. [[His words "muhaymin and muqit": that is, the powerful one (al-muqtadir), or the guardian (al-hafiz). (ʿ)]]

It is reported that Shu'ayb had the staff of the prophets with him, and he said to Musa at night: "Enter that room and take a staff from those staffs." So he took a staff that Adam had descended with from Paradise, and the prophets had continued to inherit it until it came into the possession of Shu'ayb. He touched it, and he was blind, and he was reluctant to give it up, saying: "Take another." But nothing came into his hand except it, seven times, so he knew that it had a significance.

It was also said: Gabriel took it after the death of Adam, and it remained with him until he brought it to Musa at night. And it was also said: an angel in the form of a man entrusted it to Shu'ayb, and he commanded his daughter to bring him a staff, and she brought it to him, and he threw it back seven times, and nothing came into her hand except it, so he gave it to him. Then he regretted it, because it was a deposit (wadi'a), and he followed him, and they disputed over it. They agreed that whoever arrived first should judge between them, and the angel came to them and said: "Cast it down; whoever lifts it, it is his." The old man struggled with it and could not manage it, and Musa lifted it.

From al-Hasan: it was nothing but a staff of wood that came in his way by chance. From al-Kalbi: the tree from which he was called was a thorn-bush (shajarat al-'awsaj), and from it was his staff.

When morning came, Shu'ayb said to him: "When you reach the fork in the road, do not take on your right, for although there is more pasture there, in it is a serpent (tinnin) [[His words "a serpent": that is, a large snake (tha'ban). (ʿ)]] I fear for you and for the sheep." So the sheep took the right, and he could not restrain them, so he walked in their tracks, and there was pasture and lush greenery the like of which he had never seen. He slept, and suddenly the serpent came, and the staff fought it until it killed it, and returned to Musa's side, bloodied. When he saw it bloodied and the serpent dead, he was pleased with that. When he returned to Shu'ayb, he touched the sheep and found them full-bellied and abundant in milk, and Musa informed him, and he rejoiced and knew that Musa and the staff had a significance. He said to him: "I have given you of the young of my flock this year every spotted and speckled one."

Then in a dream it was revealed to him: "Strike your staff against the watering-place of the sheep." He did so, and then he watered them, and not one of them missed without bearing spotted and speckled young, and so he fulfilled his condition to him.

﴿...﴾ the water of Madyan, the water from which they drew. It was a well, according to what is narrated. Wurud (arriving) means coming to it and reaching it. ﴿He found upon it a community (ummah) of people﴾, a dense, large group of people of various kinds, ﴿and beside them he found two women driving back﴾, in a place lower than theirs. Al-dhawd means driving away and pushing back. The two women were driving back (their flock) because there were stronger people at the water who would prevent them from watering. It is also said that they disliked crowding at the water. It is also said that they did this so that their sheep would not mix with the sheep of the others. It is also said that they were driving back (the sheep) and screening their faces from a viewer's gaze. ﴿What is your matter (khatbukuma)?﴾ meaning, what is your affair? Its literal sense is "what is your maktub (the thing sought)," i.e., your objective, from al-dhawd. So the sought thing is called khatb, just as the affair (sha'n) is called sha'n in your saying "ma sha'nuka?" It is said: sha'nat sha'nahu, meaning, I aimed at his aim. It has been read as ﴿lā nasqī﴾ (we do not water) and ﴿yuṣdira﴾ (until the shepherds send back). And al-ri'a', with a damma on the nun, the ya' and the ra': al-ri'a' is a collective noun like al-rikhal and al-tha'a'.[[His statement "lā nasqī, yuṣdira, al-ri'ā' with a damma on the nūn, the yā' and the rā'" indicates that the well-known reading is with a fatḥa on the nūn and the yā' and a kasra on the rā'. Al-rikhāl: its singular is rakhl, which is the female of young sheep. Al-tha'ā': the tether of a camel or the like, from a twisted rope, as stated in al-Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿ)]]

As for al-ri'ā' with a kasra, it is analogical, like ṣiyām and qiyām. ﴿An old man﴾, meaning, an elderly man of great age. ﴿So he watered for them﴾, meaning he watered their flock on their behalf. It is narrated that the shepherds used to place upon the mouth of the well a stone which only seven men could lift. It is said: ten. It is said: forty. It is said: a hundred. Yet he lifted it alone. It is narrated that he asked them for a bucket of water, and they gave him their bucket and said: "Draw water with it." It was a bucket that only forty men could draw up. He drew water with it, poured it into the trough, and prayed for blessing, and he gave their flock drink and sent them back. It is narrated that he pushed them away from the water until he had watered for the two women. It is also said there was another well, over which was a stone. He did this out of eagerness for doing good and relieving the distressed. The meaning is: he reached that water when a community of people of differing, dense numbers had crowded around it, and he saw the two weak women behind them with their small flock, waiting for them to finish. His resolve did not fail to seize that opportunity in the religion of God, despite the fatigue he had, the tearing of the sole of his foot, and his hunger. Rather, he showed them mercy and relieved them, and he took care of the watering for them in such a crowd by the strength of his heart and the strength of his arm, and by the excellence God had given him in firmness of nature and solidity of constitution. And in this, together with the intent to relate his story and the strength and power he had been given, and what he did not neglect despite his exhaustion, there is an encouragement to goodness, a seizing of its opportunities, and an impulse to follow the righteous in that and to take up their conduct and ways.

If you ask: why was the object omitted in ﴿yasquna﴾ and ﴿tadhūdāni﴾ and ﴿lā nasqī﴾? I answer: because the purpose is the act, not the object of it. Do you not see that he showed mercy to them only because they were driving back while the others were watering, and he did not show mercy because their flock was of sheep and the others' was of camels, for example? Likewise their saying ﴿lā nasqī ḥattā yuṣdira al-ri'āʾ﴾, where what is intended is the watering, not the watered thing.

If you ask: how did their answer correspond to his question? I answer: he asked them about the reason for their driving back, and they said: the reason for that is that we are two weak women, veiled, unable to compete (musājala) with men or crowd with them, so we must delay watering until they finish. We have no man to do that, and our father is an old man whom age has weakened, so he is not fit to do it. So they presented their excuse for taking on the watering themselves.[[His statement "abalatā ilayhi ʿudhrahumā" is probably a distortion; its original is abdatā, as in the wording of al-Nasafī. (ʿ)]]

If you ask: how was it permissible for the prophet of God, who is Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, to be content for his two daughters to water the livestock? I answer: the matter in itself is not forbidden, and religion does not reject it. As for manliness (murū'ah), people differ in that, and customs vary regarding it. The condition of the Arabs in this differs from that of non-Arabs, and the custom of the people of the desert differs from that of the people of the settled towns, especially when the situation is one of necessity.

﴿Indeed, I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need﴾, whether little or much, lean or fat. Faqīr is followed by lām because it implies the meaning of "one who asks" and "one who seeks." It is said: he mentioned that, though the greenness of the herb showed through his belly from emaciation, he asked God only for a single meal. It may also mean: "I am poor in worldly things, on account of what You have sent down to me of the good of religion, which is salvation from the wrongdoers," because he had been in wealth and prosperity at Pharaoh's court. He said that out of contentment with the noble exchange, joy in it, and gratitude for it.

﴿And the shade was the shade of a sumur tree﴾ and ﴿she came walking to him with modesty﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: modestly, shyly, veiled. It is said: she had drawn her garment about her.

It is narrated that when the two of them returned to their father earlier than the people, their flock came back with full udders. He said to them: "What has hastened you?" They said: "We found a righteous man who had pity on us and watered for us." So he said to one of them: "Go and call him for me." Then Musa followed her, but the wind pressed her garment against her body, and she described him. So he said to her: "Walk behind me and direct me to the way." When he related his story to him, he said: "Do not fear; there is no authority of Pharaoh in our land."

If you ask: how was it permissible for Musa to act on the word of a woman, and to walk with her though she was a stranger? I answer: as for acting on the word of a woman, it is like acting on the word of one (single reporter) in reports, whether free or slave, male or female. She was only reporting about her father that he was calling him to reward him. As for walking with a foreign woman, there is no harm in it in similar circumstances, together with caution and abstinence.

If you ask: how was it valid for him to take a wage for righteousness and kindness? I answer: it is possible that he did that for the sake of God and as a form of righteousness and kindness. It is also said that Shu'ayb's feeding him and his beneficence was not in the manner of taking a wage, but as an accepting of a kindness begun by him. How (could it be otherwise), since he had related his story to him and he had made him know that he was of the house of prophethood, from the descendants of Ya'qub? Such a man deserves to be hosted and honored, especially in the house of a prophet of God's prophets. And it is not objectionable that he should do so out of the necessity of poverty and need, seeking reward.

And there is narrated something that supports both views: it is reported that when she said "that he may reward you," he disliked that. And when the food was set before him, he refused and said: "We are a household that does not sell its religion for the filling of the earth with gold, nor do we take a price for kindness." Until Shu'ayb said: "This is our custom with everyone who comes down upon us."

It is related from ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib: he raised his voice in supplication so that they would hear him. That is why it was said to him: ﴿that he may reward you for what you watered﴾, i.e., the recompense for your watering.

Al-qaṣaṣ (the story) is a verbal noun like al-ʿilal, and the narrated account is named after it.

The elder of the two was called Ṣafrāʾ, and the younger Ṣufayrāʾ. Ṣafrāʾ is the one who went with him and asked her father to hire him, and she is the one he married.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās that Shu'ayb was seized by jealousy and said: "And what do you know of his strength and trustworthiness?" So she mentioned the lifting of the stone and the drawing of the bucket, and that he lowered his head when his message reached him and when her father commanded her to walk behind him.

Her saying ﴿Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong, the trustworthy﴾ is a wise, comprehensive statement to which nothing can be added, because when these two qualities are combined, I mean sufficiency and trustworthiness in the one who manages your affair, your mind is at ease and your goal is achieved. She has been content with sending this saying, whose context is that of a proverb, and the wisdom is that you say: hire him for his strength and his trustworthiness.[[Mahmud said: "This is a wise and comprehensive statement to which nothing can be added, because if strength and trustworthiness are combined in the one who manages your affair, your mind is at rest, and she has been content with sending this saying, whose context is that of a proverb and maxim, rather than saying: 'He is strong and trustworthy.'" Aḥmad said: This is also more beautiful as praise by women of men than specific praise, and more preserving of modesty, especially if she understood that her father's aim, peace be upon him, was to marry her to him. How well the Fārūq (ʿUmar), may God be pleased with him, took this meaning when he said: "I complain to God of the weakness of the trustworthy and the treachery of the strong." In the content of this complaint is a request to God that He grant him one who combines the two qualities, strong and trustworthy, whom he could rely upon in what he was undertaking, may God be pleased with him. And this ambiguity, from the daughter of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, was also taken by Zulaykha with Yusuf, peace be upon him. But how different is natural modesty from acquired modesty: kohl in the eyes is not like the kohl. When she said to her master: ﴿What is the recompense of one who intended evil to your wife, except that he be imprisoned or a painful punishment?﴾, she meant: what is the recompense of Yusuf for having intended evil toward me, except that you imprison him or punish him with a painful punishment? But shame and modesty prevented her husband's mind from her speaking the word of chastity while attributing the indecency to herself, indicating that this modesty in her, which prevented her from speaking this matter, prevented her from soliciting Yusuf by a more fitting and better means. And God knows best.]]

If you ask: how did he make ﴿the best you hire﴾ the subject of ﴿inna﴾ and ﴿the strong, the trustworthy﴾ the predicate? I answer: it is like his saying:

"Surely the best of people, alive and dead, is the captive of Thaqīf among them in chains."[[Surely the best of people, living and dead, is the captive of Thaqīf among them in chains. By my life, if you have made the prison abode of Khalid and made him tread it with the tread of one burdened. He was one who rose up to every calamity, and gave generous gifts, great in bounty, abundant in extra gifts. This is by Abu al-Shaghb al-ʿAbsī, lamenting over Khalid ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī when Yusuf ibn ʿUmar captured him. "The best of people" is an elative in the form of a comparative, annexed to a definite with al, and it is the subject of inna. "Living and dead" (ḥayyan wa-mayyitan), and in one narration "perishing" (hālikan), are two circumstantial clauses from it. "Captive" (asīr) is the predicate of inna, annexed to Thaqīf, the name of the tribe. A proper name is more definite than what is definite by al, so the predicate annexed to the proper noun is more definite than its subject which is annexed to the definite by al, and there is no obstacle to this when both refer to the same thing intended by the speaker. "Among them in chains" is a circumstantial clause or a predicate after a predicate. "By my life" is an oath. "If you have made...": that is, you put Khalid into prison and settled him there. "And made him tread it": that is, you made him tread the ground with his foot like the tread of one burdened with something heavy, meaning you put the shackles on his feet, so this is a metaphor for that. "He was one who rose up..." is the answer to the oath. The answer to the condition is omitted, meaning he was quick to rise to every heavy calamity. "Giver of al-lahā" with a fatḥa is the plural of lahāh, like ḥaṣā and ḥaṣāh, meaning the piece of flesh at the farthest part of the mouth, but here it means the mouth itself. The more likely is that with a ḍamma it is the plural of luhwah, like ghuraf, plural of ghurfah, meaning gift of any kind. "Ghamran" means abundant overflowing gift, and he was one with many additions in giving. He treated "muʿṭī" in the manner of a nominative for the sake of the meter.]] in that care is the cause of the fronting, and she has spoken truly, so that what is more worthy of being the predicate was made a noun. And the verb's coming in the past tense indicates that it is a matter that has been tested and known. From this is their saying: "The least of what you have worked with is the tongue of one who disowns."[[His statement "the least of what you have worked with is the tongue of one who disowns (mamkh)" in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: tamakhkhaytu min al-shayʾ and amkhaytu minhu: when one disowns something. So perhaps mamkh is an active participle from amkhaytu. (ʿ)]]

It is narrated from Ibn Masʿūd, may God be pleased with him: "The shrewdest of people are three: the daughter of Shu'ayb; the companion of Yusuf in his saying ﴿perhaps he will benefit us﴾; and Abu Bakr concerning ʿUmar."

It is narrated that he married him to Ṣafrāʾ.

His saying ﴿these two﴾ (hātayn) is evidence that he had other daughters besides them. ﴿That you hire me﴾ (ta'jurunī) is from ajara, meaning to hire someone out, if you were his hired man, like your saying abawtuhu if you were his father. ﴿Eight years﴾ (thamāniya ḥijaj) is its adverbial object. Or it is from ajartuhu kadhā, when I gave it to him as a wage. From this is the condolence of the Messenger of God, ﷺ: "May God reward you (ajarakum) and have mercy on you."[[It was recorded by Abu Nuʿaym in Taʾrīkh Aṣbahān from the route of Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn Ibrāhīm ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Ibrāhīm ibn al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, from his fathers, Ibrāhīm ibn al-Ḥasan, from Fāṭimah bint al-Ḥusayn, from her father, who said: "When the Messenger of God ﷺ offered condolence he would say: 'Ajarakum Allāh wa-raḥimakum,' and when he congratulated he would say: 'Bārak Allāh lakum wa-bārak ʿalaykum.'" It has a supporting mursal report recorded by Ibn Abī Shaybah from the narration of Ibn Khālid al-Wālibī: that the Prophet ﷺ offered condolence to a man and said to him: "May God have mercy on him and reward you." In al-Ḍuʿafāʾ by Ibn Ḥibbān from Ibn ʿUmar: that the Prophet ﷺ offered condolence to a Muslim for a dhimmi who had died to him, and said: "May God reward you and increase your reward." Its chain includes Ismāʿīl ibn Yaḥyā al-Taymī, who is discarded (sāqiṭ). (ʿ)]] "Eight years" is the object, and its meaning is: the pasturing of eight years.

If you ask: how is it valid that he marries him one of his two daughters without specifying? I answer: that was not a contract of marriage, but a promise and a description of a matter he had resolved upon.[[His statement "but a promise and a description (muwāṣafah) of a matter he had resolved upon" is probably muwāḍaʿah (agreement). (ʿ)]] If it had been a contract, he would have said: "I have married you," and he did not say: "I intend to marry you."

If you ask: how is it valid that he gives as her dowry the hire of his own labor in pasturing sheep, when the delivery of what is property is necessary? Do you not see how Abu Ḥanīfah prohibited a man marrying a woman on condition that he serve her for a year?[[Mahmud said: "It is quoted from Abu Ḥanīfah's school that marriage is forbidden upon his personal service, but permitted upon the service of his slave for a year, and he made a distinction: in the first case he has given himself, which is not property, while in the second he has given his slave, which is property. It is quoted from al-Shāfiʿī that marriage upon known benefits is permitted absolutely." Aḥmad said: The school of Mālik has three positions: prohibition, disapproval, and permissibility. The marvel is Abu Ḥanīfah's permission of marriage upon the benefits of a slave, but not upon the benefits of the husband, while the verse permitted marriage upon the benefits of the husband and did not touch on anything else. This is only to favor the meaning that al-Zamakhsharī pointed to, or on the basis that there is no evidence in the law of those before us, or for other reasons. And God knows best.]] He permitted that he marry her by serving her, his slave, for a year, or by housing her in his house for a year, because in the first case...

Hired himself out, not for property. In the second case, he is hired for property, which is a slave or a house. I say: the matter stands on Abu Hanifa's school as you have mentioned. As for al-Shafi'i, he permitted marriage in exchange for a hire (ijara) for certain works and services, provided that the thing the employer hires or the service rendered is a known matter. Perhaps that was permitted in that earlier law (shari'a).

The dower may be something else. He wanted him to tend his sheep for this period, and he wanted to marry him his daughter. So he mentioned the two desired things and tied the marriage to the tending, meaning: "I will do this if you do that," as a mutual pledge (mu'ahada) and not as a binding contract (mu'aqada). It is also possible that he hired him to tend for eight years at a known sum, paid it to him, and then married his daughter to him for that. His words ﴿on condition that you hire yourself to me for eight years﴾ are an expression of what passed between them. ﴿And if you complete ten years, it is from you﴾: so its completion is from you. Its meaning is: it is from you, not from me. That is, I do not obligate you to it or impose it upon you, but if you do it, it is a favour and a voluntary gift from you; and if not, there is no blame on you. ﴿And I do not want to burden you﴾ by obligating you to complete the longer of the two terms and making it binding.

If you ask: what is the reality of their saying "I burdened him" (shaqqa 'alayhi) and "the matter burdened him" (shadda 'alayhi)? I say: its reality is that when a matter becomes great for you, it is as if it has burdened you, since you are in doubt; you say at one time, "I can bear it," and at another, "I cannot bear it." Or his promise of leniency and easygoing dealing from himself, meaning that he would not burden him in what he hired him for, in tending his sheep, and would not do what the difficult employers do with those they hire, such as quibbling over observing times, strictness in demanding the completion of tasks, and assigning the shepherds labours beyond the limit of the condition. Thus the prophets, peace be upon them, always adopted the most lenient course in their dealings with people. From this is the hadith: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was my partner, and he was the best of partners; he was not stubborn, did not dispute, and did not quarrel." [[Narrated by Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah from the hadith of al-Sa'ib, that he said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "You were my partner, and you were the best partner; you were not stubborn and did not dispute."]] His words ﴿you will find me, if Allah wills, among the righteous﴾ indicate this. By righteousness he means good dealing, gentleness of manner and softness of disposition. [[His words "gentleness of manner and softness of disposition": in al-Sihah (the lexicon of al-Jawhari), "wati'a" (softness) means "gentle, easy." (Ibn Hajar? no; the marginal note reads: (ʿ).)]] It is also possible that he means righteousness in general, which includes good dealing. The purpose of conditioning the will of Allah on the righteousness he promised is reliance on Allah's granting him success in it and His help, not that he would perform righteousness "if Allah wills," and if He wills, He would make him do the opposite.

﴿That﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿between me and you﴾ is its predicate, and it refers to what Shu'ayb covenanted with him. He means: what you said and covenanted with me and stipulated upon me remains established between us both, and neither of us departs from it, neither I from what you stipulated upon me, nor you from what you stipulated upon yourself.

Then he said: ﴿whichever of the two terms I fulfil﴾, that is, the longer of them, which is the ten years, or the shorter, which is the eight years, ﴿there shall be no injustice against me﴾, that is, no one shall transgress against me by seeking more than it. If you ask: the imagining of injustice applies only to one of the two terms, the shorter one, which is the demand for completing the ten years, so what is the meaning of attaching injustice to both of them together? I say: its meaning is that just as, if I were required to add to the ten years, that would certainly be an injustice, so likewise if I were required to add to the eight years. He intended by this to establish the matter of choice (khiyar), that it is firm and fixed, and that the two terms are equal: either this or that, with no difference between them in fulfilment. As for the completion, it is left to my judgement: if I wish, I will do it, and if not, I will not be compelled to it. It was also said: the meaning is "then I am not a transgressor," and this is in negating transgression from himself, like your saying, "there is no sin upon me, and no consequence upon me."

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "whichever of the two terms I have fulfilled." It was also read as "ayyama" with a sukun on the ya', as in the verse:

*I waited for Nasr and the two Simaks, whichever of them*
*its heavy rains pour upon me.* [[By al-Farazdaq. Nasr is the son of Sayyar, king of the two Iraqs. The two Simaks are two stars: al-Simak al-A'zal, which has no star in front of it, and al-Simak al-Ramih, which has stars in front of it. The word "ayyuhuma" originally had a doubled letter, which was made quiescent out of necessity. Then it may be that it is in the accusative as a substitute for what precedes it, and that it governs a deleted element, meaning: "I do not know which of them," and it is a relative pronoun. It is also possible that it is an interrogative, and in that case it is in the nominative as the subject, and the pronoun in it refers to Nasr and the two Simaks, meaning: "I awaited Nasr and the two Simaks, whichever of them its rains pour down upon me from the cloud." "Istahalla" means its pouring became intense. "Mawatir" are clouds, and "ghayth" is rain. In linking Nasr with the two Simaks there is an indication of comparing him to them in goodness, and of the interrogative sense, so it is of the type of "feigning ignorance of one who knows" (tajahul al-arif); and likewise it denies knowledge.]]

It is also reported from Ibn Qutayb: "'udwan" with a kasra. If you ask: what is the difference between the two positions of the extra "ma" in the two readings? I say: in the widely transmitted reading it occurs as an emphasis on the indefiniteness, meaning that "ayyu" is made more general by it; and in the irregular reading it is an emphasis on the decree, as if he said: "whichever of the two terms I have resolved upon fulfilling, and I have set my firm resolve upon it."

"Al-wakil" is the one to whom the matter has been entrusted. When it is used in the place of "witness," "guardian" (muhaymin) and "sustainer" (muqit), it takes "'ala" by virtue of that. [[His words "muhaymin and muqit": that is, the powerful one (al-muqtadir), or the guardian (al-hafiz). (ʿ)]]

It is reported that Shu'ayb had the staff of the prophets with him, and he said to Musa at night: "Enter that room and take a staff from those staffs." So he took a staff that Adam had descended with from Paradise, and the prophets had continued to inherit it until it came into the possession of Shu'ayb. He touched it, and he was blind, and he was reluctant to give it up, saying: "Take another." But nothing came into his hand except it, seven times, so he knew that it had a significance.

It was also said: Gabriel took it after the death of Adam, and it remained with him until he brought it to Musa at night. And it was also said: an angel in the form of a man entrusted it to Shu'ayb, and he commanded his daughter to bring him a staff, and she brought it to him, and he threw it back seven times, and nothing came into her hand except it, so he gave it to him. Then he regretted it, because it was a deposit (wadi'a), and he followed him, and they disputed over it. They agreed that whoever arrived first should judge between them, and the angel came to them and said: "Cast it down; whoever lifts it, it is his." The old man struggled with it and could not manage it, and Musa lifted it.

From al-Hasan: it was nothing but a staff of wood that came in his way by chance. From al-Kalbi: the tree from which he was called was a thorn-bush (shajarat al-'awsaj), and from it was his staff.

When morning came, Shu'ayb said to him: "When you reach the fork in the road, do not take on your right, for although there is more pasture there, in it is a serpent (tinnin) [[His words "a serpent": that is, a large snake (tha'ban). (ʿ)]] I fear for you and for the sheep." So the sheep took the right, and he could not restrain them, so he walked in their tracks, and there was pasture and lush greenery the like of which he had never seen. He slept, and suddenly the serpent came, and the staff fought it until it killed it, and returned to Musa's side, bloodied. When he saw it bloodied and the serpent dead, he was pleased with that. When he returned to Shu'ayb, he touched the sheep and found them full-bellied and abundant in milk, and Musa informed him, and he rejoiced and knew that Musa and the staff had a significance. He said to him: "I have given you of the young of my flock this year every spotted and speckled one."

Then in a dream it was revealed to him: "Strike your staff against the watering-place of the sheep." He did so, and then he watered them, and not one of them missed without bearing spotted and speckled young, and so he fulfilled his condition to him.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 28, verses 29–32:

It was asked of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Which of the two terms did Musa fulfil?" He said: "The more distant and the longer of them." [[Al-Hakim transmitted it through Ibn Uyaynah, from Ibrahim ibn Yahya, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, in this form. I say: Ibrahim is unknown (majhul). As for the report that he said, "He fulfilled the more complete of them and married the younger of the two daughters," al-Tabarani and al-Bazzar transmitted it through Uwayd ibn Abi Imran al-Jawni, from his father, from Abd Allah ibn al-Samit, from Abu Dhar, that "the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked: 'Which of the two terms did Musa fulfil?' He said: 'The more complete and the more righteous of them.' He was asked: 'Which of the two women did he marry?' He said: 'The younger of them.'" Uwayd is weak. In Ibn Mardawayh, from a hadith of Abu Hurayrah traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Jibril said to me: 'If the Jew asks you, "Which of the two terms did Musa fulfil?", say, "The more complete of them." And if he asks you, "Which of the two did he marry?", say, "The younger of them."'" Its chain includes Sulayman al-Shadhakuni, who is weak.]]

It is also reported that he said: "He fulfilled the more complete of them, and he married the younger of the two." This contradicts the earlier report.

*Al-jadhwah* (a brand of fire), in its three vocalisations, and it was read with all three: a thick piece of wood; whether or not there was fire at its tip. Kuthayyir said:

*They spent the night, the gatherers of wood for Layla, seeking thick and dry firewood, neither weak nor smouldering.* [[By Ibn Muqbil. *Al-hawatib* are the young women seeking firewood. *Al-iltimas* (seeking), originally, derives from *al-lams* (touching), and then its usage was extended. *Al-jidhl* is thick, dry firewood. *Al-judhā* is the plural of *jadhwah*, with the *jim* vowelled in three ways in both, and it is a thick piece of wood with fire at its tip, or first. *Al-khiwar* is weakness. *Al-khawr* is a defect, except in their phrase *nāqah khuwwārah*, meaning a she-camel abundant in milk, and *nakhlah khuwwārah*, meaning a palm abundant in fruit. *Da'ara al-'ūd* (the wood) *da'aran*, on the pattern of *ta'iba*, means its smoke increased, so it is *da'ar* on the pattern of *hadhar*. *Al-da'ar* also means worm-eaten decay and corruption. *Al-di'ār* means immorality and wickedness. *Ghayra khawwār* is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of *jidhl al-judhā*.]] He also said:

*And he cast upon a brand of fire a firebrand, its heat and its blazing being fierce upon him.* [[The *jadhwah* originally means a thick piece of wood with fire at its tip, or first. But the attribute specifies what has fire at its tip. Then it is a clear metaphor (*isti'arah tasrihiyyah*) for a spear or a sword. "Heat" and "blazing" are a *tarshih* (a complementary elaboration) of it. *Shadid* is the predicate of the subject that follows it.]]

*Min* in both places (*min al-ūlā* and *al-thāniyah*) indicates the starting point of the action. That is: the call came to him from the side of the valley, in the direction of the tree.

*Wa-min al-shajarah* ("and from the tree") is a substitute for *min shāti' al-wād* ("from the side of the valley"), a substitute of inclusion (*badal al-ishtimal*), because the tree was growing on the bank, as in His saying (the Exalted): ﴿Indeed, We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful, for their houses...﴾. *Al-buq'ah* is read with a *damma* and with a *fatha*.

*Al-rahb* (fear) is pronounced with two *fathas*, two *dammas*, a *fatha* and a *sukun*, or a *damma* and a *sukun*. It means fear. If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿And draw your arm close to your side against fear﴾? I answer: it has two meanings. The first is that when Allah turned the staff into a snake, Musa (peace be upon him) was startled and agitated, and he shielded himself from it with his hand, as the one who fears something does. So it was said to him: "Your shielding yourself with your hand carries a humiliation before the enemies. When you cast it, and it turns into a snake, insert your hand under your armpit in place of your shielding with it. Then bring it out white," so that two things would be achieved: avoiding what is a humiliation for you, and displaying another miracle. *Al-janāh* (the wing) here means the hand, because a person's two hands are in the position of a bird's two wings. When he inserts his right hand under the armpit of his left, he has drawn his wing to himself.

The second is that drawing his wing to himself means restraining himself and controlling himself, and steadying himself when the staff turns into a snake, so that he does not become agitated and does not fear. This is a metaphor borrowed from the action of a bird, because when it is afraid it spreads its wings and lets them droop; otherwise its wings are folded against it, close to its body. From this is what is related about Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz: that a scribe of his was writing before him, and a gust of wind escaped from him, so he was embarrassed and shaken. He stood up and struck the ground with his pen. Umar said to him: "Take your pen, draw your wing to yourself, and let your fright be dispelled, for I have never heard it from anyone more than I have heard it from myself." [[His saying "let your fright be dispelled" means let your fear go away, as the *Sihah* states. (ʿ)]]

The meaning of His saying *min al-rahb* ("from fear") is: "because of fear", that is, if fear strikes you at the sight of the snake, then draw your wing to yourself. The fear that used to afflict him was made the cause and reason for what he was commanded to do, namely drawing his wing to himself.

The meaning of "draw your wing to yourself" and of His saying "insert your hand into your pocket" is one thing according to one of the two interpretations. But the two expressions differ, and the one meaning is repeated because the purposes differ: the purpose of one is the hand's coming out white, and the purpose of the other is the removal of fear. If you say: the wing, which is the hand, has been made folded in one place and folded-to in another, namely His saying ﴿And draw your arm close to your side﴾ and His saying ﴿And draw your hand to your side﴾, how can these be reconciled? I answer: the "wing" that is folded is the right hand, and that to which it is folded is the left hand; and each of the right and left hands is a wing.

Among the strange interpretations is the claim that *al-rahb* means the sleeve, in the dialect of Himyar, and that they say, "Give me from what is in your *rahb*." I wonder how this is sound in the language? Was it heard from reliable authorities whose Arabic is trusted? Then I wonder how it fits in the verse? And how it is applied to the *mufassal* (the final division of the Qur'an) like the rest of the words of the revelation? Moreover, Musa (peace be upon him) on the night of the private conversation was wearing only a *zurmanqah* of wool with no sleeves. [[His saying "a *zurmanqah* of wool": in the hadith, when Musa (peace be upon him) came to Pharaoh, he came wearing a *zurmanqah*, that is, a woollen cloak. Abu Ubayd said: I think it is Hebrew. So the *Sihah* states. (ʿ)]]

*Fa-dhānika* ("These two") is read with a light and with a heavy *dhal*. The light form is the dual of *dhāka*, and the heavy form is the dual of *dhālika*. *Burhānān* ("two proofs") means two clear, shining evidences. If you ask: why was the proof called *burhān*? I answer: because of its whiteness and its brightness, from the phrase used for a white woman, *barhar-hah* (with the repetition of the *ʿayn* and the *lām* together). The evidence that the *nūn* is an addition is their saying *abrah al-rajul*, meaning "the man brought a *burhān*." And the parallel is their calling it *sulṭān* (authority), from *al-saliṭ*, which is oil, because of its brightness.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 28, verse 33–34:

It is said: radi'tuhu (ردأته) means "I helped him." And ridʾ (الردء) is a noun for that which one is helped with; it is a form in the sense of the passive participle, just as dafʾ (الدفء) is a noun for that with which one is warmed. Salamah ibn Jandal said:

"And my helper, every white Mushshari (sword), its edge sharpened, keen, with nicks (in its edge)..."

[Note: Salamah ibn Jandal. He says: my helper, by which I ward off hardships, is every white sword. He used "every" (kull) because the intent is to specify the kind, not the individual. Mushshari: a nisba to Mashariq al-Yaman, villages from it; it is also said to be from al-Sham. Shahidh al-hadd: its edge made keen, from shahadh al-midyah, i.e., sharpened it. ʿAdab: cutting. Al-fulul: plural of fal (with fatha), which is a break and notch in the edge of a sword, i.e., it has fulul from clashing with the battalions.]

It is also read radan (ردا) with the sukun (lightening), as the reading "al-khabba ridan yusaddiqunī" (ردءا يصدقني) is read with raf' and jazm, as an attribute and as a response, like "waliyyan yarithuni" (وليا يرثني). If you ask: what is the benefit of his brother confirming him? I say: the purpose of his confirming him is not that he says to him, "You have spoken the truth," or says to the people, "Musa has spoken the truth," but rather that he clarifies the truth with his tongue, expands the speech about it, and argues with it against the disbelievers, as an eloquent man of strong argument does. This takes the place of an effective confirmation, just as a statement is confirmed by proof. Do you not see His saying: "And my brother Harun, he is more eloquent than me in tongue, so send him with me" (28:34)? The excellence of eloquence is only needed for this, not for saying "you have spoken the truth," for Sahban and Baqil [Note: "Sahban and Baqil are equal in it" is an example of eloquence; Baqil is an example of incoherence and inarticulateness. (ʿA)] would be equal in that. Or he joins the wing of his speech with clarity until the one he fears will deny him confirms him. So the confirmation is ascribed to Harun because he is the cause of it, as a metaphorical ascription (al-isnad al-majazi). The meaning of metaphorical ascription is: confirmation is in reality of the one who confirms, so ascribing it to him is literal, and there is no confirmation in the cause; but ascription is borrowed for it because the one who causes it is connected to the confirmation through causation, just as the doer is connected to it through direct action. The proof of this interpretation is His saying: "Indeed I fear that they will deny me" (28:34). And the reading of the one who reads: "ridʾan yusaddiqūnī" (ردءا يصدقوني) strengthens the reading with the jazm of "yusaddiqunī."

**al-Aḍud** (the upper arm): the strength of the hand, and with its strength the hand becomes strong. Ṭarafa said:

*Ābnā Libayna, lastum bi-yadin... illā yadan laysat lahā ʿaḍud*
*Ābnā Libayna, lā uḥiqqukum... wa-jadda l-ilāhu bikum kamā ajid*

[[*Abnā Libaynā, lastum bi-yadin / illā yadan laysat lahā ʿaḍud*
*Abnā Libaynā, lā uḥiqqukum / wajada l-ilāhu bikum kamā ajid*

These lines are by Ṭarafa ibn al-ʿAbd. It is also said that they are by Aws ibn Ḥajar. The *hamza* is the particle of address. *Libayna* is the name of a female slave, used as a metonymy for the fact that they are slaves. "Hand" is an explicit metaphor (*istiʿāra taṣrīḥiyya*) for the strong. Or it is an eloquent simile (*tashbīh balīgh*), meaning: you are not like any hand among hands in strength, except like a hand that has no arm, which is weak. It is also narrated as *illā yadan makhbūlat al-ʿaḍud*. One says *khabalat yaduhu*, meaning "I paralysed his hand." In the rhyme there is *al-iqwāʾ* (the irregular change of vowel in the rhyme-letter). It also contains the placing of blame in a form resembling praise, for the sake of intensifying the blame. He repeated the address for added emphasis. *Ḥaqquhu yaḥiqquhu* means "his opponent disputed with him," and also "he established it," and "he made it obligatory." So: *lā uḥiqqukum*, i.e. I will not establish you (as right), or: you are not fit for disputing with me. *Wajada ʿalayhi* means "he was angry," and *wajada bihi* means "he was sorrowful," i.e. God became angry at you on account of your deeds as I am angry, or He hated you as a grieving person hates what grieves him. This is a supplication against them for destruction.]]

It is said in a supplication for good: *shadda Llāhu ʿaḍudaka* ("may God strengthen your arm"). Its opposite is *fatta Llāhu fī ʿaḍudika* ("may God weaken your arm"). The meaning of ﴿سَنَشُدُّ عَضُدَكَ بِأَخِيكَ﴾ ("We will strengthen your arm through your brother") is: We will make you strong through him and help you. This may be because the hand grows strong when the upper arm is strong, and the body is strengthened by the strength of the hand in carrying out affairs. Or it is because the man was likened to the hand in its becoming strong through the strengthening of the upper arm, so he was made as if he were a strong hand supported by a strong upper arm.

﴿سُلْطَانًا﴾ means dominance and authority. Or it means a clear proof. ﴿بِآيَاتِنَا﴾ is connected to something similar to what it is connected to in the nine signs, i.e. "go with Our signs." Or it is connected to ﴿نَجْعَلُ لَكُمَا سُلْطَانًا﴾ ("We will give you both authority"), i.e. We will give you authority through Our signs. Or it is connected to ﴿لَا يَصِلُونَ﴾, i.e. they will be prevented from reaching you by Our signs. Or it is an explanation of ﴿الْغَالِبُونَ﴾ ("the victors"), not a relative clause complement, because it is impossible for a relative complement to precede the relative word. If it were placed after, it would only be a complement of it. It is also permissible that it be an oath, whose answer is ﴿لَا يَصِلُونَ إِلَيْكُمَا﴾ ("they shall not reach you"), placed before it. Or it is part of an idle oath (*laghw al-qasam*).

Magic, fabricated (sihrun muftaran): magic that you yourself perform and then attribute falsely to God. Or, it is manifest magic whose fabrication is evident. Or, it is described as fabricated like all other kinds of magic, and is not a miracle from God.

"In the time of our fathers" (fi aba'ina) is a circumstantial accusative (hal mansubah) referring to "this": that is, existing in the time and days of our forefathers. They mean: "We have not heard of its occurrence among them." It cannot be that they were lying in this, since they had heard of and known something similar. Or they mean that they had not heard of anything like it in its monstrousness. Or [it means] that the soothsayers (al-kuhhan) did not foretell the appearance of Moses and his coming with what he brought.

This is evidence that they were confounded and bewildered, and that they found nothing with which to repel the signs that came to them except their saying, "This is magic and an innovation (bid'ah) of which we have never heard the like."

He says: ﴿My Lord knows best﴾ who among you is most deserving of the great success, since He made him a prophet, sent him with guidance, and promised him a good final outcome. He means himself. Were he what you claim, a liar, a sorcerer, and a fabricator, God would not have made him worthy of this, because He is Self-Sufficient and Wise, does not send liars, does not grant success to sorcerers, and the wrongdoers do not prosper with Him. ﴿The final outcome of the abode﴾ is the praiseworthy outcome. The evidence for this is His saying, ﴿Those, theirs is the good final abode: Gardens of Eden﴾ and His saying, ﴿The disbelievers will know to whom belongs the final abode﴾. By "the abode" is meant this world. Its outcome, its final end, is that the servant is sealed with mercy and divine good pleasure, and the angels greet him with glad tidings at death. If you say: both the praiseworthy and the blameworthy outcome may validly be called "the outcome of the abode," since this world either ends well or ends badly, so why is its ending in good singled out with this name rather than its ending in evil? I reply: God, glorified is He, made this world a passage (majaz) to the Hereafter, and He willed for His servants that they should do only good in it. He created them only for this purpose, so that they would receive a good ending and a truthful outcome. Whoever acts in it contrary to what God established has distorted it. Its original outcome is therefore the outcome of good. As for the outcome of evil, it is not counted, because it is a result of the distortion of the wicked.

[[Mahmud said: "The outcome is the praiseworthy outcome, and the evidence for this is the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Those, theirs is the good final abode: Gardens of Eden﴾ and His saying ﴿The disbelievers will know to whom belongs the final abode﴾. The intended meaning is the abode of this world, and its outcome is that a person is sealed in it with mercy and divine good pleasure, and the angels greet him with glad tidings at death." He said: "If you say: both the praiseworthy and the blameworthy outcome may validly be called an outcome, since this world either ends well or badly, so why is its ending in good singled out with this name rather than its ending in evil? I reply: because God, glorified and exalted is He, made this world a passage to the Hereafter, and He willed for His servants that they should worship Him in it and do only good, and He created them only for this, as He said: ﴿I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me﴾. Whoever acts in this world contrary to that has distorted it, because its original outcome is the outcome of good. As for the outcome of evil, it is not counted, because it is from the distortion of the wicked."

Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: The principles of the People of Truth (ahl al-haqq) that have already been mentioned offer light on this matter. The point that needs restating here is this: his argument that the outcome of good and the worship of God are what is meant, and nothing else, by His saying ﴿I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me﴾ is contradicted by similar verses in the evidence that Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah) cite for their beliefs, such as His saying ﴿We have indeed created for Hell many of the jinn and humankind﴾, and so on. The intended meaning, and God knows best, is: We have indeed made for the punishment of Hell many created beings from the two weighty creatures. Among this is what is related from al-Faruq (ʿUmar), may God be pleased with him, that he said: "Indeed you are the offspring of al-Mughirah, the fuel (dhurʾ) of the Fire," meaning its creation. If the verse of al-Dhariyat apparently indicates that God created the two weighty creatures so that their outcome would be Paradise as reward and recompense for their worship of Him, then the verse of al-A'raf indicates that He created many of the two weighty creatures so that their outcome would be Hell as recompense for their disbelief.

At that point it is necessary to reconcile the two verses, and to restrict the general sense of the verse of al-Dhariyat to the particular sense of the other verse. The intended meaning becomes: "I did not create the blessed among the two weighty creatures except for My worship," reconciling the evidences. It is established that both outcomes are intended by God, Exalted is He, after the concurring rational proofs for this. The reason that the absolute term "outcome" often comes and means the good by it is that God guided people to it, promised them what is reported regarding treading its path of salvation and lasting bliss, forbade them its opposite, and threatened those who follow it with painful punishment of various kinds. He placed in them intellects that guide them to the outcome of good, enabled them to attain it, removed their obstacles, and supplied their motives. It was therefore their duty not to turn away from the outcome of good, nor to take any path other than its path, and to set it before their eyes. So the term "outcome" was used absolutely, meaning by it the good, as a consequence of this, and God knows best. The summary is: since it is what is commanded and urged, it is treated as what is willed, even if it is not willed for many of the creatures.

Someone said to me: "What prevents you from saying that the absolute outcome is not understood to be the outcome of good from its being used absolutely, but from its being attributed to its people with the preposition lam (لـ) in the verses mentioned, such as His saying ﴿Whose will be the outcome of the abode﴾, ﴿The disbelievers will know to whom belongs the final abode﴾, and ﴿The outcome is for the God-fearing﴾? The lam conveys that it is the outcome of good, since it belongs to them, while the outcome of evil is against them, not for them, just as they say: 'the turn (al-dāʾira) is for so-and-so,' meaning the turn of victory and triumph, and 'the turn is against so-and-so,' meaning the turn of abandonment and evil." I said: "I would have had something to say on that, had it not been for the verse ﴿Those, for them is the curse, and for them is the evil of the abode﴾, where it does not say ʿalayhim (عليهم, 'against them'). So the use of lam in place of ʿala (على) is evidence that the argument through lam fulfils the meaning of the outcome of good, and God knows best."]] Ibn Kathir recited ﴿قال موسى﴾ without the conjunction waw (و), according to what is in the codices (masahif) of the people of Mecca. This is a good reading, because the context calls for a question and discussion about what Moses, peace be upon him, answered when they called such clear signs "fabricated sorcery." The other reading (with waw, وقال موسى) has this rationale: that they said that, and Moses said this, so that the observer may weigh the statement against what is said, and perceive the corruption of one and the soundness of the other. As the poet says: "And by their opposites things are made clear." 

[[He said: "Whoever wrongs his peers in their obligations, by wanting them to be equal to him, has put them under hardship. And he disparages them, and through them we know his excellence; and by their opposites things are distinguished."

These are lines of Abu al-Tayyib al-Mutanabbi, in praise of Harun ibn Abd al-Aziz. That is: he has wronged his peers by making them obligated to be equal to him, which is a hardship for them. This is a metaphor (kinaya) for the fact that no one equals him. His saying "and by their opposites" to the end is an illustration of what precedes it. It is also narrated as "تتبين الأشياء" (tatabayyanu al-ashya', "things become clear"), and the meaning is the same: things are known by knowing their opposites.]]

It is recited as ﴿تكون﴾ with both the ya' (يـ, third person) and the ta' (تـ, second/feminine form).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 28, verse 38:

It is related that when he (Pharaoh) ordered the building of the lofty palace (sarh), Haman gathered the workers until there were fifty thousand builders, apart from the followers and the hired labourers. He ordered the baking of bricks (ājurr) and gypsum (jiss), the carpentry of wood, and the driving of nails. They built it until it reached a height that no building of any created being had reached, so that the builder could not stand at its top while building. Then God sent Gabriel (Jibril), peace be upon him, at sunset, and he struck it with his wing and cut it into three pieces. One piece fell on Pharaoh's army and killed a million men, one piece fell into the sea, and one piece fell in the west, and none of his workers remained without perishing.

It is also related in this story that Pharaoh climbed to the top of it and shot an arrow towards the sky. God wished to test them, so the arrow came back to him stained with blood, and he said: "I have killed the god of Moses." Thereupon God sent Gabriel, peace be upon him, to demolish it. God knows best its authenticity.

The meaning of his denial of knowing any god other than himself is the denial of his existence. The sense is: ﴿I do not know for you any god other than me﴾, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: Do you inform God of what He does not know in the heavens or in the earth?﴾ (Q. 10:18), meaning: of what is not in them. That is because knowledge follows the known; it relates only to what the thing is. If the thing is non-existent, then no existent is related to it. Therefore the negation of knowledge of its existence is the negation of its existence itself. He expressed the negation of its existence by the negation of knowledge of its existence. [[Mahmud said: "He expressed the negation of the known by the negation of knowledge, and it is so because knowledge relates to the known only as it is: if it is existent, then it is existent, and if it is non-existent, then it is non-existent. Therefore he expressed the negation of its being existent by the negation of its being known." Ahmad said:

Because of how far delusion had reached him, he did not consider how the arrow falls. It came from the fact that God, exalted is He, often expressed the negation of the known by the negation of knowledge, as in His saying: ﴿Say: Do you inform God of what He does not know in the heavens or in the earth?﴾ and ﴿Or do you inform Him of what He does not know in the earth?﴾ (Q. 13:33). When this usage became consistent for him, he imagined that this expression of the negation of the known by the negation of knowledge covers every knowledge, even if it does not relate to the known as it is. This is not so. Rather, this expression is permissible only in the knowledge of God, the Eternal, owing to a matter specific to eternal knowledge, namely the comprehensiveness of its relation, so that nothing escapes it. Hence, if knowledge does not relate to the existence of a thing, it must follow that the thing does not exist, for if it existed, it would be related to by knowledge. This is unlike the knowledge of creatures. There is no necessary connection between the negation of a thing and the negation of created knowledge of its existence, but it is not so with eternal knowledge. Between the negation of its known object and the negation of its relation to existence there is a necessary connection which permits the aforementioned expression. But it is well known that Pharaoh claimed divinity and treated his knowledge as the knowledge of God, the Exalted, in that nothing escapes it. Hence he transgressed and became arrogant. He expressed the negation of his knowledge in place of the negation of the known, to deceive his chiefs and to confuse their foolish minds, and God knows best.

His exaltation of himself is suited to His saying: ﴿So kindle for me, O Haman, upon the clay﴾ (Q. 28:38). He did not say "bake bricks for me," and this is from self-exaltation, as God, exalted is He, said, and His are the greatness and the pride, and whoever wraps himself in His two garments, He breaks him: ﴿And of that which they kindle upon in the fire, seeking an ornament﴾ (Q. 13:17). He mentioned this comprehensive expression of the varieties of disbelief in a manner of pride, treating them with contempt, and that is the arrogance of kings, may God be exalted and glorified. Among Pharaoh's self-exaltation also: his calling to his minister by name, with the particle of address, and placing his call in the midst of the command; his building of the palace; and his hope of looking (upon the god of Moses) is evidence that he was not determined in denial. Al-Zamakhshari said: That contradicts the decisive denial he displayed in his saying: ﴿I do not know for you any god other than me﴾. Either this contradiction was hidden from his people because of their stupidity and the dullness of their minds, or they perceived it and feared his vengeance, and so they persisted.

Ahmad said: One may say, and God knows best, that his saying ﴿I do not know for you any god other than me﴾ may be understood as doubt, and as the negation of his knowledge specifically, and as placing it in the same category as the knowledge of ordinary creatures, in that the negation of its relation to the existence of something does not necessitate the negation of that thing, since it is possible that it exists and escapes his knowledge. In that case it is not a contradiction. And if this interpretation were not the primary one, we would not have been justified in removing the contradiction from his speech, since he is too contemptible for that.]] It is also permissible that it be taken literally, and that a god other than Him was not known to him, but was only supposed. This is shown by his saying: ﴿And indeed I think him to be among the liars﴾ (Q. 28:38). If Moses, peace be upon him, thought (the claim of) a god other than Him to be false, without knowing it to be false, then he thought that there is in existence a god other than Him. Even if the forsaken one was not supposing with a supposition like certainty, but rather knowing the truth of Moses' words, then Moses' saying to him: ﴿You know that none sent these down but the Lord of the heavens and the earth as insights﴾ (Q. 17:102), would not have made him undertake that great building, nor toil in building it as he toiled, perhaps so that he might, in his supposition, rise up to the god of Moses, peace be upon him. Yet he was ignorant to an extreme degree of Him and of His attributes, since he reckoned that He is in a place as he himself was in a place, that He is approached by ascent as he would ascend to Him when he sat in his upper chamber, and that He is king of the heavens just as he is king of the earth.

You will not find clearer proof of his extreme ignorance and dullness, and the ignorance and dullness of his chiefs, than that they sought to attain the means to the heavens by a palace they would build. I wonder: was he deceiving the people of his land and mocking their minds, since he encountered the most foolish of people, the emptiest of intelligence and most like beasts in this? Or was he in himself of that description? And if it is correct what is related of the arrow returning to him stained with blood, then this was a mockery by deed, as mockery by speech occurs in more than one place in the Book of God concerning his like among the disbelievers.

It is also permissible to interpret the supposition in the first view as certainty, as in the verse:

I said to them: Be assured of two thousand armored men,
I endured every torment of the lover except (that of) a woman; I did not meet my death at my ambush.
I gave counsel to Aridh and the companions of Aridh, and the clan of Banu al-Sawda, and the people of Shahd.

This is said by Duraid ibn al-Simma, warning his people of an enemy attack. Duraid is Mu'awiya ibn al-Harith ibn Bakr ibn Alqama al-Juhani, who killed a polytheist on the day of Hunayn. That is: every hardship that the lover encounters from his beloved, I encountered. Al-hatf is destruction. Al-marsad and al-mirsad are the path; in his attributing it to himself there is a subtle meaning: I did not take a path in which destruction awaited me, but took another which had no harm in it. Nasaha and nasaha lahu: he was sincere, purely. Al-shahd, with shadda, is the plural of shahid. Dajjaja tadjij: he covered it thoroughly. Al-dajja, with shadda, is darkness; al-daj is walking with deliberation. Al-mudajjaj is the fully armed. It is said that it, with a fatha, is the horse, and with a kasra, the rider. Al-sarah are the chiefs and nobles, with a fatha on the sin; originally it is the upper back of an animal, and it was borrowed for them. It may also be pronounced with a damma; its form is fa'lah, the plural of sariy, of the form fa'il against analogy, since its analogical plural is af'ila'. Originally it is a small stream, borrowed for a leading good man. Al-farisi denotes coats of mail made in Persia. Al-sard and al-tasrid mean continuous weaving. He says: be certain of the attack of a great army. The two thousand is a metaphor for multitude, that is, a large army covered with weapons, its nobles in the continuously woven Persian coats of mail. The adverbial form of place indicates the full extent of the coats of mail for them. It is also related as al-musawwad with a waw, but that is not so.]]

Then the building of the palace would be a contradiction of his claim of knowledge and certainty, and it was hidden from his people because of their stupidity and foolishness.

Or it was not hidden from them, but each one feared for himself his whip and his sword. He said ﴿So kindle for me, O Haman, upon the clay﴾ and did not say "bake the brick for me and make it," because he was the first to make bricks, so he was teaching them the craft. And because this expression is better in its correspondence (tibaq) to the eloquence of the Qur'an and its high rank, and more fitting to the speech of tyrants. He commanded Haman, who was his minister and his companion, to kindle upon the clay, calling him by his name with the particle of address in the middle of the speech, which is evidence of exaltation [[the phrase "evidence of exaltation" perhaps is "of exaltation" (ʿ)]] and tyranny. It is related from Umar, may God be pleased with him, that when he travelled to Syria and saw the palaces built with brick, he said:

I did not know that anyone built with brick except Pharaoh.

Al-tula' and al-it-la' are ascending; it is said: the mountain rose (ṭalaʿa) and ascended (aṭlaʿa), with the same meaning.

Arrogance with respect to the truth belongs only to God Most High; He is the true Proud (al-Mutakabbir) in reality, that is, the One who exceeds all in the greatness of His majesty. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said, relating from his Lord: "Pride is My cloak and greatness is My garment; whoever contends with Me over either of them, I will cast him into the Fire." [Narrated by Muslim from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah and Abu Sa'id, from the Prophet (ﷺ), from his Lord.] And every other arrogant person's arrogance is without right. (يُرْجَعُونَ) is read with a damma and with a fatha. ﴿So We seized him and his hosts, and cast them into the sea﴾ is from the majestic speech by which He indicates the greatness of His affair and the majesty of His dominion. He likened them, belittling them and considering their number insignificant, even if they were a great multitude and a vast throng, to pebbles that a taker grasps in his palm and throws into the sea. [End of his words. He said: "His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So We seized him and his hosts, and cast them into the sea﴾, is a counterpart to his arrogance, expressed by an act whose form is taking contemptible pebbles and then casting them into the sea with disdain. This is an image of His treating him with contempt and destroying him with this kind of destruction. And God knows best."] Similarly is His saying: ﴿And We set in it lofty mountains﴾ (Q. 77:27), ﴿and the earth and the mountains are lifted and crushed with a single blow﴾ (Q. 69:14), ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure, while the earth entire will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be rolled up in His right hand﴾ (Q. 39:67). These are only depictions and images of His power, and that every created thing, however great and mighty, is belittled beside His power.

Arrogance with respect to the truth belongs only to God Most High; He is the true Proud (al-Mutakabbir) in reality, that is, the One who exceeds all in the greatness of His majesty. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said, relating from his Lord: "Pride is My cloak and greatness is My garment; whoever contends with Me over either of them, I will cast him into the Fire." [Narrated by Muslim from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah and Abu Sa'id, from the Prophet (ﷺ), from his Lord.] And every other arrogant person's arrogance is without right. (يُرْجَعُونَ) is read with a damma and with a fatha. ﴿So We seized him and his hosts, and cast them into the sea﴾ is from the majestic speech by which He indicates the greatness of His affair and the majesty of His dominion. He likened them, belittling them and considering their number insignificant, even if they were a great multitude and a vast throng, to pebbles that a taker grasps in his palm and throws into the sea. [End of his words. He said: "His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So We seized him and his hosts, and cast them into the sea﴾, is a counterpart to his arrogance, expressed by an act whose form is taking contemptible pebbles and then casting them into the sea with disdain. This is an image of His treating him with contempt and destroying him with this kind of destruction. And God knows best."] Similarly is His saying: ﴿And We set in it lofty mountains﴾ (Q. 77:27), ﴿and the earth and the mountains are lifted and crushed with a single blow﴾ (Q. 69:14), ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure, while the earth entire will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be rolled up in His right hand﴾ (Q. 39:67). These are only depictions and images of His power, and that every created thing, however great and mighty, is belittled beside His power.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 28, verses 41–42:

If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying, ﴿And We made them leaders calling to the Fire﴾? I say: its meaning is: "We counted them as leaders, callers to the Fire" [[His saying "We counted them as leaders, callers to the Fire" — this interpretation, and what follows it in his saying "It is permissible that We forsook them ..." to the end:

are both based on the premise that it is obligatory for Him, exalted is He, to do what is good, and that it is not permissible for Him to create evil. This is the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah. As for the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah, it is that nothing is obligatory upon Him, exalted is He, and it is permissible for Him to create evil just as He creates good. This has been verified in the discussion on Divine Unity (tawhid), so there is no need to interpret the verse with such strained reasoning. (Ibn 'Atiyyah / al-'Ta' [editor's marker])]], and we said: they are leaders calling to the Fire, just as the rightful successors are called leaders calling to the Garden. It is from your saying: "He made him stingy and wicked," when you call him so and say that he is stingy and wicked. [[Mahmud said: "Its meaning is: We called them leaders, callers to the Fire, just as you say: 'I made him stingy, wicked,' when you call him so." Ahmad said: There is no difference, according to the People of the Sunnah, between His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And He made the darknesses and the light﴾ and ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs﴾ and this verse. Whoever takes "making" to mean "naming" in our present case, fleeing from the belief that their calling to the Fire is created by God, exalted is He, is in the same position as one who takes it to mean naming in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs﴾, fleeing from the notion that night and day are created by God, exalted is He. There is no difference between denying one created thing from His power and denying every created thing. We seek refuge in God from that.]] The people of language explain his wickedness and stinginess as: "He made him stingy and wicked." From this is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And they made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾. The meaning of "calling them to the Fire" is calling them to its causes, which are disbelief and sins. ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped﴾, as the leaders who call to the Garden are helped. It is also permissible to read: "We forsook them until they became leaders of disbelief." The meaning of forsaking (khidhlan) is:

the withholding of divine favours (alutaf). He withholds them only from one whom He knows they would not benefit, namely the one who is determined upon disbelief, for whom signs and warnings are of no avail. Its manner is that of metonymy (kinayah), because withholding favours entails determination, while the purpose of mentioning it is:

the determination itself. It is as if it were said: they were determined upon disbelief until they became leaders in it, callers to it and to its evil consequence.

If you ask: what is the benefit of omitting the thing that follows (the mardūf) in favour of the thing that implies it (the radifah)? I say: mentioning the implying thing indicates the existence of the implied thing, so the existence of the implied thing is known together with the evidence attesting to its existence, and this is stronger in establishing it than mentioning it directly. Do you not see that you say: "Were it not that he is determined upon disbelief, his affair decided and his judgment fixed, the favours would not have been withheld from him"? By mentioning the withholding of favours, knowledge of the existence of determination upon disbelief is gained, and more: the establishment of proof of its existence.

This interpretation is supported by His saying, ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped﴾, as if it were said: "We forsook them in this world, and on the Day of Resurrection they are forsaken." As He said, ﴿And We followed them in this world with a curse﴾, that is, expulsion and removal from mercy, ﴿and on the Day of Resurrection they are of the despised﴾, that is, of the expelled and removed.
