He withholds them only from one whom He knows they would not benefit, namely the one who is determined upon disbelief, for whom signs and warnings are of no avail. Its manner is that of metonymy (kinayah), because withholding favours entails determination, while the purpose of mentioning it is:

the determination itself. It is as if it were said: they were determined upon disbelief until they became leaders in it, callers to it and to its evil consequence.

If you ask: what is the benefit of omitting the thing that follows (the mardūf) in favour of the thing that implies it (the radifah)? I say: mentioning the implying thing indicates the existence of the implied thing, so the existence of the implied thing is known together with the evidence attesting to its existence, and this is stronger in establishing it than mentioning it directly. Do you not see that you say: "Were it not that he is determined upon disbelief, his affair decided and his judgment fixed, the favours would not have been withheld from him"? By mentioning the withholding of favours, knowledge of the existence of determination upon disbelief is gained, and more: the establishment of proof of its existence.

This interpretation is supported by His saying, ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped﴾, as if it were said: "We forsook them in this world, and on the Day of Resurrection they are forsaken." As He said, ﴿And We followed them in this world with a curse﴾, that is, expulsion and removal from mercy, ﴿and on the Day of Resurrection they are of the despised﴾, that is, of the expelled and removed.

Basa'ir (insights): accusative, in the sense of a circumstantial state (hal). Basira (insight) is the light of the heart by which one gains insight, just as sight (basar) is the light of the eye by which one sees. The meaning is: We gave Moses the Torah as lights for hearts, because they were blind, unable to gain insight or to distinguish truth from falsehood. And guidance, because they were floundering in error. And mercy, because if they acted upon it they would attain the attainment of mercy. La'allahum yatadhakkarun (so that they might take heed): the desire that they should take heed. The desire has been likened to hope (tarajji), so the word is used metaphorically for it.

It is also permissible that what is meant is the hope of Moses (ʿalayhi al-salam) that they would take heed, as in His words, exalted is He: la'allahu yatadhakkaru (perhaps he will take heed). [[Mahmud said: "Its meaning is the desire for their taking heed, because desire resembles hope, so the word is used metaphorically for it. Or what is meant is the hope of Moses (peace be upon him) that they would take heed." Ahmad said: The second aspect is the correct one, and beware of the first, for it is Qadari.]]

Al-Gharbi (the western side): the place on the western side, which is the place where Musa's (peace be upon him) appointed meeting from Mount Tur took place, and where God wrote for him on the tablets. And the decreed command given to Musa (peace be upon him): the revelation that was revealed to him. The address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), saying: "And you were not present at the place where We revealed to Musa (peace be upon him)," nor were you among those who witnessed the revelation to him, or [who were] witnesses to the revelation to him, namely his chieftains whom he chose for the appointed meeting, so that you could have witnessed from direct observation what took place in Musa's (peace be upon him) appointed meeting. [And] the scribing of the Torah for him on the tablets, and other than that.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 28, verse 45:

If you say: How does His saying ﴿But We brought into being many generations﴾ connect with this discourse, and in what respect is it a corrective (istidrak) to it? I say: Its connection with it, and its being a corrective to it, is in that its meaning is: "But We brought into being, after the era of revelation up to your era, many generations, so that the span (al-'umur) lengthened over them, and the last of them is the generation in which you are, namely the period of the cessation of revelation and the effacement of knowledge. Therefore it was necessary to send you to them, so We sent you and We gave you knowledge (kasabnaka [[His saying "wa-kasabnaka al-'ilm": kasaba is transitive to two objects, as one says kasabtu ahli khayran and kasabtu al-rajula malan, as in al-Sihah. (Gh.)]]) of the stories of the prophets and the story of Moses, peace be upon them, as if He said: 'You were not a witness to Moses and what befell him, but We revealed to you.'" So He mentioned the cause of the revelation, which is the prolongation of the interval, and He indicated the effect by it, in accordance with God's habit, glory be to Him, of brevity in His discourse. Thus this corrective is similar to the two corrections that follow it: ﴿Nor were you a dweller among the people of Madyan﴾, that is, a resident among them, ﴿reciting to them Our verses﴾, that is, reading them to them, learning from them. He means: the verses in which is the story of Shu'ayb and his people. "But We sent you and informed you of them and taught them to you."

When We called (ﷺ)... He means the calling of Musa (peace be upon him) on the night of the secret conversation (munajat) and His speaking to him. "But" (We sent you as) a mercy. It is also read *rahmatun* with the nominative (رفع), meaning: it is a mercy (هي رحمة) that there came to them no warner (ما أَتاهُمْ من نذير) in the time of the interval (fatra) between you and Jesus, which was five hundred and fifty years. A similar statement is His saying: ﴿that you may warn a people whose fathers were not warned﴾.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 28, verse 47:

The first *lawla* is *imtina'iyya* (expressing the non-fulfilment of a condition due to the absence of its consequent), and its response is omitted. The second *lawla* is *tahdidiyya* (exhortative). One of the two *fa'*s is for conjunction (*'atf*), and the other is the response of the *lawla*, because it has the force of a command (*amr*), since a command motivates an action, and the motivator and the one who urges belong to the same category. The meaning is: "Had it not been that they would say, when they are punished for what they had sent forward of polytheism and sins: 'Why did You not send to us a messenger?', arguing against us with that: 'We would not have sent to them.'" That is, the sending of the messenger to them is only so that they bear the proof and do not impose it [on Us]. This is like His saying ﴿so that people will have no argument against God after the messengers﴾, and ﴿lest you say: "There came to us no bringer of good tidings and no warner."﴾ and ﴿"Why did You not send to us a messenger, so that we might follow Your signs?"﴾

If you say: How does this meaning hold, when you have made the punishment the cause of the sending, not the saying, given that the particle of prohibition (*imtina'*) is attached to it and not to the saying?

I say: The saying is the intended thing, that it be a cause for the sending of the messengers. But since the punishment is the cause of the saying, and its existence depends on the existence of the punishment, the punishment is treated as if it were the cause of the sending through the medium of the saying. So *lawla* was attached to it, and the saying was brought in as coordinated with it by the *fa'* that gives the meaning of causation. [[Mahmud said: "*Lawla* the first is *imtina'iyya*, and the second is *tahdidiyya*. The first *fa'* is conjunctive and the second is the response of *lawla*.

The meaning: Had it not been that they would say when they were punished: 'Why did You not send to us a messenger, so that we might argue with that, [and] We would not have sent anyone to them.' If you say:

How does this meaning hold, when you have made the punishment the cause of the sending, not the saying, given that the particle of prohibition is attached to it and not to the saying?

I say: The punishment is the cause of the saying, and it is the cause of the cause, so it was made a cause, and the original cause was coordinated with it by the causal *fa'*." Ahmad said:

Similar to this is His saying ﴿lest one of them should err, so that one of them may remind the other﴾. The secret in making the cause of a cause a cause, and coordinating the original cause with it, is two matters. The first: that the increase of concern requires precedence, and this is the secret that Sibawayh revealed. The second: that in this arrangement there is an indication of the causality of each of them. As for the first, it is due to its being joined to the particle of causation, which is *an*. As for the second, it is due to its being joined to the *fa'* of causation, and this meaning is not conveyed except by your saying ﴿lest one of them should err, so that one of them may remind﴾, not by the speaker saying: "that one of them remind the other if she errs."

Some grammarians used to raise this verse as a difficulty for the grammarians and for the *Ahl al-Sunna* (the Sunni theologians; the people of the prophetic custom and community). They would say: *lawla*, according to the specialists, indicates the non-occurrence of its response because of the existence of what follows it. In that case, what follows it in the verse, namely the punishment of these mentioned people, would be existent on the assumption of the absence of the sending of messengers, and its omitted response, the non-sending, would not occur, because it is impossible by the first. And when the non-sending does not occur, the sending must occur. So the event after it becomes problematic for the *Ahl al-Sunna*, because they say: there is no injustice before the sending of messengers, so the punishment cannot be conceived on the assumption of the absence of the sending, since it is an event that is a recompense for violating the rulings of the Law, and if there is no Law there is no violation and no punishment. The response is also problematic for the grammarians, because it would entail that it not occur, namely the absence of the sending of messengers, but the event after it requires its occurrence. Then the one who raised this difficulty answered it by postulating an omitted element. The original reading: "and had it not been that the dislike that a calamity should befall them [...]". And then the difficulty disappears from both groups.

The verification in my view regarding the response is contrary to that. The difficulty arose only from the grammarians' refusal to admit the meaning of *lawla*, which they hold to indicate that what follows it exists and that its response is impossible because of it. The correct description of its meaning is that it indicates that what follows it prevents its response, the reverse of *law*, whose meaning is the necessity of its response by what follows it. Then the preventer may be existent or may be assumed, and the verse belongs to the category of assuming the existence of the preventer. Likewise the necessity in *law* may be one thing necessitating two things, so the negation of one of its necessitators does not necessitate the negation of the other. On this description the difficulty raised against *law* in his saying: "Excellent servant is Suhayb; had he not feared God, he would not have disobeyed Him" disappears. So reflect on this discussion; I have opened it, and it has benefits for the reflecting one. And God is the Granter of success.]]. Its meaning returns to your saying: "And had it not been for their saying this when a calamity befell them, We would not have sent." But this method was chosen for a subtle point: namely, that if they were not punished, for example, for their disbelief, and they had witnessed what compelled them to certain knowledge, they would not have said ﴿"Why did You not send to us a messenger?"﴾. The cause of this saying is only the punishment and nothing else, not regret over what they missed of faith in their Creator. In this there is, as is evident, a strong testimony to the firmness and deep-rootedness of their disbelief, like His saying ﴿and if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden﴾. And since most actions are performed by the hands, every action was expressed by "committing with the hands" and "sending forward the hands," even if it is an action of the hearts. This is a broadening in speech, making the minority follow the majority, and giving the majority precedence over the minority.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 28, verse 48:

When the Truth came to them, namely the Messenger who confirms the Book, with the miraculous Book and with all the other miracles, and their excuses were cut off and the path of their argument was blocked, they said: ﴿Why was he not given the like of what was given to Musa?﴾ — namely the Book sent down all at once, and the turning of the staff into a live serpent, the splitting of the sea, and other signs. So they came up with proposals founded on obstinacy and stubbornness, just as they said: ﴿Why was no treasure sent down to him, or why did no angel come with him?﴾ and the like. ﴿Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Musa?﴾ — meaning: their fellows of the same kind, whose way is their way and whose obstinacy is their obstinacy, and they are the disbelievers of the time of Musa, peace be upon him. ﴿...in what was given to Musa?﴾ And al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The Arabs had a root in the days of Musa, peace be upon him; so its meaning on this reading is: did not their forefathers disbelieve? They said of Musa and Harun: ﴿Two sorceries that support each other﴾ — i.e., they cooperated. It was also read as ﴿tazahharā﴾ (idhhār, without assimilation of the letters). And ﴿siḥrān﴾ means: two possessors of sorcery. Or they made them two sorceries as an exaggeration in describing them as sorcery. Or they meant two kinds of sorcery, ﴿each of them﴾ with regard to each one of them.

If you ask: With what did you connect the phrase ﴿min qabl﴾ ("before") in this interpretation? I say: with ﴿lam yakfurū﴾ ("did they not disbelieve"). I may also connect it with ﴿ūtiya﴾ ("was given"), so the meaning becomes that the people of Makkah who made this statement, just as they disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ) and in the Qur'an, had also disbelieved in Musa, peace be upon him, and in the Torah. They said of Musa and Muhammad, peace be upon them both: ﴿Two sorcerers that support each other﴾. Or, regarding the two Books: ﴿Two sorceries that support each other﴾. That was when they sent a delegation to the leaders of the Jews in Madinah to ask them about Muhammad (ﷺ), and they informed them that his description and attributes are mentioned and that he is in their book. The delegation returned to Quraysh and told them what the Jews had said, and at that they said: ﴿Two sorcerers that support each other﴾.

He (the Qur'an) is more guided than both of them, the Torah revealed to Musa (peace be upon him) and that revealed to me.

This conditional is of the kind I mentioned: a condition used to establish a matter whose truth is certain, because the impossibility of bringing a book more guided than the two books is a known and established matter, with no room for doubt. It is also permissible that the particle of doubt (in) is intended for mockery of them (al-tahakkum bihim).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 28, verse 50:

If you say: what is the difference between the verb of response (istijaba) in the verse and its use in His saying:

"فلم يستجبه عند ذاك مجيب" [[The line's first half is: "وداع دعا يا من يجيب إلى الندى"

Alayan (the editor's note).

I say: The explanation of this line has already been given in the first volume, page 456, so refer to it if you wish. (Note by its corrector.)]]

where it is followed by no preposition (lam)? I say: This verb takes its object directly as the supplication (du'a'), and takes the one who supplicates with the preposition lam. The supplication is generally omitted when it is followed by the one who supplicates, so one says: "istajaba Allahu du'a'ahu" (God answered his supplication) or "istajaba lahu" (He answered him), and one hardly says "istajaba lahu du'a'ahu." As for the line, its meaning is: "fa-lam yastajib du'a'ahu" (he did not answer his supplication), with the noun elided (hadhf al-mudaf). If you say: "Response requires a supplication, and there is no supplication here." I say: His saying "fa-'tu bi-kitabin" is a command to bring a book, and a command urges the act and calls to it. So it is as if He said: "If they do not respond to your call to bring the more guided Book, then know that they have been rendered helpless, and no proof remains for them except following their desires." Then He said: "وَمَنْ أَضَلُّ مِمَّنِ لا يتبع في دينه إلا هَواهُ بِغَيْرِ هُدىً مِنَ اللَّهِ" meaning: sealed upon his heart, deprived of divine kindnesses. "إِنَّ اللَّهَ لا يَهْدِي" meaning: He does not show kindness to the people who persist in wrongdoing, those for whom one who shows kindness is a mocker. His saying "بغير هدى" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: forsaken, left to himself and his desires.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 28, verse 51:

It is read as "waṣṣalnā" with shaddah and as "waṣalnā" without it. The meaning is that the Qur'an came to them consecutively and continuously: promise and warning, stories and lessons, admonitions and counsel, in the hope that they would take heed and prosper. Or it means that it was sent down to them in a continuous manner, some of it following right after another, like His saying: ﴿Never does there come to them a new reminder from the Most Merciful except that they turn away from it.﴾ (Q. 26:5)

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 28, verse 52:

It was revealed concerning the believers among the People of the Book. It is also reported from Rifa'ah ibn Qurzah that he said: "It was revealed concerning ten people, of whom I am one." It was also said: it was revealed concerning forty of the Muslims among the People of the Gospel (Injil): thirty-two of them came with Ja'far from the land of Abyssinia (al-Habasha), and eight from al-Sham (Greater Syria).

The pronoun in "min qablihi" (before it) refers to the Qur'an.

"If you ask: what is the difference between the two resumptive clauses, 'innahu' and 'inna'? I answer: the first is a reason (ta'lil) for believing in it, since its being the truth from God makes it fitting that one should believe in it. The second is an explanation (bayan) of their saying 'We believed in it', because it could be a faith of recent date or of long standing; so they informed that their belief in it is ancient, for their earlier forefathers read of its mention in the former Books, and their sons after them ﴿from before it﴾, that is, before its existence and its descent, ﴿Muslims﴾, being on the religion of Islam, because Islam is the attribute of every monotheist who confirms the revelation."

Their patience (*bi-ma sabaru*): by their patience in holding fast to faith in the Torah and faith in the Qur'an.

Or, by their patience in holding fast to faith in the Qur'an before its revelation and after its revelation.

Or, by their patience in bearing the harm of the polytheists and the People of the Book.

Similar to this is ﴿He will give you a double portion of His mercy﴾ (57:28). And ﴿repelling evil with good﴾ means obedience repelling the earlier disobedience. Or, forbearance repelling harm.

"Peace be upon you" (salamun ʿalaykum) is a farewell and a parting of ways. It is reported from al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him, that it is "a word of forbearance from the believers." "We do not seek out the ignorant" means: we do not want to associate with them or keep their company. If you ask: whom did they address with their saying "to you your deeds"? I say: the idle talkers, whom His saying "and when they hear idle talk" points to.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 28, verse 56:

"You do not guide whom you love" (lā tahdī man aḥbabta): you cannot bring into Islam everyone you wish to enter it from your people and others, because you are a servant who does not know who has a seal upon his heart from among others. "But God guides whom He wills" (wa-lākinna Allāha yahdī man yashā'): He, who knows that he is not sealed upon his heart, and that the subtle favours (al-alṭāf) benefit him, so He joins His subtle favours to him until they call him to acceptance. "And He knows best those who are guided" (wa-huwa a'lamu bil-muhtadīn): those who accept, from those who do not accept. Al-Zajjaj said:

The Muslims are agreed that it was revealed concerning Abu Talib. When Abu Talib was at the point of death he said: "O assembly of the Banu Hashim, obey Muhammad and affirm him, and you will prosper and be rightly guided." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Do you order them to give counsel to themselves and leave it for yourself?" He said: "What do you want, nephew?" He said: "I want one word from you, for you are at the last day of the days of this world: that you say, 'There is no god but God,' and I will bear witness for you with it before God." He said: "Nephew, I know that you are truthful, but I dislike that it be said that I faltered at death [[His saying "I dislike that it be said I faltered at death": in al-Sihah, kharu'a al-rajul (with kasra): he became weak, so he is khari'. (ʿ)]], and were it not that it would be a reproach upon you and upon the sons of your father after me, I would have said it, and would have gladdened your eye with it at parting, because of what I see of the intensity of your grief and your sincere counsel. But I shall die upon the religion of the elders: ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, Hashim and ʿAbd Manaf."

Quraysh said [[I did not find this. The story of Abu Talib's death in the two Sahihs, related by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib from his son, is in a different context or is shorter than this.]] It is also said that the speaker was al-Harith ibn Uthman ibn Nawfal ibn Abd Manaf: "We know that you are upon the truth, but we fear that if we follow you and oppose the Arabs in that, they will snatch us from our land," and "we are only a handful (ukla ra's), that is, few in number." So God silenced them (fa-alqamahum Allah al-hajar, "God silenced them with the stone") by stating that He had established them in the sanctuary (haram) which He made secure through the sanctity of the House (the Ka'bah), and made its inhabitants secure through its sanctity. The Arabs in the pre-Islamic period around them were raiding and fighting one another, while they themselves were secure in their sanctuary and feared nothing. By the sanctity of the House they dwelt in a valley without crops, and fruits and provisions were brought to them from every direction. If God granted them security and provision by the sanctity of the House alone, while they were disbelievers worshipping idols, how could it be consistent for Him to expose them to being snatched away and to strip them of security when they add to the sanctity of the House the sanctity of Islam?

The attribution of security to the people of the sanctuary is literal (haqiqa, literal usage), and its attribution to the sanctuary itself is figurative (majaz, figurative usage). Yujba ilayhi means "is brought or gathered to it." It has been read with the yā' and with the tā' (yujba and tujba). It has also been read tujna, with the nūn, from al-jany (gathering fruit), and its transitive use with ilā is like the poet's line: "yujnā ilayya fīhi" (it is gathered to me in it), and "yujnā ilā al-khāfah" (it is gathered into the khāfah). [[His words "and yujnā ilā al-khāfah": in al-Sihah, "al-khāfah" is a leather container in which honey is gathered. It also says "yashtār" means "yajtanī" (is gathered).]] "Thamarat" is read with two dammas, and with one damma and a sukūn. The meaning of "kull" (all) here is abundance, as in the verse ﴿and she has been given of everything﴾, and ﴿but most of them do not know﴾. The phrase ﴿from Us﴾ is connected to ﴿provision﴾, meaning: a few of them acknowledge that this provision is from God, but most of them are ignorant, do not know this, and do not perceive it. Had they known that it was from God, they would have known that fear and security are from Him, and they would not have feared being snatched away if they believed in Him and renounced His rivals.

If you ask: with what is "rizqan" (as provision) in the accusative? I say: if you make it a verbal noun (maṣdar), it may be in the accusative by the sense of what precedes it, because the meaning of "is brought to it the fruits of every thing" and "is provided the fruits of every thing" is one. It may also be an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu). If you make it in the sense of "provided" (marzuq), it is a circumstantial state (hal) of "the fruits," since it is specified by its annexation, just as an indefinite noun is put in the accusative as a state when it is specified by a qualifier.

This is a warning to the people of Makkah about the evil end of a people who were in a situation like theirs, enjoying God's blessing of resting in the shade of security and ease of livelihood. They were ungrateful for the blessing and met it with insolence and exultance, [[His words "they were ungrateful for the blessing and met it with insolence and exultance" mean: they treated it lightly and belittled it. Al-ashr and al-batar: intense exultation; al-marah: intense joy, as stated in al-Sihah. (Ṭ)]] so God destroyed them and ruined their dwellings. The word maʿīshatahā (its livelihood) is in the accusative either by removing the preposition and letting the verb reach it directly, as in God's words ﴿Musa chose seventy men of his people﴾, or as an adverb of time in itself, as in your saying, "Zayd is in my opinion (ẓannī) steadfast," or by supposing an omitted temporal noun in apposition, the original being: "its livelihood's days were insolent," as in "the rising of the star" and "the arrival of the pilgrim." Or by implying in "batirat" the meaning of: disbelieved and ungrateful. [[His words "as in your saying, Zayd is in my opinion steadfast" mean: in my opinion. (Ṭ)]] It was said: al-batar is the poor handling of wealth, which is that one does not observe God's right in it. ﴿But only a little of their dwellings was lived in afterward﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him, said: none dwelt in them except the traveler and the passerby for a day or an hour. It is also possible that the ill omen of the sins of those who were destroyed remained in their dwellings, so whoever dwelt in them of their descendants did not remain there except briefly. ﴿And We were the inheritors﴾ of those dwellings from their inhabitants, meaning: We left them in a state where no one could inhabit them, or We ruined them and leveled them with the ground.

Traces remain behind their owners for a while, and then annihilation overtakes them and they follow.

[[Where is the one whose building was the two pyramids? What of his people, what of his day, what of his place of death?

Traces remain behind their owners for a while, and then annihilation overtakes them and they follow.

Said by Abu al-Tayyib (al-Mutanabbi) when he entered Egypt and saw the pyramids that king Surand had built. It was also said: Sinan ibn Mushalshal. It was also said: Idris, peace be upon him. "Al-Harmān" is the dual of "haram" (as in sabab), and he meant by the two the ones near Egypt. "Yawmuhu" is the time of his reign, and it may be that it is the day of his death, just as "al-maṣraʿ" is the place of death. The question about this after the question about his people serves to bring both images to mind and the difference between the two states. Then he said "tatakhallaf" (remain behind), meaning: the traces, of buildings, trees and other things, are delayed for a long time after their owners.

Then annihilation overtakes them and they follow their owners, however long their delay. It is also possible that the meaning is: "for a little while," so the tanwin is for magnification or diminution.]]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 28, verse 59:

﴿Your Lord was never one to destroy the towns, until He had sent to their mother-town a messenger reciting to them Our verses.﴾ That is, to its origin and its capital, which are its affairs and dependencies, a messenger to establish the proof and cut off excuse, although He knew that they would not believe. Or: it was not within God's judgment and prior decree that He would destroy the towns on earth until He had sent to Umm al-Qura (meaning Makkah) a messenger, who was Muhammad (ﷺ), the Seal of the Prophets. It is also read as ﴿umminha﴾, with the hamza vowelled by a damma or a kasra, following the case of the genitive that precedes it. This is a statement of His justice and His exemption from wrongdoing, since He informs us that He will not destroy them except when they deserve destruction through their wrongdoing. [[Mahmud said: "This is a statement of His justice and His exemption from wrongdoing, in that He informs us that He will not destroy them except when they deserve punishment, and they do not deserve it until the proof is firmly established against them by the sending of messengers." Ahmad said: This is a lapse by al-Zamakhshari into an answer that falls short of a question directed at the Qadariyya (the advocates of human free will and of the rational obligation of justice), for which they have no answer. The question arises in this verse as follows: if reason could establish divine obligations, the proof would stand against people even without the sending of messengers, since reason is an authority; and they have no way to escape this question.]] He would not destroy them while they are wrongdoers except after the proof has been firmly established and the obligation made binding through the sending of messengers. He does not make His knowledge of their conditions a proof against them. He exempts His essence from destroying them while they are not wrongdoers, as God, exalted is He, says: ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns wrongfully while their people were reforming.﴾ In His words ﴿wrongfully﴾ He explicitly states that if He destroyed them while they were reformers, that would be an injustice on His part, and that His state of self-sufficiency and wisdom is incompatible with injustice. He indicated this with the negative particle together with its lam, as God, exalted is He, says: ﴿And God would never waste your faith.﴾

Whatever thing you have been given from the provisions of this world, it is nothing but enjoyment and adornment for a few days, and that is the duration of the passing life. "But what is with Allah" — that is, His reward — "is better" in itself than that, "and more lasting," because its permanence is everlasting and never-ending.

It is also read "ya'qilun" (with the letter ya', i.e., "they reflect"), and this is more forceful in admonition.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that Allah created the world and made its people three kinds: the believer, the hypocrite, and the disbeliever. The believer takes provision (from it), the hypocrite adorns himself (with it), and the disbeliever enjoys it.

This verse is an affirmation and clarification of the one before it. "Al-wa'd al-hasan" (the good promise) means the reward, because it is lasting benefit given in a manner of honour and entitlement, and what could be better than that? For this reason God named Paradise "al-husna" (the best). "Laqiyahu" (meeting him) is like God's words: ﴿And He gave them radiance and joy﴾ [76:11], and its opposite: ﴿but they will meet error﴾ [25:68]. "Min al-muhdarin" (among those brought forward) means among those who are brought forward to the Fire. A similar usage is found in ﴿I would certainly be among those brought forward﴾ [37:57], and ﴿so they denied him, and indeed they will be brought forward﴾ [37:158]. It was said: it was revealed concerning the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and Abu Jahl. It was also said: concerning Ali, Hamzah and Abu Jahl. And it was said: concerning Ammar ibn Yasir and al-Walid ibn al-Mughira.

If you ask: explain to me the two fa's and thumma, and inform me of their positions. I answer:

The verse before it mentioned the enjoyment of the life of this world and what is with God, and the difference between them. Then he followed it with His words ﴿Is one to whom We have made a good promise﴾, meaning: after this manifest disparity, are the people of the Hereafter equated with the people of this world? This is the meaning of the first fa' and an explanation of its position. As for the second, it is for causation, because meeting the one promised is caused by the promise, which is the guarantee of good. As for "thumma" (then), it is to indicate that the state of being brought forward is delayed relative to the state of being given enjoyment, not that its time is delayed relative to its time.

It is also read "thumma huwa" with the ha' pronounced with sukun (as "thumma hu"), in the manner in which it was said "'udh" for "'udhd" (ʿaḍd), likening the separated to the joined. The sukun of the ha' in "fa-huwa", "huwa" and "lahuwa" is preferable, because a single letter is not pronounced on its own, so it is like the joined form.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 28, verse 62:

"My partners" is built on their supposition (za'm), and there is mockery in it. If you say: "zaʿama" (to suppose, assert) requires two objects, as in the verse of the poet:

"... And that which has lived, O Umm Malik, will die, and I did not suppose you to be a place of isolation from that."

He says: every living thing, however long its life, will die. I did not suppose you, O Umm Malik, to be a place of isolation (maʿzal) from that judgment or death. The maʿzal is the place of seclusion and solitude; meaning: I did not think you were in a place of isolation from it, or a person of isolation, or one who isolates herself, or that the saying itself is an intensification.

Then where are the two objects? I say: they are omitted, and the estimate is: "those whom you used to suppose as my partners." It is permissible to omit both objects in the category of "ẓanantu" (I thought), but it is not correct to limit oneself to only one of them.

Those against whom the Word has been justified: the devils, or the leaders of disbelief and its heads. The meaning of "the Word has been justified against them" is: its requirement became binding upon them and was established, namely His saying, "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind, all together." "These" is the subject (mubtada'), "whom We led astray" is its description (sifah), the returning pronoun to the relative clause is omitted, and "We led them astray" is the predicate (khabar).

The kaf (in "as We led astray") is a description of an omitted verbal noun (sifat masdar), its estimated form being: "We led them astray with a leading astray like that by which we were led astray." They mean: we were not led astray except by our own choice, not that there were above us misleaders who incited us by compulsion and coercion. Or: they invited us to error and made it attractive to us; so these likewise went astray by their own choice, because our leading them astray was nothing but whispering and enticement, not compulsion and coercion. There is therefore no difference between our going astray and their going astray. Even if our enticement was a summons for them to disbelief, there was set against it God's summons to them to belief, through the proofs of reason He placed within them, the messengers He sent to them, and the books He revealed to them, filled with promise and threat, admonitions and restraints; and that is sufficient as a deterrent from disbelief and a summons to belief. This is the meaning of what God related of Satan: "Indeed, God promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you, but I failed you. I had no authority over you except that I invited you, and you responded to me. So do not blame me; blame yourselves" [Qur'an 14:22].

God placed this meaning first, when He said to Iblis: "Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you among the misguided" [Qur'an 15:42]. "We disown before You them and what they chose of disbelief for themselves, out of their own desire for falsehood and hatred of truth, not by any power of ours to coerce them, nor any authority; they were not worshipping us, but were only worshipping their own desires and obeying their appetites." The two sentences are left without a conjunction because they confirm the meaning of the first sentence.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 28, verses 64–66:

﴿If only they had been guided.﴾ This has several possible senses: (a) a way of finding a means by which to ward off the punishment; (b) or, "If only they had been guided and believers, they would not have seen it"; (c) or, they wished that they had been guided; (d) or, they were bewildered at the sight of it and were confounded (wa-sadaru), so that they could not find any path. [[Shaykh's note: "wa-sadaru" means "they were bewildered." So noted by al-Sihah. (ʿA.)]] He first relates what will rebuke them for taking [the gods] as partners, then what the devils or their leaders will say when they are rebuked. For when they are rebuked for worshipping the gods, they make the excuse that the devils were the ones who led them astray and made their worship seem attractive to them. Then [he relates] what amounts to a mockery of them: their calling upon their gods, the gods' abandonment of them, and their inability to help them. Then [he relates] what they will be silenced by, namely the argument against them through the sending of messengers and the removal of excuses.

﴿Then the reports will be blinded to them﴾: the reports will become like blindness to them all, so that they cannot be guided to them. ﴿So they will not question one another﴾: they will not ask one another as people question each other about difficult matters, because they are all equal in the blindness of the reports to them and in their inability to answer.

Another reading is: "fa-ʿamiyat" (so it was blinded).

By "the report" (nabaʾ) is meant the information about what the one sent to them answered his messenger. Since the prophets, because of the terror of that Day, will stammer in answering such a question and will leave the matter to the knowledge of God, [this is] His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the Day when God gathers the messengers, and says, "What answer were you given?" They will say, "We have no knowledge. Surely You are the Knower of the unseen."﴾ So consider what is the case with the misguided among their peoples.

Then as for one who repents from among the polytheists, renouncing polytheism, and combines faith with righteous deeds, perhaps he will be among the successful in the sight of God. And "perhaps" (ʿasā) from the Generous (al-Karīm) is a certainty. It is also permissible that it be understood as expressing hope and aspiration on the part of the penitent, as if he had said: let him hope to be successful.

The word khayra (choice) is from takhayyur (choosing), like tiyara (omen) from tatayyur (taking omens). It is used as a verbal noun meaning "choosing," and also in the sense of "the one chosen," as in the saying: "Muhammad is God's chosen one (khiyara) from among His creation." The phrase "They had no choice" (مَا كانَ لَهُمُ الْخِيَرَةُ) is an explanation of His words "and He chooses" (وَيَخْتارُ), because its meaning is "and He chooses whatever He wills," and for this reason the conjunction (al-'atif) is not inserted. The meaning is that choice belongs to God Most High in His acts; He knows best the aspects of wisdom in them, and it is not for any of His creatures to choose over Him. It has been said that the cause of this revelation was the statement of al-Walid ibn al-Mughira:

"Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from the two cities?"

That is, God does not send the messengers by the choice of those to whom they are sent. It has also been said that the meaning is "and He chooses what is a choice for them," i.e., He chooses for the servants what is better and more suitable for them, and He knows their interests better than they do themselves. This is from the expression used for two matters: "there is no choice for the chooser in them." If you ask: where is the returning pronoun (al-raji') from the relative clause to the relative pronoun when you take ma as a relative pronoun? I answer: the original sentence is "what they had a choice in" (ما كان لهم فيه الخيرة), so "fihi" (in it) was omitted, just as "minhu" (from it) was omitted in His words "Indeed that is among the resolute matters of affairs" (إِنَّ ذلِكَ لَمِنْ عَزْمِ الْأُمُورِ), because it is understood. "Glory be to God" (سُبْحانَ اللَّهِ): God is free of their associating partners with Him, and of the audacity that drives them to act against God and to choose over Him what is not for them to choose.

Their breasts conceal (from) the enmity toward the Messenger of Allah and his envy, and what they openly display of their slander against him.

And their saying: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of importance from the two cities?" (Others are then chosen over him for prophethood.) "He is Allah, and He is the One who alone possesses divinity, specially reserved for it. There is no god but He" is an affirmation of that, like your saying: "The Ka'bah is the qiblah; there is no qiblah but it." If you ask: praise in this world is apparent, so what is praise in the Hereafter? I answer: it is their saying, ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has removed from us grief﴾, ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us﴾, and it was said, ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾. And the glorifying there is out of pleasure, not burden. In a hadith: they are inspired with tasbih (glorification of Allah) and taqdis (sanctification of Allah). [[Narrated by Muslim from the hadith of Jabir, within a longer report describing the people of Paradise, in which it says: "They are inspired with tasbih and tahmid as they are inspired with breathing." And in another narration from him: "tasbih and takbir."]] "And to Him belongs the judgment": the judgment (qada') between His servants.

And their saying: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of importance from the two cities?" (Others are then chosen over him for prophethood.) "He is Allah, and He is the One who alone possesses divinity, specially reserved for it. There is no god but He" is an affirmation of that, like your saying: "The Ka'bah is the qiblah; there is no qiblah but it." I answer: it is their saying, ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has removed from us grief﴾, ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us﴾, and it was said, ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾. And the glorifying there is out of pleasure, not burden. In a hadith: they are inspired with tasbih (glorification of Allah) and taqdis (sanctification of Allah). [[Narrated by Muslim from the hadith of Jabir, within a longer report describing the people of Paradise, in which it says: "They are inspired with tasbih and tahmid as they are inspired with breathing." And in another narration from him: "tasbih and takbir."]] "And to Him belongs the judgment": the judgment (qada') between His servants.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 28, verse 71–73:

أَرَأَيْتُمْ (ʾara'aytum): it is also read as "araytum" with the hamza omitted, though this is not a regular (qiyasi) omission. Its meaning is: "Tell me, who has power to do this?" Al-sarmad (al-sarmad): that which is lasting and continuous, from al-sard, which means successive continuity. From it comes their saying concerning the sacred months: "three in succession (sard) and one singly (fard)." The letter mim is an added letter, and its pattern is fa'mal. Its parallel is dalamas, from al-dalas [[His saying "its parallel is dalamas from al-dalas": in al-Sihah, al-dalas means soft and glossy, and al-dalamas means glossy. It is said: dalasat al-dir' (with a fatha on the first letter). (ʿ)]]. If you ask: why was it not said "by day in which you move about (tatasarrafun)," just as it was said "by night in which you rest (taskununa)"? I answer: he mentioned the light, which is the sunlight, because the benefits connected with it are numerous, and it is not limited to earning a livelihood alone. Darkness does not hold that same status. For this reason, the light is paired with "Will you not then hear?" because hearing perceives what sight does not perceive, namely the mention of its benefits and the description of its advantages. The night is paired with "Will you not then see?" because others see from the benefit of darkness what you see, and you see from the rest and similar things. And from His mercy He paired the night and the day for three purposes: that you may rest in one of them, which is the night; that you may seek of God's bounty in the other, which is the day; and for the sake of your giving thanks.

With this verse I have followed the method of *laff* (grouping several elements under a single treatment) in repeating the rebuke concerning the taking of partners, to indicate that nothing brings about the anger of God more than associating partners with Him (*shirk*), just as nothing brings about His pleasure more than affirming His oneness (*tawhid*). O Allah, just as You have admitted us among the people of Your *tawhid*, admit us among those who are saved from Your threat.

And We will draw out from every nation a witness, who is their prophet, because the prophets of the nations are witnesses over them, bearing testimony to what they were upon. Then We will say to the nation, "Bring your proof" concerning what you were upon of polytheism and opposition to the Messenger. Then they will know at that time that the truth belongs to Allah and to His Messenger, not to them and their devils, and what they used to fabricate will be lost to them, absent from them as a lost thing is absent.

Qarun (Qarūn) is a foreign (non-Arabic) name, like Harun (Hārūn), and it is not declined because of its foreignness and definiteness. Had it been a pattern of the form fā'ūl derived from qarn, it would have been declined. It has been said: the meaning of "from his people" is that he believed in him. It has also been said that he was an Israelite, a cousin of Musa:

He is Qarun ibn Yasihar ibn Qahith ibn Lawi ibn Ya'qub, and Musa ibn 'Imran ibn Qahith. It has been said that Musa was his paternal uncle's son, and he was called al-Munawwar (the Illuminated) for the beauty of his appearance. He was the most proficient of the Children of Israel in the Torah, but he was hypocritical, just as the Samiri was hypocritical, and he said: "If prophethood belongs to Musa, peace be upon him, and the altar and the sacrifice to Harun, then what about me?" It is narrated that when Musa led them across the sea, and the prophetic mission and the priesthood (al-hibarah) passed to Harun, who would offer the sacrifice and become the head among them, while the sacrifice had been (assigned) to Musa, and Musa handed it over to his brother, Qarun felt resentment and envied the two of them. He said to Musa: "The matter belongs to you two, and I am of no account. Until when shall I endure?" Musa said: "This is the doing of God." He said: "By God, I will not believe until you bring a sign." So he commanded the leaders of the Children of Israel that each one should bring his staff. He bundled them and placed them in the tent where revelation used to descend upon him. They used to guard their staffs at night. In the morning, behold, Harun's staff was trembling and had green leaves, and it was of almond wood. Qarun said: "This is no more wondrous than what you do by magic." So he "transgressed against them" (fa-baghā 'alayhim), from al-baghy, which means injustice. It has been said: Pharaoh had appointed him over the Children of Israel, and he oppressed them. It has also been said: from al-baghy, which means arrogance and haughtiness: he displayed pride over them through the abundance of his wealth and children. It has been said: he made his garments a span longer than theirs.

Al-Mafatih (the keys) is the plural of miftah (with a kasra), which is that by which something is opened. It has been said that they are the treasuries; the analogical singular of it would be mafhat (with a fatha). It is said: "al-hamlu nā'a bihi" when the load weighed him down until it made him lean. Al-'Usbah means a large group, and al-'usabah is similar to it. Ista'sabu means they gathered together. It has been said: sixty mules used to carry the keys of his treasuries, one key for each treasury, and no key exceeded a finger in size, and they were made of leather. Abu Razin said: one key would suffice for Kufa. The matter is greatly exaggerated in the mention of this, with the wording: the treasures, the keys, the weighing down, the group, and the people of strength.

Badil ibn Maysara recited "la-yanū'u" with a ya'. Its justification is that al-mafatih is explained as the treasuries, and it is given the judgment of what it is attached to, because of their connection and association, as in your saying "dhahabat Ahl al-Yamamah" (the people of Yamama went away). The place of "idh" is in the accusative, governed by "tanū'" and by "lā tafraḥ", as in His saying: "and do not rejoice in what He has given you" (57:23), and in the words of the poet:

Nor am I one who exults when fortune delights me, nor one who grieves at its changing turns.
Nor do I seek evil; but when evil leaves me, I mount it when I am provoked to it.

These are by Hudba ibn Khashram, when Mu'awiya led him to al-Harra to take retribution from him for Ziyad ibn Zayd al-'Udhri. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Hassan met him and asked him to recite, and he recited these verses. Al-mifrah means one who rejoices greatly. The intent is the negation of rejoicing at its root. Sarf al-dahr means its vicissitudes. "Idha" is conditional, so after it there must be a verb, meaning: "if evil has left me." "Uhmal" is in the passive voice and "arkab" in the active. The meaning is: I have tested fortune, and when it is treacherous, yet I still do not abase myself.

That is because one does not rejoice in this world except one who is content with it and at rest in it. As for one whose heart is set on the Hereafter and who knows that he will soon depart from what he possesses, his soul does not prompt him to rejoice. How excellent is what the poet said:

The greatest grief in my eyes, within joy, is that its possessor is certain of departing from it.

(This is by Abu al-Tayyib: the greatest grief in my eyes is at the time of joy, whose possessor is certain to leave it, and so is all the joy of this world.)

"Wabtaghi fīmā ātākal-Lāhu al-dār al-ākhirah" (And seek, in what God has given you, the abode of the Hereafter): by doing in it deeds of goodness of the kinds of obligatory and recommended acts, and making it your provision for the Hereafter. "Wa lā tansa naṣībaka" (And do not forget your portion): this is to take from it what suffices you and sets you right. "Wa aḥsin kamā aḥsana Allāhu ilayk" (And be good as God has been good to you), or: be good by thanking and obeying God as He has been good to you. Corruption in the earth is what he was upon of injustice and transgression. It has been said that the speaker was Musa, peace be upon him. It has also been read: "wa-ittabi'" (and follow).

Qarun (Qarūn) is a foreign (non-Arabic) name, like Harun (Hārūn), and it is not declined because of its foreignness and definiteness. Had it been a pattern of the form fā'ūl derived from qarn, it would have been declined. It has been said: the meaning of "from his people" is that he believed in him. It has also been said that he was an Israelite, a cousin of Musa:

He is Qarun ibn Yasihar ibn Qahith ibn Lawi ibn Ya'qub, and Musa ibn 'Imran ibn Qahith. It has been said that Musa was his paternal uncle's son, and he was called al-Munawwar (the Illuminated) for the beauty of his appearance. He was the most proficient of the Children of Israel in the Torah, but he was hypocritical, just as the Samiri was hypocritical, and he said: "If prophethood belongs to Musa, peace be upon him, and the altar and the sacrifice to Harun, then what about me?" It is narrated that when Musa led them across the sea, and the prophetic mission and the priesthood (al-hibarah) passed to Harun, who would offer the sacrifice and become the head among them, while the sacrifice had been (assigned) to Musa, and Musa handed it over to his brother, Qarun felt resentment and envied the two of them. He said to Musa: "The matter belongs to you two, and I am of no account. Until when shall I endure?" Musa said: "This is the doing of God." He said: "By God, I will not believe until you bring a sign." So he commanded the leaders of the Children of Israel that each one should bring his staff. He bundled them and placed them in the tent where revelation used to descend upon him. They used to guard their staffs at night. In the morning, behold, Harun's staff was trembling and had green leaves, and it was of almond wood. Qarun said: "This is no more wondrous than what you do by magic." So he "transgressed against them" (fa-baghā 'alayhim), from al-baghy, which means injustice. It has been said: Pharaoh had appointed him over the Children of Israel, and he oppressed them. It has also been said: from al-baghy, which means arrogance and haughtiness: he displayed pride over them through the abundance of his wealth and children. It has been said: he made his garments a span longer than theirs.

Al-Mafatih (the keys) is the plural of miftah (with a kasra), which is that by which something is opened. It has been said that they are the treasuries; the analogical singular of it would be mafhat (with a fatha). It is said: "al-hamlu nā'a bihi" when the load weighed him down until it made him lean. Al-'Usbah means a large group, and al-'usabah is similar to it. Ista'sabu means they gathered together. It has been said: sixty mules used to carry the keys of his treasuries, one key for each treasury, and no key exceeded a finger in size, and they were made of leather. Abu Razin said: one key would suffice for Kufa. The matter is greatly exaggerated in the mention of this, with the wording: the treasures, the keys, the weighing down, the group, and the people of strength.

Badil ibn Maysara recited "la-yanū'u" with a ya'. Its justification is that al-mafatih is explained as the treasuries, and it is given the judgment of what it is attached to, because of their connection and association, as in your saying "dhahabat Ahl al-Yamamah" (the people of Yamama went away). The place of "idh" is in the accusative, governed by "tanū'" and by "lā tafraḥ", as in His saying: "and do not rejoice in what He has given you" (57:23), and in the words of the poet:

Nor am I one who exults when fortune delights me, nor one who grieves at its changing turns.
Nor do I seek evil; but when evil leaves me, I mount it when I am provoked to it.

These are by Hudba ibn Khashram, when Mu'awiya led him to al-Harra to take retribution from him for Ziyad ibn Zayd al-'Udhri. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Hassan met him and asked him to recite, and he recited these verses. Al-mifrah means one who rejoices greatly. The intent is the negation of rejoicing at its root. Sarf al-dahr means its vicissitudes. "Idha" is conditional, so after it there must be a verb, meaning: "if evil has left me." "Uhmal" is in the passive voice and "arkab" in the active. The meaning is: I have tested fortune, and when it is treacherous, yet I still do not abase myself.

That is because one does not rejoice in this world except one who is content with it and at rest in it. As for one whose heart is set on the Hereafter and who knows that he will soon depart from what he possesses, his soul does not prompt him to rejoice. How excellent is what the poet said:

The greatest grief in my eyes, within joy, is that its possessor is certain of departing from it.

(This is by Abu al-Tayyib: the greatest grief in my eyes is at the time of joy, whose possessor is certain to leave it, and so is all the joy of this world.)

"Wabtaghi fīmā ātākal-Lāhu al-dār al-ākhirah" (And seek, in what God has given you, the abode of the Hereafter): by doing in it deeds of goodness of the kinds of obligatory and recommended acts, and making it your provision for the Hereafter. "Wa lā tansa naṣībaka" (And do not forget your portion): this is to take from it what suffices you and sets you right. "Wa aḥsin kamā aḥsana Allāhu ilayk" (And be good as God has been good to you), or: be good by thanking and obeying God as He has been good to you. Corruption in the earth is what he was upon of injustice and transgression. It has been said that the speaker was Musa, peace be upon him. It has also been read: "wa-ittabi'" (and follow).

"On knowledge" means: on the basis of entitlement and merit, because of the knowledge in me by which I was preferred over people. That is because he was the most knowledgeable of the Children of Israel regarding the Torah.

It was said: it is the knowledge of alchemy (al-kimiya'). From Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib: Musa (peace be upon him) used to teach the knowledge of alchemy, and he bestowed a third of it upon Yusha' ibn Nun, a third upon Kalib ibn Yufuna, and a third upon Qarun. Qarun deceived them until he added their knowledge to his own, and he would take lead and copper and turn them into gold.

It was also said: God taught Musa the knowledge of alchemy, Musa taught it to his sister, and his sister taught it to Qarun. It was also said: it is his insight into the various kinds of trade, agriculture (al-dahqana), and all other means of earning. Some have said that "indi" (ʿindī) means "in my estimation," as one says "the matter is thus according to me" (ʿindī), as if he said: "I was only given it on knowledge," like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then when We bestow upon him a favour from Us, he says, "I was only given it on knowledge."﴾ Then he added "ʿindī," meaning: it is in my estimation and my opinion, thus.

It is permissible that this be an affirmation of his knowledge that God had destroyed before him generations that were stronger than him and richer, because he had read that in the Torah, Musa had informed him of it, and he had heard it from the memorizers of histories and days. As if it was said: "Did he not know, among what he possessed of knowledge, this?" so that he would not be deceived by the abundance of his wealth and his strength.

It is also permissible that it be a negation of his knowledge of that, because when he said, "I was given it on knowledge that is with me," he became puffed up with knowledge and exalted himself by it. It was said: "Did he have the like of that knowledge which he claimed, and by which he saw himself deserving of every blessing, and did he not know this beneficial knowledge by which he could protect himself from the fates of the destroyed?" ﴿And more abundant in wealth⦆ — that is, in gathering wealth, or more numerous in group and number. If you say: what is the connection of His saying, ﴿And the guilty will not be asked about their sins﴾ with what precedes it? I say: when he mentioned Qarun, and those generations before him who had been destroyed, who were stronger and richer than him, He said, by way of threat to him: God is aware of the sins of the guilty; He has no need to ask them about them or to inquire of them. And He is able to punish them for them, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And God is Acquainted with what you do﴾, and ﴿And God is Knowing of what you do﴾, and what is similar to that.

fī zīnatihi (in his adornment). Al-Ḥasan said: "In red and yellow." It was also said: he went forth on a white mule upon which was an arghuwān [Note from the commentator: In al-Ṣiḥāḥ, the arghuwān is a red velvet cloth (qaṭīfa ḥamrā' arghuwān). Also in it: al-arghuwān is a very red dye; it is said to be Persian arghawān, and it is a tree with a red blossom, the finest of its kind. (ʿ)], and upon it a saddle of gold, and with him four thousand upon his dress. It was also said: upon them and upon their horses was red brocade (dībāj), and on his right were three hundred boys, and on his left three hundred girls, white, upon whom were ornaments and brocade. It was also said: [he went forth] with ninety thousand, upon them the mu'aṣfarāt (saffron-dyed garments), and that was the first day the saffron-dyed garment was seen. Those who wished for it were Muslims, and they only wished for it out of desire for wealth and self-sufficiency, as is the habit of humankind. It is reported from Qatādah: they wished for it so that they might draw near to God by it and spend it in the paths of good. It was also said: they were a people who were unbelievers.

Al-ghābiṭ (the one who envies in the sense of admiring) is the one who wishes for the like of his companion's blessing without its being removed from him. Al-ḥāsid (the envier) is the one who wishes that his companion's blessing be his own instead of the other's. From the ghibṭa is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Would that we had the like of what Qārūn was given﴾, and from ḥasad is His saying: ﴿And do not wish for that by which God has favoured some of you over others﴾. It was said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Does envy (ghabṭ) harm?" He said: [Note from the commentator: Thābit al-Sirqusṭī mentioned it in al-Gharīb in this form without an isnād. Ibrāhīm al-Ḥarbī recorded it in al-Gharīb through the route of Ibn Abī Ḥusayn: "A questioner asked the Prophet (ﷺ): Does envy harm people? He said: Yes, as the ʿiḍāh (thorny trees) is harmed by al-khabṭ (beating the tree with a stick to shake off its leaves)." al-Ṭabarānī recorded it with this wording from the narration of Umm al-Dardāʾ, who said: I said, "O Messenger of God," and he mentioned it, but he said "the tree" (al-shajar) instead of "the ʿiḍāh."

Al-Ḥarbī said: al-ghabṭ means the desire for abundance. Thābit said: al-ghabṭ is envy.]]: "No, except as the ʿiḍāh is harmed by the khabṭ." Al-ḥaẓẓ (fortune) is luck, which is fortune and prosperity; they described him as a man of good fortune, favoured by luck. It is said: so-and-so is dhū ḥaẓẓ, ḥaẓīẓ, and maḥẓūẓ, and the world is nothing but aḥāẓ and judūd.

Woe to you! Originally it is an invocation of destruction, then it came to be used for rebuke, deterrence and urging to abandon what is not approved, as in "lā abāka" (may you have no father). Its origin is an invocation against a man with ruin (al-iqrāf), that is, with the corruption of his father (ʿAlī's note: "the invocation against a man with al-iqrāf," meaning with the corruption of the father, as stated in al-Ṣiḥāḥ), used in urging to an action. The pronoun in "wa-lā yulaqqāhā" refers either to the word that the scholars spoke, or to the reward, since it carries the sense of a recompense or Paradise, or to the way and manner, which is faith and righteous deeds. [It is the ones who are] patient in obedience, patient in refraining from desires, and patient with what God has apportioned of little rather than much.

Qārūn used to harm the Prophet of God Mūsā, peace be upon him, at all times, and he tolerated him because of the kinship between them, until the zakāt was revealed. He then reconciled with him on the basis of one dīnār out of every thousand dīnārs and one dirham out of every thousand dirhams. He calculated it, found it to be a large amount, and his soul grudged it. So he gathered the Children of Israel and said: "Mūsā has ordered you to do everything, and he wants to take your wealth." They said: "You are our elder and our master, so command us as you wish." He said: "Hire the adulteress woman so that she accuses Mūsā of himself, and the Children of Israel will then abandon him." So he gave her a thousand dīnārs. It was said: a basin of gold. It was said: a basin of gold filled with gold. It was said: [he made her] swear [to it].

Then, when it was the day of a festival, Mūsā stood and said: "O Children of Israel, whoever steals, we shall cut off his hand; whoever slanders, we shall flog him; whoever commits fornication while unmarried, we shall flog him, and if he is married, we shall stone him." Qārūn said: "Even if you are the one?" He said: "Even if I am the one." He said: "The Children of Israel claim that you committed fornication with so-and-so." She was summoned, and Mūsā adjured her by Him who split the sea and sent down the Torah to tell the truth. God then took hold of her, and she said: "They lied. Rather, Qārūn gave me a reward on condition that I accuse you for his own sake." Mūsā fell prostrate, weeping, and said: "O Lord, if I am Your messenger, then be angry for my sake." So it was revealed to him:

"Command the earth to do whatever you wish, for it is obedient to you." He said: "O Children of Israel, God has sent me to Qārūn just as He sent me to Pharaoh. Whoever is with him, let him remain in his place, and whoever is with me, let him withdraw." They all withdrew except for two men. Then he said: "O earth, seize them!" It seized them up to their knees. Then he said: "Seize them!" It seized them up to their waists. Then he said: "Seize them!" It seized them up to their necks, while Qārūn and his companions were pleading with Mūsā, peace be upon him, and adjuring him by God and by kinship, but Mūsā did not turn to them because of the severity of his anger. Then he said: "Seize them!" and it closed over them. [Footnote: Reported by ʿAbd al-Razzāq and al-Ṭabarānī, through ʿAlī ibn Zayd from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Nawfal al-Hāshimī, who said, and mentioned it as a mawqūf report. al-Ḥākim linked it to Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "When Mūsā came to his people, he commanded them to pay zakāt, and Qārūn gathered them," and mentioned it in abridged form. As for his statement "and the reports and traditions indicate it," meaning the terror that falls on the hearts of all people on the Day of Standing, this may be supported by the lengthy hadith of intercession. In the agreed-upon hadith from Abū Hurayrah, in the hadith of intercession, he said: "God will gather the first and the last in one plain; the beholder will see them, the caller will make them hear, and the sun will draw near to them, so that people will suffer such distress and anguish that they cannot bear or endure it." In it is the saying of Ādam and others: "Myself, myself." Both agreed on it from the hadith of Anas similarly.]

God revealed to Mūsā: "How harsh you are! They called upon you for help many times, and you did not show them mercy. By My might, if they had called upon Me alone just once, they would have found Me near and responsive." The Children of Israel then began to whisper among themselves: "Mūsā only prayed against Qārūn so that he could take sole possession of his home and treasures." So he prayed to God until his house and wealth were swallowed up.

*"Among those who were helped"*: among those who avenged themselves on Mūsā, peace be upon him, or among those who protected themselves from the punishment of God. It is said: "He helped him against his enemy, so he was helped," meaning: he protected him from it, so he was protected.
